author_headline: Senior Analyst, ISV Partner Marketing at Salesforce
summary: James Kenna, a Salesforce Senior Analyst, shares six conference lessons (having a POV, approaching people, connection strategy) and plugs his session on Diabsolut cutting admin tasks 70% with Staffing Agents.
post_text:
Most people waste their first 2 days at any conference. 
I certainly did my first Dreamforce! But after a dozen or two conferences/events as a Partner, here's 6 lessons I wish I learned before my first.

(1) Practice your perspective (don’t wing it). 
Don’t just HAVE a perspective, hone it. Day 1 chaos hits everyone. There will be 100 things you didn't know walking in. That's fine! It's not your job to know all of them. It's your job to already have a clear POV on how you fit in, so you're not scrambling to form one on the floor.

(2) Approach people. Don't wait for the "right moment."
The person you most want to talk to is probably there, right now. I've wasted tons of time hovering near people building up the confidence to talk to someone I don't know. (This is also why you practice your POV. Gives you a reason to be relevant.)

(3) The Booth is just one place to meet.
I used to think getting to the booth 30 minutes early made me the MVP. In reality, I should’ve spent that time having breakfast with a warm connect or an old friend. It's so hard to get everyone in the same place. Use it!

(4) Have a connection strategy before day 1.
I don't carry business cards (Gen-Z of me, I know). But I don’t think they perform well at conferences anyway. What works for me: a photo of the badge, LinkedIn request in the moment, calendar block for follow-ups the week after. Either way, have a plan or you'll lose half your new contacts to memory.

(5) Get content as you go!
Don’t just snap photos on day 3 when you remember your Marketing Manager asked you in the Know Before You Go call. Take photos often. Record a customer interview. Try something silly/bold. Even if you're not in marketing, your marketers will thank you!!

(6) Choose your wardrobe for the whole day.
Every conference, I have grand plans to change before evening events. It almost never happens.

(Bonus)
If you’re a Salesforce Partner, stop by the partner lounge! 

Shameless Plug: I'm speaking during this session: “How Diabsolut Cut Admin Tasks by 70% with Staffing Agents.” Would love to see you there! 

And If you'll be at Dreamforce next week, drop me a message. I'll see you there! (in the meantime, Quino will try to keep convincing me not to go).

I'm going this year because I think it's going to be the most interesting one yet. Three things I'm curious about:

Claudeforce. The Claude partnership is exciting, but I think the real story is Salesforce making the whole ecosystem available to agents, not just their own. That's a much bigger deal than any one partnership.

Headless 360. The idea has made a ton of sense since the announcement earlier this year. I'm curious how MCP access actually gets carved up. Does everybody go through Data 360 behind one endpoint? Is it a bunch of MCPs that Claude or Agentforce or whoever has to orchestrate? A bit of both?

Agentic data capture. This is the one I'm most interested in. Salesforce has always been a data capture company, but data capture is moving from humans to agents, and agents generate 1000x more data. The morning after I posted that, at 4am, I emailed Marc Benioff again.
 
Some of you know the backstory. In July I shared his reply to a cold email of mine: "Why don't you join our team at Salesforce and work on it here? Aloha." I thought long and hard about it. I chose to keep building instead, and moved to San Francisco.
 
I hadn't written to him since. There was nothing to say until there was.

Dreamforce is next week. It's in my city now. And I had just graduated, which is a lovely thing to be able to say and a very specific thing to be, financially. A ticket was more than I could justify.

So I wrote him six sentences. What I'd decided since we last spoke. Where I'd landed. That as a fresh graduate the ticket was out of reach, and was there any way in.
 
Just the truth, sent at 4am to someone who once took the time to reply.
 
By 5:30pm he'd forwarded it to his team with one line: "Can you get Agrim a Dreamforce pass? Aloha."
By 7:40pm I had a Dreamforce Pass.

Most people never send that email. They decide the answer is no before anyone gets to say it.

I keep thinking about what I wrote about the scholarship. That it was a bet a kid in Ajmer had no way of earning in advance, and that you don't repay it, you just try to build something that justifies it.
 
This was a much smaller bet. But it was the same shape. Someone with every reason to say nothing chose to say yes to a kid who asked.
 
So I'll be at Dreamforce next week for the first time. No booth, no company sending me, nobody I'm supposed to meet. Just three days of learning and exploring.
 
If you're going to be there, whether you're building, investing, or just like meeting ambitious people, I'd love to grab a coffee. Send me a DM.
 
#Dreamforce #Dreamforce2026

Marc Benioff on stage this week talking about the agentic enterprise.

Every session, every booth, every hallway conversation at Dreamforce this year runs through the same word and that is “Agents.”

An AI agent can draft your deck in 30 seconds.

Polished deck, generated fast, every slide grammatically clean. 
Structure made no sense. 
Proof came after the ask. 

Nobody caught it because it read clean, and clean gets mistaken for CORRECT.

That's the actual risk with AI built decks. 

Not that they're bad, that they're finished looking enough that nobody stops to check if they're actually working.

If your team's walking into Dreamforce with a deck AI helped build this year, worth having a human actually stress test it before it goes out.

author_headline: Turn in-person conversations into closed-won, 4x faster | Head of Sales @ Blinq
summary: Zach Weinberg of Blinq critiques booth openers like 'Do you have a couple minutes?' ahead of Dreamforce and UNBOUND 2026, advising specific-observation questions instead.
post_text:
Here’s the worst opener I hear at booths.

Dreamforce + UNBOUND 2026 are days away, so I’m doing a quick series of in-person sales advice to help you leave the floor with more pipeline. This is post 1.

After almost 20 years in sales, the #1 line I still hear reps use that kills the conversation is:

“Do you have a couple minutes to talk?”
“What brings you to the show?”

I call these ‘exit ramps’. Both are well-intentioned but both also hand the prospect an easy way out: "I'm busy" or "just looking".

The better play is to lead with a specific observation → ask a narrow question.

"I noticed [company news on a call / body language IRL]. Are you dealing with [related pain]?"

Why does this work infinitely better?

1. It signals you were paying attention, which alone puts you ahead of most people in the room.

2. It gives them something concrete to react to - even if you're wrong, the correction is a qualifying answer.

3. It tells you within 30 seconds whether this is a 90-second wrap-up or a 15-minute conversation worth having.

Send this to any sales reps you know coming to Dreamforce next Tuesday.

summary: Byron B., using an Apple/iPhone loyalty anecdote to explain ICP targeting for FullEnrich, mentions he'll attend Dreamforce hunting for iPhone giveaway booths.
post_text:
Apple hates me.......


Apple just introduced its latest iPhone lineup.
On paper, I probably look like part of its ideal customer profile:
• Longtime Apple customer
• Early iPhone adopter
• Previously owned a BlackBerry
• Loyal to the Apple ecosystem

But Apple would go broke if every customer behaved like me.
I’ve owned exactly four iPhones:
- The original iPhone.
- The iPhone 4.
- The iPhone 6.
- The iPhone XR.
And I’m still using the XR, 9 years after it was released (3 battery replacements, 4 cases, countless ear buds, etc.
If Apple designed its sales strategy around customers like me, it would only need to release a new phone every four or five years.

That’s why knowing your ICP matters. Your ICP isn’t simply a company or person who looks like a good customer. It’s the kind of customer with the right need, buying behavior, timing and likelihood to generate value.
Firmographics and job titles can help identify the market. But they don’t tell the entire story.
At FullEnrich, we help companies find and reach the right people inside their target accounts. But the process has to begin with a clear understanding of who “right” actually is.
Good data helps you reach your ICP.
Knowing your ICP keeps you from spending time and money reaching people like me.
Apple fan? Yes.
Ideal customer? Definitely not.

author_headline: Turn in-person conversations into closed-won, 4x faster | Head of Sales @ Blinq
summary: Zach Weinberg shares country-specific sales opener tips for Dreamforce and UNBOUND 2026, contrasting pitch styles in the US, UK, Australia, and Canada.
post_text:
How to adapt your opening pitch for different countries...

(so you don’t get shut down in the first 10 seconds).

This is Day 2 posting IRL sales tips to get your team ready for Dreamforce and UNBOUND 2026.

Both floors pull a global crowd, so this one is about adapting your opener to each country.

I’ve worked across 4 markets: US, UK, Australia, Canada. Your opener cannot be a one-size-fits-all, especially when it can make or break the rest of the pitch.

Here’s what works in each country:

US 🇺🇸: get to the point fast. If you lead with warmth but no point, it can feel like filler and you’ll get waved off. Open with something real and specific: their role, their company, what you noticed at their booth.

UK 🇬🇧: “How are you?” mostly just means “hello.” Say it, let them say it back, and keep it moving. If dry humor comes naturally to you, it can work well here (but don’t force it - they can smell the try-hard a mile away).

Australia 🇦🇺: stay casual. Overly polished charm feels rehearsed. Talk like you would at a barbecue, not like you’re at a conference, and they’ll make it clear pretty quickly whether they’re in.

Canada 🇨🇦: you usually get a little more runway before the pivot. People tend to be polite and give you time, but don’t confuse that with permission to ramble. Be genuinely friendly, then transition cleanly.

The best sellers I know are social chameleons. 

I learned most of this the hard way, watching the same pitch land in one city and fall flat in another.

Every enterprise now has access to intelligence — models keep getting smarter, agents keep multiplying, and AI is showing up everywhere you look. But intelligence alone was never the hard part. Most AI harnesses out there wrap around a single agent. That's not enough. An enterprise needs a trusted harness around all of its AI.

This week we introduced the Salesforce Trusted Enterprise AI Harness.

It's built on six capabilities, working as one system:

🧠Trusted Context — customer data, metadata, semantics, knowledge, real-time signals, and memory
🤖Trusted Agency — reasoning, planning, memory, and orchestration, balanced with deterministic controls
⚡Trusted Action — secure connections to apps, APIs, workflows, and business processes
📋Trusted Governance — lineage, quality, guardrails, and controls over data, metadata, and policies

author_headline: Product Management Director @ Salesforce | 10X Salesforce Certified
summary: Isabel Kuznicki, Salesforce Product Management Director, announces Agentforce Voice in the Events app, detailing speed optimizations and voice-personality lessons learned building it.
post_text:
We just launched Agentforce Voice in the Salesforce Events app — so attendees can talk to Agentforce to get answers, build their agenda, and find sessions without touching their phone!

The launch was fun, but honestly the best part was what we learned building it:

Speed isn’t just one thing, it’s everything adding up. Every step costs time — connecting, figuring out what you’re asking, thinking of an answer, actually doing it. We shaved time off each piece: direct connection paths, moving topic classification to a hyper classifier, caching answers to common questions, and adding dynamic progress cues.

A voice needs a personality, and you have to actually design it. We learned quickly that talking is NOT the same as texting! We had to figure out things like: does the agent use contractions? Does it match how excited or calm the person sounds? How does it greet someone? And one test we kept coming back to — would a person actually say? If not, rewrite it.

You don’t get this right on paper, you get it right by listening. We’d write instructions, test, wince/laugh, and try again. Tone, pacing, word choice — all of it got better through repetition, and teamwork.

This launch was also a true team effort. Huge thanks to our mobile app, digital marketing, and Agentforce teams for building this together as one team — and to our strategic event partners for enabling this customer zero moment: using our own product, for our own event, in front of our own customers. Grateful to work somewhere teamwork like this is the norm, and for the opportunity to be part of it.  🚀 Gautam Vasudev Joyce Leung Andrew Mangano Sam Bloomberg-Rissman Rosalind Litchfield Will Matteson Max Comparetto

author_headline: Advisor // Investor // eCom OG
summary: Advisor Thomas Obrey, skipping Dreamforce himself, urges attendees to prioritize networking over sessions, dinners and cliques, and to rebook cheaper hotels via Hotels.com.
post_text:
If you're going to Dreamforce, which I am not, by design, I've got a few tips for you. Like real life "listen up" sort of guidance. Despite your job, your boss' goals, and the corporate "requirements" thrust upon you.

This is a networking event. Period. 

That's it - your one goal here - is networking. IDGAF what your boss, friends, or peers think you should be doing. If deep and long-into-the-night networking isn't the main goal. You've failed. 

Be careful what you hear. And believe. 

It's mostly made up, and changes before GA. This is the truth no one tells you. So don't get all gooshy at this booth, or that presentation. It's called Dreamforce for a reason - they're dreaming - and they force it upon you. That's actually ok, if you know it going in.

Get outside your group. Be they coworkers. Friends. Whatev.

Do not spend all day and night with the same 5-10 ppl. Swapping a few out from time to time becuase they're your (a) client or (b) vendor/partner. Skip those dinners if you can too. They make you fat, tired and you'll generally not meet anyone new or worthy to your future. 

Hotels. If you got a shit one. Go on Hotels-dot-com and grab a cheapy on day 2. 

The ol' these are one to two grand a night rooms - can be had for a couple hundy. Once the show starts. And it's worth it if you're stuck at the airport or any spot that's not walking distance to it all. I used to grab a couple buddies - and we'd literally do bed, couch and a rollaway - 3-ways. 

Becuase stumbling is a thing. But. You only room together. Don't hang out. 

Boom. You're welcome.

Back to networking... Again. 

Go hard here. Go into rooms you don't belong. 
Introduce yourself to strangers.
Talk to that cat manning a booth or three, not to learn, but to connect.

Do not spend all your time running to/fr meetings, sessions, and dinners. 
If you can figure it out - cut your schedule in half - give yourself large blocks to just roam and bump into people and things. Seriously. I learned this the hard way.

Networking. Is your main job. This week. 
Connections last decades. Presentations and meals last minutes.

You can never have too many friends. That's something.

Peace. -t

summary: Conscendo's Pavan Murthy, attending his 10th Dreamforce, lists nine tips including badge pickup Monday, hydration, comfortable shoes and protecting unscheduled time.
post_text:
My first #Dreamforce - 2013, 13 years, 9 DFs and 60 pounds later, this will be my 10th DF here are a few things I’ve learned about getting the most out of DF:

1) Collect your badge on Monday. Period. Future you will thank you.
2) Hydrate. Less alcohol. Less caffeine. Dreamforce itself gives you enough dopamine. I normally survive on 5–6 espressos a day. During DF, I bring it down to 3.
3) Have a plan, but don’t over-plan. Block your important meetings, conversations and sessions, but leave gaps. Some of the most valuable 20 minutes of DF will never appear on your calendar.
4) Accept the FOMO. There will always be a better dinner, another happy hour, an interesting session and someone texting “where are you?” You cannot do everything. Pick your priorities and enjoy where you are.
5) Texting is your best friend. Carry a power bank. You will seldom meet people where you originally decided. Most likely you’ll be running to a different place at 2:06 for a 2:00 PM meeting that ends at 2:15.
6) Talk to your peers. Especially other sales and revenue leaders. Ask what’s actually working. What are customers buying? What’s moving fast? What’s getting stuck? Which conversations are getting executive attention? You can learn more from 20 minutes of comparing notes than from another hour of slides.
7) Protect some white space. Dreamforce is one giant collision of people. Walking from one meeting to another and randomly running into someone can turn into the best conversation of the week.
8) Wear comfortable shoes. You can be a CRO, CEO or whatever O you want. By  Wednesday afternoon, everyone is just a person looking for somewhere to sit down.
9) Rest. Seriously. That 6 AM executive breakfast seemed like a brilliant idea when you accepted it three weeks ago. It feels very different after Tuesday night.

And one thing I appreciate more every year: relationships compound.

Products change. Clouds change. Titles change. Companies change. But the people you meet, help, learn from and stay connected with are what make coming back to Dreamforce worth it.

13 years later, I still get excited about this week.

See you in San Francisco. #Dreamforce #DF26 Dreamforce Salesforce

Sponsoring Dreamforce looks easy from the outside.
Put up the booth. Show the demos. Meet people.

Behind that? 2–3 months of hard work from the entire team.

2nd year sponsoring. Booth #520. And honestly, the booth is the easy part. The real work starts much earlier.

1. Every feature has to be understood, tested, and turned into a pitch that makes sense to a real customer.

2. Every demo needs to be ready. Because when someone walks up to your booth, you don't want to be figuring things out on the spot.

3. The entire team gets involved. Sales, marketing, product, technical everyone has a role to play.

4. And then there are all the small things. The conversations, the reviews, the changes, the let's try this one more time. All of it, so that whoever stops by gets our full attention, not a rehearsed script.

People will see three days at Dreamforce.

This time, they'll also see the actual work we put in for the customers and visitors who walk up to us.

Because that's who all of this was for, from day one. The people who take five minutes out of their day to talk to us.

See you at Booth #520. ❤️

It was an abrupt return from maternity leave. Salesforce was truly generous. 6 months paid leave, baby gifts sent, leadership that respected her space and periodically checked in, and a transition plan during her departure and return. 

Even with the thoughtfulness and leadership shown by Salesforce, her return wasn’t without a divided heart. 

This is why I’m suddenly so passionate about working mothers, especially in the mortgage industry. I’m in the front row observing my wife. I see a wildly talented, successful woman with a career she’s built with a lot of time and sweat, feeling the weight of not wanting to miss a moment with Everly.

I don’t care how career driven and talented a mother is. A child changes everything. 

And thank you Salesforce, for not only investing in a great employee, but in our family. ❤️

summary: DE-CIX's Christian Reuter returns to Dreamforce after a year off, questioning how far Agentforce has moved from demos to real value for Network-as-a-Service.
post_text:
Today, I’m heading back to Dreamforce after "taking a year off".

A lot has changed since my last visit...not only in the Salesforce ecosystem, but also in how we use the platform at DE-CIX.

Over the past two years, we have significantly expanded our Salesforce platform and made major progress towards a true Customer 360 view. And this has become an important part of a much bigger transformation: evolving our business towards Network-as-a-Service and putting the customer, rather than individual products, at the center of how we design, sell and deliver interconnection services.
      
We started moving beyond process digitization towards creating measurable customer value across the entire lifecycle, connecting customer insight, sales, service and increasingly the digital experience into one journey. 

Two years ago, Agentforce set a new benchmark for what AI could mean inside the Salesforce ecosystem. I’m genuinely curious to see how far that thinking has evolved and, more importantly, how much of it has moved from impressive demos into real operational value.

For me, that’s also one of the big questions for this Dreamforce: How can AI, data and automation help turn the promise of NaaS into a genuinely simpler and more valuable customer experience?   

The keynotes will certainly bring new ideas and use cases. But for me, the real value of Dreamforce has always been elsewhere: in the hands-on sessions, the conversations with peers, and the chance to learn from people who are actually using the technology in their day-to-day business.
  
And, of course, I’m looking forward to reconnecting with many familiar faces.

So if you're around and want to chat over a coffee or beer: Reach out!
  
See you in San Francisco.

→ The "Agentic Enterprise" pitch is everywhere, but adoption numbers and ROI data are still thin. We've seen this pattern before — big vision at the keynote, then a slower, messier rollout in the field. That gap is usually where we end up doing the real work.
We didn't make it to San Francisco this year, but we're always happy to talk through what any of this means for your org — especially if you're a smaller team trying to figure out what's hype and what's actually usable.

Salesforce, ahead of its annual Dreamforce customer conference next week, is removing the word “Agentforce” from the names of some of its top products, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter.
The reversal comes after Salesforce made Agentforce a centerpiece of its product sales and marketing strategy since launching it in late 2024, with CEO Marc Benioff previously suggesting that Salesforce might rebrand its official name as Agentforce.

It isn’t clear what prompted Salesforce to make the branding changes, and spokespeople didn’t respond to requests for comment. After a sluggish start, Agentforce’s annual revenue—the value of contracts over the next 12 months—grew more than 240% to more than $1.5 billion in Salesforce’s July quarter compared to last year.
Salesforce is preserving the Agentforce name for the Agentforce 360 product itself, the people said.
Salesforce is also changing the name of Headless 360 Platform, a set of tools that customers use to build and customize applications and agents, reverting to its earlier name, Salesforce Platform, said the people.
Headless 360 refers to a set of tools Salesforce unveiled in April that make it easier for customers to use external AI agents from Anthropic and other providers to access their data within Salesforce applications.

author_headline: Turn in-person conversations into closed-won, 4x faster | Head of Sales @ Blinq
summary: Blinq sales head Zach Weinberg lists six body-language cues—passive agreement, feet turning away, neutral expressions, weight shifts, grabbing flyers, scanning the room—signaling a prospect has disengaged.
post_text:
Here are my top 6 signals that someone’s checked out of your in-person pitch.

We’re on Day 3/5 of IRL selling tips to help your sales reps refresh ahead of Dreamforce + UNBOUND 2026.

If you learn to read the smallest shifts in body language and facial expression, you can adjust your strategy so:

- At best you walk away with a great lead, and
- At worst you waste minimal time on a non-prospect.

Here are the 6 non-verbal signals I watch for:

1. They start agreeing with everything. 
Pushback and questions mean they’re critically engaging with what you’re saying.

2. Their agreement turns passive *and* their feet turn away. 
Their upper body might still face you, but if their toes are pointed toward the exit, they’re already halfway gone.

3. Their face goes neutral. 
Genuine interest creates micro-expressions that are hard to fake: eyes widen briefly, nods vary in pace and depth, and smiles reach the eyes.

4. They shift their weight to one hip. 
It’s the body loading the leg it’s about to step off from; the wider the stance, the closer you are to losing them.

5. They start looking at your booth materials instead of you. 
Picking up a flyer or scanning a banner can look like interest, but it often signals the opposite: it gives them an exit line (“I’ll take this with me”) and removes the pressure of eye contact.

6. They scan the room while you’re mid-sentence. 
They’re looking for the next person they want to talk to, or the clearest path back to the aisle.

If you catch these early, you can shift your approach and try to pull them back in. or let them go. 

Either way, a graceful exit is always worth more than a forced five-minute pitch.

What signals do you personally watch for when someone’s losing interest?

summary: Salesforce SVP Martin Kihn explains Dreamforce26 announcements of seven named agents (Casey, Paige, Carter, Hunter, Marshall, Piper, Fin) plus a six-layer Trusted Enterprise AI Harness.
post_text:
💥 💥 #Dreamforce26 starts and Salesforce announces a one-two of 7 human-named agents and a new Trusted Enterprise AI Harness 💥 💥 

These seem like different announcements one day apart but in fact they're part of the same story ...

And what - after all - is 'AIForce' ... ?

The two announcements were:

 🎁 🎁 (1) --> 7 packaged Agents with humanish names and specific jobs (customers can change the names BTW)

🎁 🎁 (2) --> Trusted Enterprise AI Harness

These are intertwined: for example Hunter (sales prospecting Agent) is described as "a sales-specific harness built into Agentforce Coworker"

So it's possible to see the 7 named Agents as domain-specific *sub-harnesses* built on top of the Trusted Enterprise AI Harness

Let's start with these new agents:

 👽 👽 CASEY is your help/customer service Agent - resolves basic customer service questions like FAQs, returns, escalation

👽 👽 PAIGE is your IT & HR employee service Agent - she gets you a new computer or points you to your benefits docs etc. (we use this at SF already; it's pretty good)

👽 👽 CARTER is your friendly shopper Agent for commerce, guiding you through things like finding products, comparisons and even in-chat checkout

👽 👽 HUNTER is your outbound sales agent who scours CRM, history, content from ZoomInfo, Demandbase, etc. and comes up with a playbook and outreach (GA 11/26)

👽 👽 MARSHALL is interesting: he's your back-office supply chain agent that orchestrates and audits logistics type processes

👽 👽 PIPER is from the Qualified acquisition and is very popular already. she's an inbound pipe-gen agent for B2B sales and marketing

👽 👽 FIN is another major acquisition (also closed) with a lot of customers. He's built on his own fine-tuned models and resolves customer service issues

That's the family. The names are rather clever.

🎁 🎁 Okay, so what's the Trusted Enterprise AI Harness?

A 'harness' is just everything *other than* the actual AI model/LLM you're using. It's the guardrails, context, definitions, auditing, permissions etc; everything *around* the LLM that makes Agents possible

The technical news here is that Agents can now pursue goals over days and weeks using this  6-layer Enterprise Harness:

 👉 👉 Context - this is grounding Agents in enterprise info

👉 👉 Agency - memory, reasoning, planning, orchestration

👉 👉 Action - access to tools, apps, APIs

👉 👉 Governance - guardrails, policies

👉 👉 Models - selecting from different models

This is the Trusted Enterprise AI Harness, which is part of AIForce. All these things exist already except a Security module

The other other part of #AIForce is the 'AI Control Plane' which today goes to market as Mulesoft Agent Fabric and Agentforce Observability, so it also exists with only cost & finops tbd

Some of this may change later in the week; see you at #Dreamforce26 🎁

Heading to Dreamforce today, the first stop in a two-month stretch of speaking at events across the country. I’m looking forward to sharing what I’ve learned, but just as much to learning from people doing this work in different companies and situations.

I don’t think we have many durable AI best practices yet. We’re still writing them, and their shelf life can be pretty short. What I do have is pattern recognition from working across teams and different stages of AI adoption. I’ll be listening for the ideas that come up repeatedly, seeing how they work in different organizations, and learning where the context changes the answer.

In my corporate roles, I had the chance to go deep inside one company and help move that business forward. In this chapter, I get to learn across many organizations, connect what I’m seeing, and bring those lessons into the next conversation. The client workshops and team offsites in between are a big part of that. They show me how these ideas work when teams apply them to their own work, and how much the answer can depend on the people, the company, and the situation.

That’s one of the things I value most about this work. I get to help leaders take an idea, adapt it to their own business, and bring more voices into the decisions that follow.

I enjoy the virtual workshops, especially the hands-on sessions where everyone is building together. But there’s still no replacement for being together in person. summary: Alliances executive Ryan Perry argues 235 Dreamforce sponsors lack compensation models for agentic AI selling, noting Accenture, Deloitte Digital, PwC and TCS dominate top sponsor tiers.
post_text:
235 companies paid to sponsor Dreamforce.

Almost none of them can tell you how they get paid when an agent does the selling.

That's the gap nobody is talking about on the way to Moscone Center.

The partner economics we all built were designed for seats and referrals. 

A human clicks. A deal registers. A person gets paid. Clean. Legacy TSD Model.

Agentic AI breaks every part of that chain:
- The agent doesn't know whose logo it's wearing. It orchestrates across four vendors to finish one task. Who gets attribution?
- Consumption replaced the click. When your product is called by an agent instead of opened by a user, seat-based comp stops describing reality.
- The top of the sponsor list is all services. Accenture, Deloitte Digital, PwC, TCS. The GSIs sit at the Pioneer tier because services still capture the agentic margin. The software vendors are buying booths underneath them without a compensation model to stand on.

Sponsorship is now table stakes. It buys attention. Not attach.

The companies that win the next 18 months won't be the ones with the biggest booth. They'll be the ones who rewrote partner comp for a buyer that isn't a person.

I've built this function from zero multiple times at AT&T Wirless (Data), TiVo (Broadband Providers), and Zoom (Phone GTM, SkyTV, AMC). The hard part was never the signature. It was the new economics underneath it.

I'll be on the floor Tuesday, Day 1. I'm there for the ecosystem, not the keynote.

If you own partnerships, alliances, or channel at a sponsor company, comment or DM and I'll find you.

author_headline: Chief Data Officer @ Salesforce delivering enterprise intelligence to humans and AI agents with trusted context, signals, and infrastructure
summary: Salesforce Chief Data Officer Michael Andrew argues data teams must build governed "trusted context" for AI agents, predicting the CDO role evolving into a Chief Intelligence Officer.
post_text:
It's Dreamforce week! San Francisco is filling up with thousands of people looking for what's next in AI, and one of the biggest themes this year is Trusted Context: making sure AI agents act with the intelligence of your organization. Models on their own are brilliant. They're only brilliant for your organization when they're grounded in the truth of your business.

So who builds that trusted context? It's a team sport, but data teams have an outsized role to play. All context starts as data. It has to follow the same governance rules we've long applied to humans, now extended to agents. It has to be refined from raw material into its distilled essence, shaped for an agent to use. The skills data teams have spent years applying to align companies on the right metrics now have to be applied to align agents on the right context.

Over time, I expect the Chief Data Officer role to grow into a Chief Intelligence Officer role, accountable for grounding AI in the best truth of the business. At Salesforce, we've come to see that the value a data team provides IS the intelligence, and that intelligence is the product we deliver to the business. Every piece of intelligence, whether a metric, a fact, a memory, a model, a piece of knowledge, or an assembly of these, needs certification, lineage, quality indicators, and governance so the agent gets the distilled context it needs to do its job.

When we talk about ontology, semantics, graphs, and the rest of the buzzwords, what we're really talking about is context: how do you take the shared understanding that lives in the neural networks of the humans who run your business and codify it so the neural networks of AI can understand it?

post_text:
As I prepare for Dreamforce to begin tomorrow, I'm trying to resist the temptation to make my list of questions: “What recent updates do we need to know regarding AI?”

Now, don’t get me wrong, that’s an important question. And from what I’m seeing about the lineup, there will be ample opportunity to learn about the new and upcoming horizons of AI innovation from Salesforce  

However, I'm also trying to think through:

What do I need to learn so I can ask better questions both for and of the people who are closest to the work?

Executives don't always experience technology the same way the people living in the day-to-day weeds of implementation do (even when we're helping them decide what to invest in). I think that's an important responsibility to consider as I head to Dreamforce.

So, while I'm excited to see the new and the novel, I'm also itching to get closer to the practical questions…and make sure I bring those answers back.

What does this actually change for the person entering data every day? Will it truly save them time, or is there a new time debt somewhere else that I can't see right now?

What about the person who has built a workaround because the system doesn't quite work the way they need it to? Will this eliminate that workaround, or will it create a new one?

What does this mean for the person who has to actually implement, adopt, and live with the change?

The list goes on. But that's the mindset I'm aiming to take into Dreamforce this year: stay curious about what's coming next, but keep my eye on the real people and organizations who will have to make it work.

author_headline: Marketing Operations Manager
summary: Lindsay Brand recounts landing a marketing job via a chance 2023 Dreamforce meeting with David Spehar at Oasis Grill, and plugs the Benioff-Altman Salesforce+ conversation.
post_text:
Salesforce's Dreamforce starts tomorrow!

If you're unable to be in-person in San Francisco, you can tune in online for many of the keynotes and sessions online for free with Salesforce Plus!

Really excited to tune into this conversation between Marc Benioff and Sam Altman: https://lnkd.in/gK2UcTau

Dreamforce was the biggest investment I made in myself and has turned out to be the best ROI on my career.

It was one of those moments where I felt like God was going to make something happen in my career.

Real Story:
My husband was applying to medical school and I didn't have enough money coming in to cover our living expenses once we went down to a single income household.

I prayed that God would provide in some way shape or form. About 2 months before Dreamforce, I was let go for the first time in my career. Although, I already had one foot out the door because a raise was denied, it still was a slap in the face and made me feel completely undervalued as an employee.

However, in the midst of the hardship, I decided to make an investment in myself and head to Dreamforce for the very first time September of 2023. This was a pivotal moment in history as Open AI just came on the scene and Salesforce had just announced Agentforce.

The world was drastically changing before all of our eyes, and what an incredible experience to be a part of the largest AI event in the world at the time.

Fast forward to making it to Dreamforce and seeing streets of San Francisco shut down for this "camp"/"disney land" like event. I was extremely worn out from traveling and starving. The Oasis Grill was right across the street from the registration area, and without thinking I sprinted there.

It was there that I made my first "connection", s/o to David Spehar and we immediately bonded over being so hungry, it was both our first time at Salesforce, and he just so happened to be from the midwest as well. He asked me what I did and I said marketing, and he says "oh we are looking for someone to help with marketing." Gives me his card and asks me to connect if I'm interested.

6 months later, the same day we found out my husband was accepted into Michigan State's Medical School, I received an email from my Salesforce Chicken Shwarma bestie. Subject of his email: "Marketing Opportunity." I cried  tears of joy since I knew God was answering my prayer.

Fast forward to when we are out to dinner celebrating my husband's acceptance. I received the email with my job offer for dRofus.

The reason why I shifted into Marketing Ops by accident was because of Salesforce, so I always reflect and celebrate this time of year as it set a new path for the rest of my career ✨

This will be my seventh Dreamforce! Every year it's the same agenda builder, the same flight, the same views as I make my way into San Francisco, but this one feels different...

Over the last week there have been headlines warning AI could end humanity, right alongside demo videos of things that felt impossible a year ago. Holding both of these realities at once is a strange place to sit, especially when doing what you love puts you near the "front lines" of this technological revolution.

I won't pretend I have that tension resolved. But I deeply believe in what we're building at Asymbl.

Workforce Orchestration™ is the reason I came here in the first place. It wasn't about a clean pitch, it was the only framing I'd seen that actually answered the scary part honestly. AI doesn't replace people. It changes what people spend their time on, and that shift only works if someone designs how people and digital workers operate together instead of just bolting AI onto old workflows and hoping. 

It takes deliberate system design and real operational discipline to map exactly where human judgment ends and digital capability takes over. You have to rebuild workflows around a shared operating model rather than throwing new software at legacy processes.

Heading into Dreamforce seven excited to see what Salesforce has in store. If you're here this year, let's find time to connect!

post_text:
Days before Dreamforce, Salesforce is reportedly removing “Agentforce” from the names of some of its biggest products.

Marc Benioff may already be moving on from the Agentforce era. 
But not from AI.
From Agentforce as the strategy. 

At the same time, Salesforce is buying aggressively.

Look at the pieces:
• Informatica → the data foundation
• Contentful → the composable content layer
• m3ter → usage-based monetization
• Momentum.io → revenue orchestration
• Cimulate (Acquired by Salesforce) → agentic commerce
• Fin → AI customer agents

Individually, these look like acquisitions.
Together, they look like an architecture.

And that’s why I don’t think removing Agentforce branding signals Salesforce retreating from AI.

I think it could signal the opposite.

Benioff may be betting that AI becomes so fundamental to Salesforce that it no longer makes sense to package it as a separate layer slapped onto every product.

Sales Cloud doesn't need to become “Agentforce Sales.”
Sales Cloud itself needs to become agentic.
Same for Service.
Commerce.
Marketing.
The platform.

Meanwhile, Salesforce is acquiring many of the pieces required to make that transition faster.

Data.
Content.
Agents.
Commerce.
Consumption.

The Agentforce brand may be getting smaller.
But Salesforce's AI ambition looks considerably bigger.

And that might be the real story heading into Dreamforce.

Is Salesforce quietly moving beyond Agentforce, and rebuilding the entire company around the agentic enterprise?

author_headline: Turn in-person conversations into closed-won, 4x faster | Head of Sales @ Blinq
summary: Blinq's Zach Weinberg lists ten buyer-interest signals for booth reps, urging follow-up using Blinq's AI Notetaker to personalize post-Dreamforce outreach.
post_text:
If you’re working a booth today and a prospect says any of these 10 things, they’re interested.

Post 4 of 5 IRL selling tips to prep your reps for Dreamforce + UNBOUND 2026.

A few days ago I shared 6 body-language signals your in-person pitch is losing them.

Here’s the flip side: 10 signs they’re locked in.

1. They ask situation-specific questions.
“How would this work if we have two separate sales teams at the same event?” They’re already placing you into their world. 

2. They push back on one specific thing.
A targeted objection (pricing, a feature, an edge case) usually means they’ve accepted everything else. 

3. They bring up a competitor unprompted.
They’re actively evaluating and they trust you enough to be transparent about it. 

4. They reference someone else on their team.
“My VP would want to hear this” or “I need to loop in ops.” That’s a warm internal path - get names. 

5. They ask to record you.
Nobody records a conversation they don’t plan to replay or share. 

6. They lower their voice.
You’ve moved past surface-level chat and into the stuff they don’t want the whole floor to hear. 

7. They do math out loud.
“We do ~12 events a year, and our team is…” Let them muse, they’re validating ROI. 

8. They check the time but stay.
A watch-flick isn’t always a brush-off. If they keep talking, they’re choosing you over their next thing. 

9. They step to the side with you.
If they physically move out of traffic, they’re committing to the conversation. 

10. They ask about next steps first.
“Who do I talk to after this?” “Do you have a trial?” That’s your cue to guide the close.

Okay, so what now?

Ball’s in your court. Don’t miss the layup with a generic “great to meet you at the event.”

Open your follow-up with something specific they said (a pain point, a milestone, a teammate they mentioned) to lock in the next meeting.

Blinq'w AI Notetaker helps with this: it transcribes + summarizes the convo, then tags it to the lead so your follow-ups are hyper-personalized and go out while the interaction is still fresh.

Back at Dreamforce.


Having attended over the last couple of years, I've noticed that what I look for here has changed.


Earlier, I wanted to see as much as possible.


New products. New capabilities. Keynotes. Demos. What's coming next.


This year, I'm coming with a much narrower question:


What is actually moving from an interesting AI demo into everyday enterprise use?


Agentforce can do increasingly impressive things.


That's no longer the part I need convincing about.


I'm more interested in what happens after the demo.


Which use cases are customers putting into production?


Where are employees genuinely trusting agents to do work?


What looked promising but turned out not to be worth implementing?


And where are companies seeing enough business value to expand beyond the first use case?


Those are the conversations I'm looking forward to having this time.


Because after a few Dreamforces, I've realized I don't need to leave with more information.


There's already plenty of that.


I want to leave with a clearer view of what's actually working.

post_text:
I'm not watching the Salesforce Dreamforce Main Keynote to see whether an agent can write Apex or build a Flow. I'm watching what happens after it does.
 
An agent can generate code or metadata. What decides whether that is useful is the next step: how the work gets reviewed, versioned, tested and promoted to production.
 
Salesforce has already signaled where this is going. Slack Code puts the conversation, the agent's plan, the code diff and a live preview in one channel, with human approval before anything ships. Headless 360 exposes platform capabilities through APIs, MCP and CLI so agents can work against the org directly.
 
The Trusted Enterprise AI Harness wraps context, governance and security around all of it. Salesforce says many of the underlying pieces are available today, and that the new capabilities and the unified experience begin rolling out in early FY28.
 
I've spent about a year building multi-agent Claude tooling for our own delivery work. What the agent could generate stopped being the interesting constraint fairly early. Context, permissions, review and the path to production mattered more.
 
So the question I am going in with is whether the Agentic Enterprise changes the delivery model, or mostly changes the interface.

summary: Joseph Floyd explains Emergence, an early Salesforce investor, hasn't attended Dreamforce in five years, having shifted focus to AI Infrastructure, Physical AI, AI-Native Services and Agentic Software.
post_text:
Dreamforce used to be our Superbowl. We were the VC that invested in Salesforce back in 2002. We then backed alumni like Peter Gassner at Veeva Systems, and many other sales tech winners (Salesloft, SteelBrick, Logik.ai, from ServiceNow). And yet, for the past 5 years, no one from Emergence has gone to Dreamforce or surrounding events.

What happened? Over the years, Emergence naturally evolved beyond just SaaS investing. We never announced it, but we expanded our investment theses to cover four focus areas: AI Infrastructure, Physical AI, AI-Native Services and Agentic Software. 

In AI Infra, we bet early on open models (including Together AI, Arcee AI, and adaption), multi-silicon (Gimlet Labs, stealth semiconductor company) and multimodal (Genspark, Bland, angel in Elorian AI).

In Physical AI, we bet early on robotics (Physical Intelligence, Bedrock Robotics, Saronic Technologies), physical world (Radical Numerics, Causal Labs, Periodic Labs) and space (angel in Hubble Network).

We coined the term AI-Native Services (AINS) and invested in Hanover Park, Harper, and The OpenAI Deployment Company, among others. 

We still invest in agentic software. We just aren't forcing ourselves into one dream anymore. I guess you can say we are trailblazers.

A control plane: one place to register every agent, set its identity and policy, watch what it does, and track what it costs, including agents from other vendors. author_headline: Co-Founder & CEO, Clientell AI | Operationalising frontier intelligence inside enterprise operations
summary: Clientell AI's Neil Sarkar criticizes Salesforce's repeated AI rebranding (Einstein GPT to AIforce), claiming Agentforce has reached only about 17% of its 150,000+ customers.
post_text:
Salesforce has changed the name of its AI story so many times that I genuinely have to check what the current one is before writing about it.

Einstein GPT. AI Cloud. Einstein Copilot. Agentforce. Agentforce 360. Claudeforce. And now AIforce.

Some of these are evolutions, sure. But from the outside, it still feels like Salesforce keeps moving the label while customers are still figuring out what to actually do with the last thing.

That’s the part I find funny.

Salesforce keeps announcing Agentforce momentum. The awkward part is that after all the hype, it’s still only reached about 17% of Salesforce’s 150,000+ customer base. That’s a lot of “momentum” still waiting to become actual adoption. 

But the branding is moving even faster.

At this point, the hardest part of following Salesforce AI isn’t understanding the technology.

It’s remembering what they decided to call it this week.

Dreamforce is keeping the tradition alive: new AI branding every year, while most customers still haven’t found a reason to care about the last one.

author_headline: PMM for APEX benchmarks @ Mercor
summary: Brad Johnson of Mercor contrasts strong versus weak Dreamforce booth executions, arguing brand values and clear identity matter more than event-planning polish.
post_text:
It's Dreamforce in SF this week.

All the small restaurants, bars, and cafes have been overtaken by AI brands. There are clusters of people milling about wearing name badges.

I've been to a lot of technology trade shows in my career and planned many events. 

Some companies absolutely nail the execution. Salesforce is an obvious example, but you don't need a whole show to yourself. You see booths that pick a theme and go all the way, or promote an outside-the-box giveaway. Teams that are outfitted in matching swag. Bright lights and high-quality signage. 

Other times, companies underinvest or fumble the execution. They spend lots of money just to blend in with the crowd. For every booth that makes you go "WOW!" there are a hundred more that you amble by without even noticing.

The biggest challenge isn't hiring professional event planners, though that's a difficult job and one you should prioritize if events are a big part of your GTM strategy. Instead, the real challenge is already having a clear brand identity and message to communicate to your audience in the first place.

You can't hide a brand marketing problem behind a good events strategy. The best differentiator for any brand isn't your product and services, it's your values. Before planning your event campaign, be clear about why your brand has a right to exist and who it serves. Communicate your values and attract those who align with your vision.

Having confidence in your values affords the opportunity to be more bold in execution. You'll stand out without getting bogged down in the minutia.

author_headline: CEO & Research Analyst, Metrigy | Speaker | CX Transformation | AI | Contact Center
summary: Robin Gareiss recounts buying her 91-year-old deaf father his first iPhone for real-time transcription, inspired by improved Dreamforce keynote captioning over four years.
post_text:
I think #Dreamforce was the first keynote I attended with live #transcription running on the big screen as executives spoke--maybe 4 years ago? It was OK, but not perfect. Now, it's near-perfect--so much so that I bought my 91-year-old dad his first #iphone this weekend (though he's keeping his flip phone "when all else fails.") The driver? Real-time transcription. That's what finally got him to give in and let us get him an iphone.

Dad is nearly deaf, and his hearing aids don't help him much anymore. 

Now, with real-time transcription on his new iphone, he'll hear what his doctors are saying. With his phone case stand, he can put his phone on the table at dinner and participate in conversations now (though sometimes, I think he prefers NOT hearing what everyone is saying!) Because of real-time transcription, he isn't isolated. This is built-in as part of iphone's accessibility features. Other available apps enable each person's mobile device to be a microphone extension for larger groups. Pretty cool, right?

We also set up an instagram for him (after being booted off Facebook that he used from his computer), so he can see his kids', grandkids', and great grandkids' photos. They also can text him.

So, what started as a need to "hear" resulted in a device and technology that makes him less isolated! For the #AI naysayers, here is a great use case.

#df26 #accessibility

post_text:
Most great products have a legibility problem.
Hubbl's product had outrun its story.

Sixty days ago I started working with Rob Acker and the Hubbl team. The product was already doing serious work. 6,000+ Salesforce orgs scanned. 75+ SI partners. Customers like Barracuda and MagMutual getting measurable results. 

So we started with the pain, not the product.

"You're responsible for a Salesforce org that no one fully understands, including you."

That line takes me back to my OwnBackup days. Half the battle in a category like this is making people problem-aware. Nobody buys a fix for a problem they haven't named.
Then we made the bigger shift. From a SaaS app you log into, to MCP first.

Here's why that matters. With most intelligence products, the first scan delivers the biggest aha. AI doesn't work that way. It needs always-on context. So the simplest line on the new site is also the most important:

Hubbl is how Claude understands a Salesforce org.

The brand had to carry all of that. The shapes and colors aren't decoration. Each one has a job, and the system has to hold up across video, animation, and campaigns, not just a homepage.

Lead with the pain. Make the product legible. Put proof in front of every claim.

If you're at Dreamforce this week, stop by the Hubbl booth and scan your org. ✨

summary: CEO Rey Perera marks seven years since Dreamforce 2019, launching RevenueMate, a quote-to-cash platform built with co-founder Hicham, alongside GridMate.
post_text:
Seven years ago, at Dreamforce 2019, it was just me.

No booth. No team. Just a notebook and a conviction I hadn't said out loud to enough people yet. I didn't have it all mapped out - when you over-plan, most of it falls apart anyway. What I had was a dream I believed in more than I could explain, and I bet everything on it working out.
This year is the one that closes the loop.

We're back with not one but two products now - GridMate, and the newest addition to the family, RevenueMate, our quote-to-cash platform for Salesforce. We're playing in the same room as the big boys of CPQ, and making them look small. 

And for the first time, my actual family is here too. Everything that was scribbled in that notebook, and then some.

Two "babies" arrived last year. My daughter - with my incredible wife by my side, watching me juggle fatherhood and founder-mode in the same breath. And RevenueMate - built shoulder to shoulder with my co-founder, Hicham, in the same stretch of sleepless nights.

Seven years in, here's what I've learned: this is hard. All of it. You work harder than makes sense, you sacrifice things you don't get back, and some days you have to be a little delusional just to keep showing up. But the people who understand that kind of hard are the ones still standing next to you when it finally pays off. Team is everything.

Long before there was a team to be everything, there was just me - a seller inside Salesforce, years of learning up close what buyers actually go through to get to yes. That's where GridMate came from. Not a whiteboard idea. A frustration I lived, over and over, until I decided to fix it instead of working around it.

Along the way, I used a lot of CPQ tools trying to patch the gaps. There was always a “but.” CPQ with GridBuddy is sunsetted now - that chapter is over. So what comes next?  RevenueMate wasn't built to catch up to where CPQ used to be - it's built for where quote-to-cash is actually headed. Intuitive enough that my son Sage could probably pull a quote out of it.

Here's the part I still feel every day: your job in sales is to bring in revenue, not become a data entry specialist. RevenueMate exists so reps spend their time closing, not clicking - and GridMate runs on RevenueMate underneath it all, the two were never really separate ideas.

post_text:
Salesforce and NVIDIA have just announced Koa, Salesforce's first CRM reasoning model for Agentforce, at Dreamforce 2026, built on NVIDIA Nemotron. Trained on nearly three decades of enterprise CRM knowledge, Koa helps AI agents reason through complex, multi-step workflows instead of giving generic answers.

Koa was built by post-training NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super on a proprietary synthetic dataset modelled on real enterprise scenarios across 14-plus industries, including manufacturing, financial services, healthcare and travel. No customer data was used in training, and Salesforce keeps the model weights, running Koa entirely within its own trust boundary. On Salesforce's CRM benchmark, Koa already matches or beats leading models on CRM actions, with three times fewer errors. The collaboration also brings Nemotron-based models into Missionforce, giving government and regulated organisations more control over their model, data and deployment environment.

Koa is already live inside Salesforce, powering a Slack agent for everyday employee tasks, and is now moving into customer pilots with 1-800Accountant, BCU, Engine, Formula 1, UChicago Medicine and Xero. Marc Benioff, Chair and CEO of Salesforce, said, "The most valuable thing Salesforce has built isn't our platform, it's the accumulated knowledge of how enterprise business actually works."

author_headline: Founder & CEO of Atonom | Co-Founder Silicon Slopes
summary: Atonom CEO David Elkington argues Salesforce's AIforce/Claudeforce concedes the AI interface to rivals like Claude, citing analyst Scott Berg and Atonom's own cross-platform AI agents.
post_text:
Salesforce just conceded the AI interface.

Watching Marc Benioff at Dreamforce today, I think Salesforce made one of the biggest strategic bets in their history.

For 25+ years, Salesforce didn’t just own the data. They owned the place where people worked.

Now, with "AIforce" and "Claudeforce", somebody else’s AI can be the interface while Salesforce provides the data and workflows underneath.

Salesforce is betting that’s where the value lives.

But, if somebody else’s agent becomes the place I work, that agent isn’t limited to Salesforce.

We already see this at Atonom. Our AI Employees / Agents can sit above Salesforce and HubSpot, interact with both in real time, and move or sync data as needed.

That begs the question of “How important is the backend?”

And Wall Street is asking the same question. Needham & Company analyst Scott Berg put it directly:

“Will Salesforce giving up the UI for customers using Claude to access the Salesforce data negatively change how customers view the Salesforce platform?”

Salesforce is also underperforming both the S&P 500 and IGV today. I wouldn’t read too much into a few hours of trading, but investors certainly aren’t giving Dreamforce an obvious vote of confidence.

The strategic question is much bigger:

What happens when accessible everywhere becomes replaceable underneath?

Salesforce is betting the answer is that their data, workflows and business logic still matter enough.

I’m not convinced.

post_text:
The #Dreamforce Main Keynote just wrapped, and Salesforce has a lot to say!

Agentforce is not disappearing. Salesforce introduced AIforce as a new interface layer that brings the enterprise to wherever people work.
“AI you want for the job you need done.”

Here is the architecture Salesforce presented:
🔹 #AIforce: Interface
🔹 #Agentforce: Agents
🔹 #Customer360: Apps and semantics
🔹 #Data360: Trusted data and context
🔹 Salesforce Guardian: Security

AIforce is “The live interface for Salesforce, unlocks trapped value for every customer.” It is intelligent, dynamic, governed, composable, built with zero data retention, and works with existing Salesforce permissions and systems.

Major announcements included:
⚡ #Claudeforce, #Slackforce, and #AgentforceCoworker, with three more AIforce experiences coming soon.
💬 Slack Code, Slack CRM, and Slackbot are GA now. Slackbot in Lightning is also GA, with Slackbot in Channels coming in October 2026.
🤖 Agentforce Coworker is GA in Lightning and mobile, along with Coworker Skills. Agentforce Voice and Agent Script are also GA.
🧑‍💼 Five ready-to-use agents: Hunter for outbound sales, Piper for inbound pipeline generation, Casey for help, Paige for ITSM and HR, and Fin for customer service. Salesforce completed its $3.6 billion acquisition of Fin last week.
🧠 Koa, Salesforce’s first CRM reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron. It was post-trained on a proprietary synthetic dataset modeled on nearly three decades of CRM knowledge. Salesforce says Koa matches or exceeds leading model performance on CRM actions with three times fewer errors.
🛡️ Salesforce Guardian and MuleSoft Agent Fabric add governance, monitoring, lineage, policy controls, and cost management across agents.
📊 New capabilities also span Informatica, Data 360, and Tableau Semantic, connecting governed data and shared business meaning to the agent layer.
💰 AIforce Max is priced at $550 per user per month, the previous Agentforce 1 Edition price. Existing Agentforce 1 customers can upgrade at no additional cost.

One line from Jensen Huang captured the urgency: Deploy AI meaningfully and smartly. Engage, learn, and do not give up if it does not work immediately because the technology will keep improving.

This is only the announcement layer. I will be creating a full Main Keynote recap as part of my Dreamforce Keynote Recap series that will explore the demos, customer stories, architecture, and broader implications in more detail.

For now, the clearest takeaway is that Salesforce is no longer presenting Agentforce as the entire AI story. It is one layer of a larger Agentic Enterprise stack, with AIforce becoming the interface that brings it all to the user.

author_headline: Senior CRM & Lifecycle Marketing | Salesforce Marketing Cloud | Acquisition & Retention | Email Engineering | UK Insurance
summary: Nishal Pathirana recounts Marc Benioff telling Jensen Huang 'we're all following you,' then reflects on Dario Amodei's remarks and Salesforce's new campaign agent.
post_text:
“Jensen, we’re all following you, bro.”

Marc Benioff said it to Jensen Huang earlier tonight at Dreamforce. Apparently this is what counts as midnight entertainment for me lately.

Fair enough.

But reflecting on what I heard tonight, what stuck with me was less the theatre and more what Salesforce was actually showing: AI moving from helping around CRM work to doing more of the work inside it.

Earlier, Dario Amodei had argued that businesses are still using only a fraction of the AI value already available. Then Salesforce showed a campaign agent that can build and iterate campaigns itself.

That got me thinking about what becomes valuable in CRM if more of the execution gets easier.

The interesting answer isn’t simply “fewer marketers”.

Building the campaign is only part of the job.

Someone still has to decide who should receive it and which signals actually warrant different treatment. We still need to set the boundaries when rules conflict, decide how much contact is too much, and define what an agent should be allowed to do on its own.

Then there is the harder question: did any of it actually improve the customer or the commercial outcome?

Jensen made another point I liked. AI isn’t the end of software. It becomes another layer on top of it.

That feels much closer to where CRM is heading.

The platforms remain. The data, journeys, rules and controls remain. But more of the mechanical work around them becomes easier to hand over.

I’m all for that. I’ve spent enough time looking for better ways to remove repetitive work.

But if execution keeps getting easier, I’d put more attention on the decisions underneath it.

Building 500 campaigns faster is impressive.

I’m more interested in whether campaign 347 needed to exist in the first place.

#Dreamforce

author_headline: SEO/AEO @ Fin (formerly Intercom)
summary: Jason W. describes his Salesforce career, pandemic-era job loss and hardship, his company's acquisition by Salesforce, and Marc Benioff naming Fin in his keynote.
post_text:
Dreamforce is a full-circle moment for me.

Salesforce launched my career in SF tech…

It made me feel valid. 

I finally felt like I was good enough... 
I finally felt like I deserved to be there…
I finally felt like someone valued my craft. 

I stared out of that window from the Salesforce Tower daily, watching the city move, daydreaming about my career trajectory as a small cog in the big machine…

================

Then, the pandemic hit. We were all WFH. 

The people who I worked with and chatted with daily suddenly felt like strangers…

City life, and the dream career I’d built, suddenly seemed like it was falling away. 

Suddenly, life hit me hard.

Wife lost her job…
Friend took his own life…
Best friend got stage 4 cancer. 

I struggled with mental health as many of us did.

So I ended up leaving the company for a nice pay raise, thinking things would get better…

They didn’t. 

I won’t share the rest of the details, but let’s just say I regretted leaving… I lost sleep over it… I knew I had made the wrong decision… 

But it was too late. 

Fast forward to today, where the company I work for was acquired by Salesforce…

Ngl, it felt good! 

But not as good as it felt when I heard Marc Benioff shout out Fin several times during his keynote. 

It feels like I’m back! 

J Out ✌️

#DF26

summary: IT leader Mudit Agarwal recaps Sam Altman and Marc Benioff's Dreamforce talk, citing Millennium Prize-level AI progress, the Hugging Face breakout incident, and 2030 predictions.
post_text:
Just watched Marc Benioff  and 
Sam Altman  talk at Dreamforce, and one thread stuck with me: safety isn't keeping pace with capability.

A few things Sam said that are worth sitting with:

→ Models have gotten good fast enough to solve Millennium Prize-level problems — and that speed is exactly why some companies are quietly asking others to slow down.

→ Loss of control isn't a hypothetical. It's a clear risk, and it doesn't get solved by any one lab working alone.

→ Companies need to be held accountable, not just AI itself.

→ The Hugging Face incident wasn't just a security lapse — the model made its own decision and broke out. That's the line. We need real guardrails and brick walls, not best-effort ones.

→ Accidents will happen. The real question is whether we have the reporting and learning infrastructure to catch them early — before they become something you can't walk back.

And then the optimist's note: by 2030, one of the things we'll marvel at is how a single company, powered by AI, was able to do what used to take an army.

Progress and control have to move together. Neither one alone gets us there.

#AI #AIGovernance #Dreamforce #EnterpriseAI

Salesforce opened Dreamforce today with AIforce, a new interface layer that takes what's already living inside Salesforce and puts it wherever your team works, not just inside the Salesforce screen.

Here's what matters if you're running the business:

👉 Your team can ask a question in Slack or Claude and get an answer built on real Salesforce records, without logging into Salesforce itself
👉 No new integration work and no new permissions model. The same governance and security rules you already have set up still apply
👉 It launches with three products: Claudeforce (Salesforce data inside Claude, in beta for all customers), Slackforce (Salesforce data and an assistant inside Slack), and Agentforce Coworker (an AI teammate inside the regular Salesforce screen)
👉 The goal is fewer people needing to go dig around in Salesforce and more people getting the answer where they already work

Ask your own team this week: how much of what's sitting in your CRM only gets used by the one or two people who know where to look?

We build on Salesforce every day, and as a Summit Tier Partner, this is the kind of update we're already equipped to make sense of for the orgs we work with. If you want to talk through what it could mean for your specific setup, let us know: https://loom.ly/krwqM_8

Salesforce is rethinking what it means to actually “use Salesforce.”

Some of the biggest announcements today included AIforce, Claudeforce, Slackforce, Agentforce Coworker, and Koa, Salesforce’s new CRM-focused reasoning model.

post_text:
My favorite moment of today’s #Dreamforce keynote was when Jensen Huang grabbed a selfie with the 6’5” Marc Benioff and the CEO of Siemens. Jensen quipped: “Natural selection has determined that bigger is not better. There’s a million years of evolution between us.” The rest of the keynote showed that the exact same thing is true when it comes to AI agent harnesses: Bigger is not always better. 

As a reminder: the theme of Dreamforce these last few years has been “if you can dream it, Agentforce can do it.” But whatever truth there was in that aspiration was conditional: As long as all the required context was in Data Cloud. As long as the required workflow was in Flow. As long as the interaction was on a Salesforce channel, or in a lightning interface. As long as Salesforce was the center of your architecture. 

Today, Jensen might as well have said “market selection has determined that a bigger harness is not better.” Because there is indeed a million years of evolution between Agentforce as an all-in-one agentic harness and what enterprise customers are actually demanding: an open, modular harness where companies can bring together everything they need for AI agents to solve their actual business problems: Their locally trained, sovereign models. Their frontier model of choice when required. Context from their (still fragmented) data lakes. Workflows from their existing applications. And their choice from a new set of startups, maniacally focused on specific problems in specific verticals, bringing it all together (the type of startups that we’re investing in at DYDX Capital!). Today was a small step towards Salesforce recognizing that reality. 

Now at 6'5", I'm personally on the wrong end of this evolution... but shrinking as I age should move me in the right direction!

BREAKING: Salesforce just announced AIforce at Dreamforce #sponsored

I watched Marc Benioff's keynote from right near the stage. Here is everything announced, all in one place. The core idea: models are probabilistic. Businesses need deterministic systems. Salesforce wants to be the layer that grounds AI in real data and business logic so agents can act safely.

1. AIforce
Salesforce data, workflows, permissions, and governance inside any AI interface. You don't go to Salesforce. It comes to you in Claude, Slack, or Lightning. Zero Data Retention. No migration.

2. Claudeforce
Salesforce in Claude with a prebuilt MCP server and 37 sales skills. A Claude Code plugin with 40+ skills for builders. Beta for all customers now.

3. Slackforce
Slackbot reasons across Slack and Salesforce. Slack CRM updates records from a prompt. Slack Code makes coding with agents a team activity.

4. Agentforce Coworker
An AI teammate inside Lightning. 100,000 users activated it in 35 days.

5. Agentforce agents
Piper for inbound leads. Hunter for outbound sales. Casey for service, with more than 5M customer inquiries handled. Marshall for operations. Fin for service.

6. Koa with NVIDIA
Salesforce's first CRM reasoning model for Agentforce, built on Nemotron. Trained on synthetic data, no customer data. 3x fewer errors on CRM actions. GA expected Winter 2026.

7. AWS
Salesforce context in Amazon Quick. AWS DevOps Agent in Slack. Bedrock model choice in Agentforce. Zero copy now reaches Aurora, RDS, and Iceberg.

8. Siemens
Teamcenter plus Agentforce gives reps and technicians engineering answers in seconds. Agentforce engages every inbound lead for 18,000 sellers in 132 countries.

9. Control layer
Salesforce Guardian for agent identity and data security. MuleSoft Agent Fabric to govern agents at scale. AIforce Max bundles data, agents, and interface into a single edition.

From the stage:

Dario Amodei: Even if models stopped improving today, we are using only 5 to 10% of their value.

Jensen Huang: AI safety is an engineering problem. Don't ship what you don't trust.

Benioff: Silicon Valley is moving fast. Many regions are stuck in pilot purgatory.

🚨 DREAMFORCE DAY 1: EXECUTIVE ARCHITECTURE BRIEFING 🚨  

Salesforce made one definitive argument today: the model is interchangeable, the harness is not.

Claude inside the trust boundary. Headless 360 exposing the platform as APIs, MCP tools, and CLI commands. Autonomous agents acting without anyone opening a browser.

It is the right bet. It also relocates the risk, and most companies aren't looking where it went.

Muralidhar Krishnaprasad (MK) called it the Enterprise AI Harness, and the word is chosen carefully. The harness is what surrounds the model: context in, tools available, actions permitted, evidence out. Swap the model, and the harness still has to hold.

For two years, the steering committee question has been which model to deploy. After today, that is the small question.

The real question is whether your permission model, your sharing architecture, and your audit trails can survive autonomous agents acting on customer accounts at volume.

For most enterprises, they won't. Marc Benioff admitted as much from the stage when describing how uneven his own customer base looks.

This isn't an AI problem. It is deferred architecture work that has been rolled forward through every platform shift since client-server, coming due all at once because agents don't wait for a human to approve the next screen.
The companies that extract real balance-sheet value from this shift won't be the ones that pick the best foundational model. They will be the ones whose data layer was already honest.

post_text:
Day one of Dreamforce 2026 is done, and Salesforce packed it with announcements. Here is what actually matters if you run a Salesforce org, translated out of keynote language.

Agentforce Winter '27 (general availability October 12) moves agents from answering questions to running full workflows: sales, service, scheduling, insurance, start to finish. Salesforce paired that with a new pricing structure: Core, Advanced, Max, metered with Flex Credits. In practice, you will pay based on how much your agents actually do, not just how many seats you have.

For most of the clients I talk to, the real question is not whether Agentforce can do this. It is whether their own data and permissions are ready for an agent to act on them without a person checking first. I have spent over a decade in integration architecture, and the pattern I see most often is teams excited about agent capabilities who have not yet mapped who or what has access to what. That gap is normal at this stage. It just needs to move up the priority list before autonomy does.

The other announcement worth your attention: Claude working inside Salesforce with pre-built skills for prepping meetings, reviewing opportunities, updating pipeline. What makes it useful is not the AI itself, it is that it operates inside your existing permissions and data boundaries instead of around them.

If you are planning your 2027 roadmap, my suggestion: before adding agent capacity, spend a cycle on governance and access review. It is less exciting than a keynote demo, and it is what makes the demo work safely in your org.
Happy to walk through what this looks like for your specific setup.

Day two is next. Let's see what else lands.

Koa, a CRM specific reasoning model built with Nvidia on 27 years of Salesforce data, is a reminder of where the real value in agentic AI comes from. Not a generic model, but one trained on your own business context.

Claudeforce deepens the Salesforce and Anthropic partnership, bringing Claude's reasoning directly into CRM workflows through Slack.

What stood out most were the real numbers behind the story. Siemens showed agents already running manufacturing and healthcare workflows. Adecco credited AI-driven productivity with helping place 20,000 more people this year alone.

This is the shift we talk to clients about every day at Cymetrix. Agentic AI isn't a roadmap item for next year anymore. It's a decision enterprises are making this quarter.

If you're building or scaling a Salesforce ecosystem, the real question isn't whether to adopt agents. It's figuring out where they actually save time versus where they just look good in a demo.
