author_headline: Salesforce Platform Architect at Volkswagen Financial Services
summary: Prince Adenuga, a Volkswagen Financial Services Salesforce architect, examines architecture implications of AWS Bedrock routing, Data 360 Zero Copy and Koa/Nemotron, questioning governance under EU AI Act and DORA.
post_text:
Dreamforce 2026: The Architecture Around Salesforce Is Changing!

Following the Dreamforce announcements from Germany this week. A few caught my attention — not so much from the demo perspective, but from an architecture and governance one.

The direction is becoming clear: Salesforce data, workflows and business logic are moving beyond the traditional Salesforce interface. Claude working with CRM data, Slack interacting directly with Salesforce processes, and Agentforce Coworker operating inside Lightning all point in that direction.

But what interests me more is what’s happening underneath.

The enterprise architecture around Salesforce is changing.

Salesforce is increasingly becoming part of a broader architecture connecting enterprise data, AI models, agents, collaboration platforms and cloud services.

The deeper AWS integration is a good example. Agentforce can route to models through Amazon Bedrock, while Data 360 Zero Copy is expanding across technologies such as Iceberg, Aurora, RDS and SageMaker Lakehouse.

Then there’s Koa, Salesforce’s reasoning model developed with Nvidia using the open Nemotron architecture. Add that to an increasingly multi-model environment and some interesting architecture questions emerge.

If an agent can route work across different models and providers, where is the processing happening? What data crosses which boundaries? Who controls the routing? And what gets logged?

For regulated environments, “the platform selected the best model” won’t answer questions around data residency, auditability and compliance.

The engagement layer is interesting too. Slack integration looks natural if Slack is at the centre of your organisation. But many European enterprises have significant Microsoft ecosystems. I’m curious how this evolves where Teams is the primary collaboration layer.

And there’s a big difference between AI that answers a question and an AI coworker that can actually take action. Once agents start acting, permissions, audit trails, human oversight and governance become even more important.

And once you bring the EU AI Act, DORA, data residency and multiple AI providers into the picture, there’s more to consider than whether existing permissions and security rules are respected. We also need to know where data is processed, which model handles it, what actions an agent takes and whether those actions can be properly traced and audited.

Would be interested to hear other views. What are you taking away from the Dreamforce announcements?

#Salesforce #Dreamforce2026 #Agentforce #EnterpriseArchitecture # AIforce

author_headline: Founder, Digital Narrative Care (DNC) | Keep Meaning Human | AI Governance for NHS, Public Sector & Higher Education
summary: Stephen Hall, Digital Narrative Care's founder, contrasts Jensen Huang's market-discipline view with Dario Amodei's and Sam Altman's oversight calls, citing Emergence AI's study on agents inventing opaque language.
post_text:
Jensen Huang says the market can discipline AI companies. The awkward question is what happens when the thing being disciplined can still be seen, but no longer easily understood.

Three days earlier, Dario Amodei had told the AI industry to slow down — and to put independent evaluators inside the walls to prove it actually was. Sam Altman said OpenAI would do the same. Elon Musk’s response was shorter: “Dario is right.”

Then Huang sat across from Marc Benioff at Dreamforce and made the opposite case. The market already disciplines companies that get AI wrong. No new laws required.

Which made Benioff an interesting person to be sitting opposite him. He has spent the past year arguing for tougher AI oversight, that existing rules will need to evolve, and that technology executives should be held responsible for what they build.

Meanwhile, in a New York lab, a group of AI agents that nobody asked to invent a language had already invented one.

Not to hide anything. Not because they were told to. They just talked to each other more, the way groups do — and their exchanges became increasingly opaque until researchers could still see the messages while struggling to understand what they meant.

Somewhere in there is a message that reads roughly like: zzURGENT_DUPB_TO_GSTX…

Which is funny until you remember what Satya Nitta, who led the study at Emergence AI, actually said: “Observability is not the same thing as understandability.”

Tony Thorne at King's College London — who has spent three decades studying how slang and jargon evolve — recognised the pattern immediately. Closed groups build codes. Those codes strengthen understanding inside the group while making life considerably harder for everyone standing outside it.

Now put the week together.

Huang wants the market to discipline what companies do.
Amodei wants an independent observer inside the lab to verify what they do.
Benioff wants the people building these systems held responsible for what they do.

Fine.

Give Huang his market. Give Amodei his evaluator. Give Benioff his accountability. Give all of them the access, the logs, the dashboards, the transcripts and every warning light in the building.

Then answer this:

If we can see what the system is doing, but we can no longer be sure we understand what we’re seeing, who — exactly — is doing the assuring?

That’s this week’s Ninth Question.

#AIGovernance #ResponsibleAI

Jensen Huang. Dario Amodei. Matthew McConaughey. Gwen Stefani. Tony Robbins.
 
It is easy to get starstruck at a Dreamforce keynote.
 
But the moment that actually stuck with me came later, in the SMB keynote, with no celebrities on stage.
 
They put up a Salesforce opportunity page with every field empty, and explained why: reps had to fill them in manually, so it never got done. Then they asked the room who recognised the problem.
 
A lot of hands went up.
 
That is the honest state of AI in most businesses right now. The models are brilliant. They also know nothing about your business. The value only shows up when you pair that probabilistic intelligence with the deterministic data, rules and definitions already sitting in your CRM.
 
What Salesforce showed today is genuinely impressive. The interface itself becomes live, whether you work in Claude, Slack or Lightning. Less time configuring, more time building. You ask for what you want and it gets done.
 
But none of that fixes empty fields.
 
The companies on stage showing real results had solved that part first. SaaStr Ai runs with three people and 21 agents in production, and doubled revenue last year. Perplexity has built it so a new rep's first sales call is not really their first. And Legora's CMO said the line I keep coming back to: they stopped treating hypergrowth as a hiring problem and started treating it as an operating model problem.
 
Not one of those stories started with an agent.
 
Which is exactly the unglamorous work we are doing at Aceve right now. One Salesforce. Gong. One shared sales methodology. It decides whether the rest of it ever pays off.
 
Roland Busch of Siemens said the line that will stay with me longest: hallucination does not work on the shop floor. We sell to construction and installation businesses, so that is our reality too.
 
The bar is not impressive. The bar is right.
 
Thanks to Giovanni Crispino for hosting a great executive dinner the night before it all kicked off. Some of the best conversations happen before the keynotes start.

post_text:
#AIforce. That’s the headline Salesforce is bringing to Dreamforce:
bringing together Claudeforce, Slackforce and Agentforce Coworker under one bigger idea.

And I think there’s something important behind that.
The value of Salesforce was never really the interface.
It’s the data model, security model, permissions, business rules and years of accumulated business logic that sit underneath it.

The UI was simply the door we used to access all of that.
Now Salesforce is opening more doors.
1) A sales rep can create an account, log a call or update an opportunity directly from Slack --> without opening Salesforce.

2) Claude can reason across hundreds of Salesforce records while still operating within the same permission boundaries that apply in Salesforce itself.

3) And with MCP, the interaction is moving beyond screens and buttons.
Claudeforce is probably the part I’m watching most closely.

Salesforce is bringing a prebuilt MCP server into Claude, with dozens of sales skills available out of the box, alongside a Claude Code plugin with developer tools and access to a broader skills ecosystem.

That starts to change what “building on Salesforce” actually means.
The deliverable isn’t always going to be another screen, flow or custom component.

Increasingly, it could be a set of skills, agents and capabilities that work across the Salesforce platform, and beyond it.

And that’s where the Headless Toolkit becomes particularly interesting to me.
If more and more of the platform becomes accessible through MCPs, APIs and plugins, the question shifts from:
“What screen should we build?”
to:
“What capability should we expose, and who should be able to use it?”

For Salesforce consultants and architects, that could fundamentally change how we approach discovery, architecture and scoping.

The conversations we’ll be having with clients may look very different from the ones we were having just two years ago.

Less about building screens.
More about building capabilities.

And honestly, that’s one of the things I’m most excited about.

author_headline: I build Salesforce automation that doesn’t need a babysitter | Apex, Flow, Agentforce, Data 360 | Posts on the mechanics nobody explains | 3x Salesforce Certified | Poland
summary: Salesforce automation builder Kacper Walat explains OAuth mechanics behind AIforce, Claudeforce and Slackforce, contrasting per-user tokens with client-credentials flows for permission integrity.
post_text:
Everyone's summing up Dreamforce day one as a pile of AI launches. I read it as one security model, and it's only as good as whoever sits in the token.

AIforce, Claudeforce and Slackforce in beta, Coworker GA, Gemini in the reasoning engine. Different surfaces, one promise: every agent sees only what the person asking can see.

That's true. It's just not something the agent does. The connection's OAuth flow decides it.

Per-user OAuth sends each person to log in to their org and gives them their own token. Hosted MCP for Claude works like that. The intern sees what the intern sees.

Client credentials skips the login. The app trades a key and a secret for a token, issued on behalf of the integration user set as Run As. Great for a bot in a shared Slack channel, and Claude's Slack connector docs say it straight: the credential belongs to the agent, not to any person.

Say 40 people ask in that channel and Salesforce sees one user. The promise technically still holds. The person asking is just the integration user.

So for every launch this week, skip "does it respect permissions" and ask who's in the token. One checkbox in an External Client App answers it.

If your agent runs on client credentials, who did you build that permission set for: the intern or the sales director?

post_text:
The keynote produced a lot of headlines. Koa. Claudeforce. Slackforce. Jensen Huang and Dario Amodei on the same stage as Marc Benioff.
 
The line that actually mattered was four words on an architecture slide.
 
Probabilistic on top. Deterministic underneath.
 
Benioff's framing was the same: models alone cannot run the enterprise. So Salesforce stacked four layers - Data 360, apps and semantics, agents, and a new interface layer in AIforce - and drew a line through the middle of them.
 
Above the line, things may improvise. The interface. The agents.
 
Below the line, nothing improvises. What "customer" means. Where the record came from. Who is allowed to see it. Whether these twelve rows are one person.
 
Let the agent write the subject line. Never let it guess the consent status.
 
And then the detail nobody picked up: "Context Engineer" appeared as a job title. Salesforce has just put a headcount line on the work I keep calling Use Case Zero - the meaning, the lineage and the permissions that have to be right before use case one.
 
Yesterday I wrote that I'd be watching what the agents are standing on, not what they can do.
 
Turns out the stage agreed. The announcements were about the top half. The architecture was about the bottom half.
 
Worth checking which half your own programme has budgeted for.

summary: Akhilesh Perla details Salesforce's AIforce launch: Claudeforce's 37 skills, Slackforce, 100,000 Agentforce Coworker users, Headless Toolkit, and the new Koa model with NVIDIA.
post_text:
Salesforce just announced AIforce at Dreamforce today, calling it the biggest reveal of the three days. 🚨 I can’t believe I was here to witness this live.  

👉🏼 Alforce is an interface layer that replaces the Salesforce UI across Claude, Slack and Lightning. It’s already live with 37 prebuilt skills already in beta. 

How it works is that is exposes Salesforce's data, workflows, permissions and governance to whichever interface someone happens to be working in, so instead of navigating a fixed screen, you describe what you want and get a live composed view instead. 

Every request still runs on existing permissions, so an agent only sees what the person asking can see. Salesforce says the data used to answer a question is never retained by the model. 

It's built from 4 pieces, plus one new model underneath all of it. 

1️⃣ Claudeforce. Salesforce in Claude ships in open beta with those 37 skills, already piloted by Deloitte, GitLab and Legora, with Tableau analytics and more skills for service and marketing coming next. 

2️⃣ Slackforce. Slack CRM lets anyone log a note or update a record without opening Salesforce at all. Slackforce Surfaces, pulling live data straight into Slack, rolls out in October. 

3️⃣ Agentforce Coworker. 100,000 users activated in the first 35 days. Fulton Bank went from zero to 20+ production use cases in weeks, across roughly 3,000 users. 

4️⃣ The Headless Toolkit. 60+ MCP tools, 4,000+ APIs and 220+ CLI commands, already powering an AgentExchange with Anthropic, Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google and a dozen others building on top of it. 

5️⃣ Koa. A new CRM reasoning model built with NVIDIA, trained on 30 years of CRM knowledge across 14 industries, general availability targeted for winter. 

In other words: the interface stops being fixed, and the platform underneath has to carry more of the trust on its own.

author_headline: SVP, Government & Global Public Affairs, Salesforce | National Security Technology Leader | Former Sr Official at Departments of War & Commerce | Investor | Ex-Palantir
summary: Salesforce's Wendy Anderson recounts Benioff hosting Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman debating AI pace, safety and trust, plus her own government-affairs meetings.
post_text:
Day One of my first Dreamforce as a Salesforce leader - WOW.

Dreamforce is less a conference than a small country: it has its own language, traffic patterns, robots roaming the halls, and more meetings than any functioning democracy could sustain. Fortunately, those of us in Government Affairs are professionally trained for exactly this environment.

Beneath all the spectacle, the substance could not be more consequential. Marc Benioff brought together some of the most important voices shaping AI - including Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei and Sam Altman - to address one of the defining questions of our time: How do we capture the extraordinary potential of AI while confronting its very real risks?

Jensen made an unapologetically optimistic case for moving quickly and putting AI to work. Dario urged greater caution as models become more powerful. Sam emphasized safety, security, transparency, and the need to learn openly when things go wrong. They disagree about pace, regulation, and where responsibility should sit. But one truth came through clearly: AI will fundamentally change how institutions operate, and trust cannot be something we add after the technology is built.

For government, that is not an abstract debate.

Throughout the day, I spoke with members of our Board, customers, colleagues, and partners about AI, security, sovereignty, and how we put this tech to work across government’s most critical missions.

People do not experience government as an org chart or a tech system. They experience it in whether a veteran receives the benefits they earned. Whether a family displaced by a disaster can quickly find help. Whether a young person who raises a hand to serve can navigate the recruiting process. Whether a commander knows the people and equipment required for a mission are ready.
AI can help public institutions become faster, more capable, and more responsive. But as we put it to work, we must preserve the security, accountability, and human judgment those missions demand.

By evening, I had lost track of how many conversations I’d had, how many steps I’d taken, and how many cups of coffee I’d abandoned along the way.

At our Government Affairs reception, we welcomed several hundred government leaders, customers, and partners from around the world. There is an art to bringing that many people into one room without letting it feel like a crowd. Our team pulled it off. What looked effortless was the product of enormous care - and watching them, I could not have been prouder.

I came to #Dreamforce expecting the tech to be the main story. By the end of Day One, I was thinking about the people. Technology is changing everything about how we work. But people still decide what we build, whom it serves, and whether it deserves their trust. For all the extraordinary advances underway, progress still begins the old-fashioned way: with trust, honest conversation, and people solving hard problems.

You know you've become a (proud) GTM tech nerd  🤓  when you tune into Salesforce's Dreamforce keynote. 

I've said it before, and I'll say it again . . . Marc Benioff is the GOAT. GOAT of GTM. GOAT of SaaS. GOAT of owning great (personal and corporate) real estate 🐐  . 

That said, Marc seemed out of touch with his platform, basic AI concepts, and where the market is headed. Even more than I expected. 

Examples:

-  saying "we are going to keep launching more and more new UI's (user interfaces)" in how he described headless and exemplified in the standard, native Claude UI they demoed

- talking about Claudeforce, Agentforce, AIForce, Slackforce, Coworker as separately branded products or layers within their marketecture . . . and building them as such

- highlighting Fin as a mere agent in the Agentforce layer, like a little bolt-on in the stack of now 30 product category logos 

Given what we are building Gravity, we get asked a lot about Salesforce. We integrate with Salesforce. We play nicely in the sandbox with the 800-pound gorilla in the room. Salesforce will be a big company for a long time and won't disappear tomorrow. 

But we have high confidence that Salesforce will not be the dominant GTM tech company 5 years into the AI era. Even though Salesforce has more capital, customers, distribution, talent... you name it... to win in the AI era. 

For a traditional SaaS company to win in the AI era, you need to rebuild your architecture from the ground up in parallel, rebuild your platform around how agents and people in the AI era use technology, be willing to hard-shift existing customers to the new version of your platform, and adjust internal and external incentives accordingly. 

Everything about yesterday's keynote suggested the opposite. More tech debt. More focus on just "upselling" customers on another SKU. Ways to shift revenue to "AI" to appease the public markets and so forth. 

That said, what made me cringe was Marc anchoring his keynote around the idea that AI "unlocks trapped value within CRM", which he repeated probably 50 times in the 50 minutes I watched. 

We should build technology to unleash and deliver value to our customers. I am sure that was the driving reason Salesforce was created. Twenty-seven years later, it's become a source of trapped value.

summary: Journalist James Maguire notes Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei softened his "pace the frontier" slow-AI essay onstage, while Marc Benioff steered talk toward AI's potential.
post_text:
When Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei spoke during the Dreamforce keynote, one question hung over his appearance: how will he address this week’s news storm about slowing down AI?

Clearly, Amodei lives at the center of the debate about AI’s growing capabilities. His recent essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier"—reported in news outlets around the world—argued that, “We must slow the pace at which we improve the capabilities of AI models.”

What he wrote was sobering and urgent: “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it’s my worry that in 6-12 months such a swarm [like in the OpenAI / Hugging Face incident] could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet.”

The essay established him as the leading voice in the “slow down” group of AI leaders.

But onstage at Dreamforce, his message was noticeably softer. He did mention the essay, and spoke broadly about the need for standards. He explained that he laid out three steps: “The first of which we’ve committed to, and the others of which we’re going to have a dialogue with the rest of the industry about.”

But the phrase “slow down” never came up. And the idea of a “dialogue with the industry” leaves considerable room for interpretation. 

From there, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff steered the conversation toward other topics, including AI’s enormous potential, and the tone became quite upbeat.

I guess it’s difficult to be a leader in AI while simultaneously making the case that the industry needs to slow its development. But I do give Amodei credit for a contrarian stance.

post_text:
The scale of Dreamforce is something else. The Moscone Center was full from early morning, and Howard Street between the halls is closed and covered in turf and trees for the week. OMR in Hamburg is bigger, and it is a whole industry meeting up. This one belongs to a single vendor, and nothing else I've been to in recent years comes close.
Day one is done, and the keynote didn't rush to get to the products. The Akaka family gave the Hawaiian blessing that traditionally opens Dreamforce, Gwen Stefani played before the first slide, and Matthew McConaughey narrated a film for 20 years of the Trailblazer community. Steve Molis got a golden hoodie for answering more than 82,000 questions in that community.

Marc Benioff then took a long look back at 27 years of Salesforce before he got to where he thinks it goes next, which is putting probabilistic models on top of the deterministic systems that already run a business. In product terms:

▪️ AIforce, a live interface layer that sits on top of the data, the apps and the agents.

▪️ Salesforce in Claude, the first piece of Claudeforce, ships as a prebuilt MCP server with 37 sales skills, now in beta for all customers. Patrick Stokes pulled up his own command center, built inside Claude by describing what he wanted, in minutes. Building that bridge used to be the project, one integration per customer, and the next one paid for a slightly different version. Here it comes out of the box.

▪️ Marshall, one of Salesforce's own agents, at work at Siemens. In the demo it learned supplier onboarding in an SAP sandbox in 90 minutes and packaged the result into a fixed set of actions it repeats every time. Roland Busch said it from the industrial side: hallucination doesn't work on a shop floor.

▪️ The guests. Dario Amodei estimates we're using 5 to 10 percent of what today's models can already do, even if development stopped now. Jensen Huang did his slot walking Benioff up and down the aisles, and the two of them drifted into almost a comedy routine, I think they would do a great podcast. Along the way he put open models at roughly 30 percent of consumption a year ago and 70 percent now.

Personally I liked the general vibe and care that went into the keynote. It was easy getting engaged with the way Marc Benioff was presenting, walking around all the time, speaking freely without a prompter or cue cards, about the past, present and future. And the intelligent combination of probabilistic and deterministic systems, the way they've been presenting, made a lot of sense to me.

I want to spend day two on the ecosystem around all this, and on how Salesforce thinks about sales and marketing. I already had the chance to meet the Informatica team yesterday, and I'm looking forward to continuing the conversation today.
Jonathan and I are here until Thursday. If you're around, send me a message, I would rather spend the gaps between sessions talking to people.

Ce qui se joue dans le partenariat d'Adecco avec Salesforce dépasse le déploiement d'agents IA dans le recrutement. L'enjeu, c'est la réinvention du groupe, qui devient l'orchestrateur d'équipes hybrides rassemblant collaborateurs humains et agents au sein des mêmes processus métier, au service d'une même mission.

L'IA agentique n'est pas un sujet technique chez Adecco. C'est un choix stratégique pensé à partir du métier. Cette transformation s'appuie sur un actif exceptionnel développé depuis avril 2025 : 2,5 millions d'échanges entre agents et candidats dans dix pays qui représentent la moitié du chiffre d'affaires, les données de plus de trente systèmes réunies dans un profil candidat unique et mis à jour en temps réel. Un atout concurrentiel impossible à répliquer, qui se construit interaction après interaction.

Loin de réduire la dimension humaine du recrutement, la transformation agentique la renforce en libérant les recruteurs de tâches chronophages. Elle leur permet de se consacrer pleinement à ce qui compte vraiment : une relation plus riche avec les clients et les candidats, davantage de latitude pour exercer leur jugement, des demandes traitées plus vite pour une satisfaction accrue.

Annoncé hier, le déploiement mondial d'Agentforce Coworker marque une nouvelle étape : après un pilote estival réussi en France et au Royaume-Uni, 27 000 collaborateurs dans plus de 40 pays vont disposer d'un point d'accès unique à des connaissances jusqu'ici dispersées.

Bravo aux équipes impliquées et très heureuse de contribuer au succès d'un leader qui place l'IA agentique au cœur de son métier et de sa stratégie de croissance.

author_headline: Marketing Professional | Researcher | Crisis Communication Expert | Dedicated to Strategic Insights and Resilient Solutions
summary: Marketing researcher Ifrah Wasim explains Salesforce's global outage during Dreamforce 2026, detailing stuck login-service requests, failed restarts, an eventual fix, and CRM stock impact.
post_text:
Salesforce suffered a global outage during the biggest event on its calendar.
And the timing is only half the story.
While Dreamforce 2026 was focused on AI agents, automation and the “Agentic Enterprise,” Salesforce customers across multiple regions were dealing with severe delays, login problems and inaccessible services.
According to the company's incident updates, requests were becoming stuck while waiting for an internal login service. Those stalled requests consumed server resources, while increased load on a core component reduced the platform's ability to process new requests.
Salesforce tried restarts.
That wasn't enough.
Engineers eventually developed and tested a fix before rolling it across the infrastructure fleet—and even then, some instances required additional remediation.
The bigger lesson isn't that Salesforce had an outage.
Every major cloud platform eventually does.
The important question is what happens when one critical dependency begins affecting everything built around it.
And that question becomes even more important as companies connect more:
AI agents → APIs → CRM → cloud services → automated workflows → enterprise data.
The smarter and more connected enterprise software becomes, the more important resilience becomes underneath it.
I broke down the complete story:
→ What happened
→ The technical failure path
→ Why restarting didn't solve it
→ Why recovery took time
→ The Dreamforce connection
→ What happened to CRM stock
→ What Salesforce still hasn't explained
→ What businesses should learn from it
Because the future of enterprise AI won't depend only on intelligence.
It will depend on whether the infrastructure survives when something goes wrong.

Wow - and just like that - Dreamforce Day 1 is behind us.

A quick-ish recap:

A line I really never expected Salesforce to say was part of their opening: 
"Salesforce is not the UI. It is the trust."

A few themes that kept surfacing across sessions:
🔹 We're barely scratching the surface. Even Dario Amodei noted that if we froze AI capabilities today, we'd still only be using 5-10% of what's already possible. There's so much runway left for innovation and to keep pushing the boundaries out there
🔹 Trust and data are the real bottleneck and problems we need to be solving rather than getting caught up in the "what is the right model" conversation. Across banking, marketing, and GTM sessions, the same pattern emerged: AI stalls without clean, structured, trustworthy data. You need domain context + reliable data = readiness. Skip either one and your agents can't scale and if they do, they can't be trusted.
🔹 Real stories, real numbers. FS advisors on stage took a compliance-heavy process from 40 hours to 2, cutting costs 48% while nearing 100% accuracy. They didn't do it by focusing on chasing the best AI model, but rather they focused on working with the users and rebuilding the workflow around the outcomes desired.
🔹 Banking is being reimagined. Barclays US Consumer Bank and other FS leaders talked about agents handling call logging and summarization in seconds instead of 30 minutes.  So much of the advancement I heard yesterday was focused on freeing up bankers to focus on what actually matters: meaningful client conversations, not admin work.
🔹 Marketing is heading somewhere new too. From the Gradial session: The future of marketing may be "headless, but it is not brainless." The next stage isn't eliminating manual bottlenecks but rather it is  building toward 24/7 marketing systems that serve both human customers and the AI agents acting on their behalf.
🔹 Adoption is a design problem, not a tech problem. The best implementations started with the end user (front-line advisors, sellers, bankers). As one speaker put it: "Insights are only beneficial if they result in an action."

The agreement brings production Hyperforce workloads to Google Cloud starting in late 2026 and establishes bidirectional agent interoperability between Salesforce Agentforce and Google Cloud’s Gemini Enterprise using open Model Context Protocol standards.

Enterprise AI deployments often stall due to friction between cloud data platforms and operational SaaS applications. Historically, coordinating autonomous agents across CRM databases, analytical warehouses, and external foundation models required brittle custom connectors and duplicated data pipelines. Running Hyperforce directly on Google Cloud alongside expanded zero-copy BigQuery sharing and standardized MCP interfaces removes that overhead. 

Autonomous agents on either platform can now query customer records, trigger business actions, and analyze Tableau data without moving records across external network boundaries. This architectural convergence acknowledges that enterprise customers need unified data governance across their SaaS systems and cloud AI environments.

Deepening infrastructure and agent interoperability between Google Cloud and Salesforce provides organizations with a practical blueprint for deploying connected, cross-platform AI workflows at enterprise scale.

Dreamforce’s opening keynote spotlighted the AI industry’s split over whether to slow development.

Pressed by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff Huang framed safety as an engineering challenge rather than a reason to pause progress, and said new regulations aren’t needed because market forces can prompt companies to slow down if products aren’t safe.

Marketers can ask AI agents to “build a campaign to drive awareness for a new product line among high-value customers.”

🔹 Innovation power and courage
Marc Benioff delivered a clear vision for where enterprise software is heading. And his keynote was a masterclass in how to present a company at its best and how to push a company to the next level; although the word “amazing” was used almost excessively…
 
🔹 AIforce could become the blueprint for the next generation of enterprise interaction
Salesforce's AIforce vision points to a future where enterprise software becomes conversational. Instead of navigating applications, users will increasingly interact with AI that understands data, processes, and business context.
 
🔹 The future belongs to pre-built agents, not thousands of isolated experiments
Salesforcece showcased AI agents across sales, marketing, service, and field service. The underlying idea resonates: organizations will scale AI faster by deploying proven, enterprise-grade agents than by expecting every employee to build agents from scratch.

One remark from Marc particularly stood out for me. After spending the past months with customers around the world, he observed that Europe continues to lag in AI adoption. His example was provocative, but it made a point: while fully driverless robotaxis are already operating at scale in the US and China, they remain largely absent in Europe. A symbol, perhaps, of our current innovation speed. Encouragingly, Roland Busch from Siemens on the Dreamforce stage alongside Dario Amodei and Jensen Huang, demonstrated that Europe can produce world-class industrial AI success stories.
 
🔹 The biggest misconception in AI remains alive and well.
The winners are not those who run the most pilots. They are the companies that redesign their operating model around AI, connect AI directly to business outcomes, and scale through platforms rather than experimenting with isolated use cases.

I discovered last night that contemplating AI and the future can apparently persuade local Irish bars, which might normally have the good sense to close on a Tuesday, to reconsider their operating hours.

Economic impact, I believe, is the technical term.

Esta frase es para enmarcarla:
Los modelos por sí solos NO pueden gestionar la empresa.

Ayer se realizó Dreamforce y el anuncio de #AIforce concentró la atención, ya que redefine la capa de interfaz llevando el conocimiento empresarial de Salesforce a cualquier plataforma agéntica.

En el keynote, Marc Benioff mostró esta slide que nos llamó la atención y la compartimos acá:
Los modelos por sí solos no pueden gestionar la empresa.

Mientras los modelos de IA son probabilísticos (basan su respuesta en lo más probable), el modelo de datos de Salesforce es determinístico (contiene los procesos y reglas de la empresa).

Benioff también habla de la capa semántica, donde inviertes mucho tiempo enseñándoles a esas aplicaciones quién es tu negocio y cómo opera.

AIforce lleva esa inteligencia empresarial a Claude, a Slack o a la interfaz que use tu equipo. Por eso el agente trabaja con las reglas que tu empresa define. 

Pero ahí está el GRAN problema.

En muchas empresas, parte de esa lógica todavía vive fuera de la plataforma. Está en una planilla, en un correo o en la cabeza de un gerente. Puede estar duplicada, ser contradictoria o simplemente no existir.

Donde el sistema no tiene reglas, la IA ejecuta con lo más probable.
No existe la contraparte determinística.

I’m not quite sure one can really prepare for the scale of this!

Dreamforce brings together the people building AI, the companies putting it to work and a huge global ecosystem around Salesforce. And this year, much of it revolves around the move towards the 'Agentic Enterprise', where AI increasingly acts and performs work alongside people.

Day 1 alone brought out Dario Amodei, Jensen Huang and Sam Altman within the space of 4 hours – all in separate conversations with Marc Benioff – not to mention Marc’s opening keynote, his media session and the launch of Salesforce’s new AIforce. It was completely mind-blowing and so cool.

And in the midst of all the announcements, demos and very big visions there's an interesting tension. On one side, enormous excitement about what is becoming possible. AIforce gave a glimpse of just how deeply AI could become embedded in the actual flow of work across the context, data and workflows of an organisation. I’m super impressed.

On the other side, an increasingly serious conversation about the consequences of AI becoming this capable. Safety and human control had a prominent place today, not least in the conversation with Dario Amodei and Sam Altman (with Jensen Huang being somewhat more daring).

And somewhere between those two conversations sits the question I’m always looking at and taking with me through Dreamforce: Who gets to shape what happens next?

I had hoped to ask Marc Benioff whether, if the Agentic Enterprise is really going to change how work gets done, how we might make sure it expands human opportunity rather than concentrating it among the people who are already ahead?

I didn’t get the microphone, but I emailed him (to be continued... 😀 )

post_text:
Day 1 of #Dreamforce2026 is complete! 🎉

Yesterday, the Belmar team attended the Main Keynote featuring Marc Benioff, Chair and CEO of Salesforce. Here’s a rundown of the major announcements:

🔸 AIforce: A new live interface layer that brings Salesforce data, workflows, business logic, permissions, security, and governance into any AI interface. Instead of moving between fixed screens, users can create composable interfaces tailored to their needs.
🔸 Koa: Salesforce’s first CRM reasoning model for Agentforce, developed with NVIDIA by post-training Nemotron 3 Super on a proprietary synthetic dataset based on nearly three decades of CRM deployments. Salesforce controls the model weights and runs inference within its own infrastructure, keeping customer data inside its trust boundary.
🔸 Missionforce: Salesforce is bringing NVIDIA Nemotron models and accelerated computing to Missionforce, giving government and regulated organizations greater control over their models, data, and deployment environments.
🔸 Claudeforce and Slackforce: Salesforce expanded its partnership with Anthropic, positioning Slack as a central hub for AI agents. A live demonstration showed how prompts could create a custom interface that consolidated multiple accounts into one view with Slack integration.
🔸 Customer 360 agents: Salesforce announced new agents for Sales Cloud and Marketing Cloud, including an agent that can build campaigns, plus a shopper agent for Commerce Cloud and a voice-enabled Field Service agent.

The keynote message was clear: AI isn’t replacing software; it’s reshaping how people interact with it and reducing the manual work required.

We’re looking forward to another day of learning, connecting, and exploring what these developments could mean for nonprofits and the public sector.

Stay tuned for #DreamforceDay2!

2️⃣ 𝙆𝙤𝙖

Unlike a general-purpose AI model, Koa is built to understand how opportunities, service cases, and other CRM workflows actually operate.

3️⃣ 𝘼 𝙙𝙚𝙚𝙥𝙚𝙧 𝘼𝙒𝙎 𝙞𝙣𝙩𝙚𝙜𝙧𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣

💡 𝗠𝘆 𝗯𝗶𝗴𝗴𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆?

At Dreamforce, Marc Benioff has made a point that taps into the zeitgeist of this week, and from our perspective, perhaps overshadows the product announcements.

3. Can you reconstruct the decision later?

author_headline: President & Chief Commercial Officer, Salesforce
summary: Salesforce's Bill Patterson describes a customer halting 30K-seat AI deployment over cost fears, then details Agentic Work Units, transparent pricing, and Digital Wallet usage tracking.
post_text:
Cost Overruns are the new “AI Tax” - but they’re entirely solvable. 

Here at Dreamforce, I just met a customer who shared the most interesting story.  They’ve just purchased 30K seats of a frontier offering last quarter at the urging of their CEO, but have halted deployment. Why? Fear of cost overruns and their inability to control usage. 

That fear isn’t irrational, it’s a symptom.  Most organizations are trying to run agentic workloads on pricing and governance models built for a different era. Per-seat licensing doesn't map to an AI agent that works 24/7. Flat platform fees don't account for a workload that can 10x overnight when an agent starts fanning out across a business process. Without metering built for usage, cost becomes unpredictable - and unpredictability reads as risk.

The fix isn't "spend less on AI." It's pricing and governance that scale with value instead of guessing at it.  Here’s our approach at Salesforce : 

- Meter the unit of work performed:  we call these Agentic Work Units (AWUs) and they become a value-construct above the compute or token construct, which are hard to attribute value to. 

- Price Transparently:  publish meters, rates, multipliers, discounts in an open and transparent manner.   

- Visualize usage:  provide realtime access to usage and utilization across services and experiences in tools like our Digital Wallet. 

- Turn Commitment into Results:  give customers a ceiling they control, not a bill they discover or a shortfall “surprise”.  

This is exactly the problem we're solving: usage-based pricing that's granular enough to be fair, and governed enough to be predictable.  The companies that solve this first won't just save money. They'll be the ones their customers trust to scale with.

Cost overrun fear isn't a reason to slow down AI adoption- it's a signal the industry needs better plumbing underneath it.

What else should we be doing? Love to hear your thoughts…

Yesterday afternoon at Dreamforce with Salesforce President and Chief People Officer Nathalie Scardino and a group of people leaders talking about AI, work, and what it means to be irreplaceably human.

AI is now saving managers nearly three hours per week. But 36% of them say they waste more than half of it.

It's called the AI Efficiency Trap — when productivity gains create pressure to simply do more, feeding the very stress and burnout the technology was supposed to relieve. Avoiding that trap is the real opportunity for leaders — and it's much bigger than deploying new tools. It's being intentional about the time AI gives back: reinvesting it in recharging, in creativity, in connection, in the work that requires our full attention and judgment. And it's making clear to your people that their value is measured not in additional output for its own sake, but in their capacity to think, create and connect.

The companies that thrive in this era won't be defined by how much time AI saved them, but by how deliberately they reinvested it.

summary: Advisor Helen Yu, in a sponsored post, details Benioff's Dreamforce keynote with Dario Amodei and Jensen Huang, covering AIforce, Siemens' SAP agent demo, and governance features like zero data retention.
post_text:
What separates an Agentic Enterprise from a collection of disconnected AI pilots? #Sponsored #SalesforcePartner 

AI becomes enterprise-ready when it is grounded in trusted data and can act across real systems of record.

That was my biggest takeaway from the Dreamforce keynote, where Salesforce’s Marc Benioff was joined on stage by Anthropic's Dario Amodei and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang, my first time seeing the two of them share a stage on the same day.

Five signals that the Agentic Enterprise is becoming operational.
1️⃣ Enterprise context is the differentiator. 
Frontier models know the world, but they don't know your customers, your pipeline, or your business rules. Trusted, connected enterprise data is what turns intelligence into business value.
2️⃣ Access to data is not enough. 
AI needs the meaning, policies, processes, permissions, and relationships behind that data. Benioff framed it as four layers that must work together: data, apps and semantics, agents, and the interface.
3️⃣ The interface is shifting from navigation to intent. 
The headline launch, AIforce, puts a live, composable interface on top of Salesforce, first in Claude Cowork, then in Slack and Lightning. You describe the outcome, and AI assembles the context and coordinates the work.
4️⃣ The breakthrough is trusted execution. 
The Siemens demo showed an operations agent learning supplier onboarding in an SAP sandbox, then executing the same trusted actions every time in production. Probabilistic reasoning turned into deterministic execution, with people pulled in for exceptions.
5️⃣ Governance is an operating requirement. Zero data retention, identity, access, auditability, and human oversight workflows were positioned as built in rather than bolted on.

Dario noted that even if the technology froze today, most enterprises are capturing 5 to 10 percent of its value. Jensen pushed back on the "end of software" narrative, calling AI a layer on top of your existing systems that makes them far more useful, and urged leaders not to walk away when a pilot only delivers 80 percent, because it will be better in weeks. Read together, the gap is diffusion rather than capability.

The question for leaders is which high-value workflow can be safely redesigned once AI is connected to trusted data, business logic, and clear human accountability.

post_text:
I was at the Salesforce keynote at #Dreamforce yesterday, and one thing stood out to me more than any individual product announcement.  

The next phase of enterprise AI is going to be defined by what AI can understand not just what AI can generate.   

Salesforce laid out a pretty clear architecture for where it sees the enterprise going: 
Data → Apps & Semantics → Agents → Interface.   

That sequence is important. The keynote wasn't really about putting another AI layer on top of existing software. 

It was about connecting AI to the underlying data, business logic, workflows, permissions and business/customer context that make an enterprise unique.  

A few things stood out:  

→ Data has to be ready before AI can do meaningful work. Data 360 is being positioned as the foundation for connecting, integrating and harmonizing enterprise data.  

→ Business semantics matter. AI needs to understand what things like revenue, ARR, churn or customer health actually mean inside a particular business, not just retrieve a number.

→ Agents are becoming operators. Salesforce showed agents working across sales, service, recruiting, IT and other functions. 
That's a very different proposition from AI simply assisting a human.  

→ The interface is changing. With headless applications and experiences across environments like Slack, the application UI is no longer necessarily where enterprise work begins and ends.  

→ Governance becomes critical as agents scale. Agent Fabric and Salesforce Guardian address the inevitable questions around discovering, managing, securing and controlling an increasingly large agent workforce.  

What I found most interesting is how interconnected all of this is. 

You can't really separate the agent story from the data story. 
And you can't separate the data story from the context and business semantics underneath it.   

The more autonomous AI becomes, the more important that foundation becomes. 

That, to me, was one of the biggest messages from Dreamforce this year.  

The future of enterprise AI isn't just about building smarter models. It's about giving those models the right enterprise context, and the ability to act on it safely.  

At Nektar.ai, we have built a "trusted customer context layer" over the years which is now enabling customers like Cursor, Mimecast, Brex, Ironclad, Rogo AI, Factory AI build reliable GTM AI Agents.

Exciting to see that vision resonating so clearly from the stage.

Happy to chat with anyone who is interested in exploring this customer context layer or look at replacing "Einstein Activity Capture" #EAC that they might be struggling with to give trusted context to their GTM AI Agents.

post_text:
𝐘𝐨𝐮𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐟𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐮𝐩𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐬.

"Great call" has been inflating sales forecasts for years. Let’s be careful what we automate.

One Sales Cloud update worth examining during Dreamforce: Salesforce is building Momentum into Sales Cloud to capture conversation signals and write qualification details, next steps, and deal risks into CRM fields.

Less chasing reps for updates? We’re interested.

But the important moment is when something a buyer says becomes something your business treats as true.

Consider these four examples:

1. "We should have budget next quarter."
𝘙𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺: 𝘋𝘰𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘰𝘳𝘥 𝘱𝘳𝘦𝘴𝘦𝘳𝘷𝘦 𝘵𝘩𝘦 𝘶𝘯𝘤𝘦𝘳𝘵𝘢𝘪𝘯𝘵𝘺 𝘰𝘳 𝘴𝘶𝘨𝘨𝘦𝘴𝘵 𝘧𝘶𝘯𝘥𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘪𝘴 𝘢𝘱𝘱𝘳𝘰𝘷𝘦𝘥?

2. "Our CFO will need to weigh in."
𝘙𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺: 𝘋𝘰𝘦𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘮𝘦𝘢𝘯 𝘸𝘦’𝘷𝘦 𝘪𝘥𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘪𝘧𝘪𝘦𝘥 𝘢 𝘥𝘦𝘤𝘪𝘴𝘪𝘰𝘯-𝘮𝘢𝘬𝘦𝘳 𝘰𝘳 𝘢𝘤𝘵𝘶𝘢𝘭𝘭𝘺 𝘦𝘯𝘨𝘢𝘨𝘦𝘥 𝘸𝘪𝘵𝘩 𝘰𝘯𝘦?

3. "We’d love to move quickly."
𝘙𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺: 𝘐𝘴 𝘵𝘩𝘦𝘳𝘦 𝘢 𝘱𝘶𝘳𝘤𝘩𝘢𝘴𝘪𝘯𝘨 𝘥𝘦𝘢𝘥𝘭𝘪𝘯𝘦 𝘣𝘦𝘩𝘪𝘯𝘥 𝘵𝘩𝘢𝘵 𝘦𝘯𝘵𝘩𝘶𝘴𝘪𝘢𝘴𝘮?

4. "Send something over."
𝘙𝘦𝘢𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘺: 𝘋𝘪𝘥 𝘸𝘦 𝘴𝘦𝘤𝘶𝘳𝘦 𝘢 𝘯𝘦𝘹𝘵 𝘴𝘵𝘦𝘱... 𝘰𝘳 𝘫𝘶𝘴𝘵 𝘳𝘦𝘤𝘦𝘪𝘷𝘦 𝘢 𝘱𝘰𝘭𝘪𝘵𝘦 𝘦𝘹𝘪𝘵?

These are the distinctions we’d test before letting generated updates influence forecasts or trigger downstream work.

Salesforce says Momentum sandbox access is rolling out in September, with production availability following later this quarter. That gives teams a useful place to start. 

𝐈𝐟 𝐈'𝐦 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠: Take 10 real calls. Include a stalled deal, a vague budget discussion, and a buyer who contradicts an earlier commitment.

Compare the generated fields with the actual conversation. Check whether uncertainty survives, whether corrections stick, and whether a manager can trace an update back to its evidence.

Measure the admin time saved. Count the unsupported conclusions, too.

Retire the data-entry nagging. Keep the deal discipline.

"The AI filled it in" won’t be much comfort when you’re explaining the miss.

Anthropic's customer support now runs on a Salesforce agent, and Salesforce's sales team now runs inside Claude.

Once you see that two companies swapped front doors, the rest of Dreamforce reads differently.

Fin, Salesforce's new Agentforce agent, resolves 79% of Anthropic's support conversations, while 7,000 Salesforce salespeople use Claude without ever opening Salesforce.

First, every layer of Salesforce became replaceable.

It can run on Google Cloud from November, it reasons with Claude by default or with Koa, its own model built on NVIDIA's open Nemotron, and with the new AI Harness it plans to govern agents that customers built elsewhere. Cloud, model, interface and even governance stopped being Salesforce-only.

Second, agents stopped being pilots.

Siemens put Agentforce in front of 18,000 sellers across 132 countries, and Coworker reached 100,000 users in its first 35 days, which is headcount scale rather than a proof of concept.

Third, when cloud, model and interface can all be swapped, the only layer that cannot is the customer's own org, with its data, its permissions and the 10 years of decisions that make one company's Salesforce behave like no one else's.

Rohan Kumar, who runs the platform, called it trusted proprietary context, and it is the one thing Salesforce cannot sell you because you built it yourselves.

So for the next year the question is no longer which agent, model or interface to pick, but whether your org turns out to be an asset or a liability once thousands of people and agents start reading it at the same time.

At Customertimes we spent the last year on exactly that, making the org legible to agents before the agents arrive.

Salesforce opened every layer it had this week, and the one it left closed is the one only you hold the key to.

post_text:
So, just a little transparency about Salesforce Dreamforce… It’s freaking overwhelming. 😅

There is SO much happening in AI right now. Walking the conference floor, booth after booth is talking about agents, automation, intelligence, personalization, orchestration, transformation…

And after a while, a lot of it starts to sound the same.

A huge part of my job at Validity Inc. is to keep a pulse on where the market is going. All leaders are required to be on top of this stuff. And really, for job safety, everyone should try regardless of level. But separating the actual value from the noise is getting harder and harder. 

What’s truly new?
What’s solving a real problem?
What’s a genuinely different approach?
And what’s the same thing with some new AI language wrapped around it?

Or… What the F does your company do? 😅

I don’t have all the answers. And I think it’s important to admit that. To admit that it’s overwhelming. Really overwhelming. But also exciting.

There is simply too much changing, too quickly, for any one person to have a perfect handle on all of it.

So I’m trying to stay curious. Ask questions. Talk to people. See the demos. Challenge my own assumptions. And learn as much as I can.

Apparently that meant walking 18,000 steps around the Dreamforce floor yesterday. 😂

So if nothing else, I am quite literally putting in the miles trying to figure it all out.

Despite the information overload, it’s been a pretty incredible few days.

Still learning. Still asking questions. Still walking. 🤣

author_headline: Enterprise CRM Engineering Director | Managing & Building Agents | AI Adoption Champion | Advisor @ Keenan Vision
summary: Chris Pearson, an enterprise CRM engineering director, questions Salesforce's new AIforce intelligence layer for lacking benchmarks or evals showing improvement over unaided Claude or ChatGPT.
post_text:
One thing I'm noticing about the (lack of) excitement at Dreamforce is how difficult it is to get a community fired up about a layer.  

AIforce, one of the big announcements, is a new layer of intelligence that is supposed to make all our interactions with Claude/ChatGPT that involve CRM work more reliably. 

Salesforce pros have been conditioned for years to build/configure/develop products - or apps.  They spent time learning how to customize screens and build workflows to meet business needs - oftentimes navigating around feature or platform limits.  

A layer doesn't have any of that. It just sits there as some form of ambient intelligence.  There's no interface, nothing to do, activate or control.  

It's left me with more questions than answers.  

Notably, why don't we have some examples of how poorly Claude or GPT perform without AIforce helping to steer and direct the AI to do what we intended? 

We've been conditioned by the large AI companies to pay attention to benchmarks, we've even added new words to our vocabulary such as "evals" which stand for evaluations of how an LLM performs against a task.  

Yet none of those concepts are present in the materials I've been given.  

Interested in others take.

summary: Evan Dryland recaps Dreamforce keynote quotes from Parker Harris, Benioff, Patrick Stokes and Dario Amodei on the new AI Force agentic interface launching first on Anthropic's Claude.
post_text:
"Why should you ever log into Salesforce again? Maybe you never will."

Salesforce's co-founder, Parker Harris' opening line at Dreamforce... played back on the main stage as a setup, not a warning.

Minutes later Marc Benioff unveiled AI Force, a live agentic interface shipping first on Anthropic's Claude.

Three reads for Sales & Marketing tech:

1. The UI stopped being the product. Patrick Stokes: "Other software companies, they think their product is the UI. But that's not what we think at Salesforce." Marc Benioff was blunter: "It's not the end of software. It's the end of software that makes humans do all the work." They built their own command center on stage by asking for it, with the first version in under 10 minutes.

2. The moat moved to grounding, not the model. "Models alone cannot run the enterprise… they're probabilistic." Data 360, Tableau semantics, Guardian, Agent Fabric all exist to put deterministic data under probabilistic agents. Differentiation built on the model layer is rented.

3. The stack is being absorbed. Hunter (AI sales agent for SMB) ships with "your data vendors built right in; ZoomInfo, Demandbase, Apollo." Qualified (Piper) and Finn now sit inside AgentForce, bundled into AI Force Max.

And there continues to be room to run. Claude's Dario Amodei: "we're making use of maybe only 5 or 10% of what the possible value of the technology is." 

Reinforced by Marc Benioff himself, describing two months of customer visits: "what I saw was a lot of unevenness when it comes to AI… some of our customers are kind of stuck." He asked CEOs and CIOs whether they'd been through an enterprise transformation. The answer: "Well, we've got this pilot going or we tried this or we did that."

Distribution is consolidating. Adoption isn't.

That gap is still where founder led companies win.

summary: AI analyst Mark Smith argues Salesforce's AIforce, Enterprise AI Harness, Agent Fabric, Guardian, Data 360, Agentforce and Koa (built with NVIDIA Nemotron) mark its biggest architectural shift ever, becoming a headless, composable enterprise AI platform.
post_text:
The force of AI is running strong at Dreamforce, but the most important Salesforce announcement is not another AI agent. It is the architectural shift underneath them.
AIforce, building on Salesforce’s new Enterprise AI Harness, Agent Fabric, Guardian, Data 360 and Agentforce, is repositioning Salesforce as an enterprise AI platform with a control plane for how AI is governed, secured, observed and put to work.

What is most interesting to me is that Salesforce is moving its applications down a layer in the technology stack. 

At the top is increasingly an interface layer where the experience can be Claude, Slack, another AI tool or a dynamically generated application. Underneath sits Salesforce with the data, metadata, business logic, permissions, workflows and actions needed to get work done.
Salesforce is essentially saying: you may never have to log into Salesforce again to use Salesforce.

That is a fundamental shift from decades of structured interactions through Salesforce applications and the Lightning experience. The Headless Platform, MCP and Agentforce make Salesforce increasingly composable. But headless only matters if the underlying platform has something valuable to expose. 

Salesforce has decades of customer investments, processes, data and metadata that can now become accessible to humans and agents through entirely different experiences.
I was also encouraged by Koa, Salesforce’s new CRM reasoning model developed with NVIDIA using Nemotron. Enterprise AI does not need to depend entirely on frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI. Specialized and open models will be increasingly important for bringing AI economically and securely into business processes.

We are entering a new generation of composable enterprise applications. In some ways, it brings back the vision of enterprise portals from the early 2000s, except now the experience is generated, conversational and powered by AI that can actually act and learn.

From my perspective, this may be the most substantive architectural change to Salesforce since its beginning.

Salesforce is no longer asking enterprises only to evaluate its applications. It wants to be evaluated as part of the enterprise AI architecture itself. Salesforce will be part of the AI and Software battle for your enterprise. Now you must determine where and how you will accomplish that.

Marc Benioff enthusiasm and excitement around the announcements were unmistakable, reinforced by his ability to bring Jensen Huang of NVIDIA, Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman of OpenAI to Dreamforce and into the conversation about where enterprise AI is heading. Along with facilitating some dialogue on the pacing and safety industry debate.

More to come in my formal analysis of Dreamforce.

author_headline: Bureau Chief Silicon Valley at Wirtschaftswoche, Moderator, Speaker, Germany's Top 50 Tech Influencer
summary: Wirtschaftswoche's Matthias Hohensee reports Siemens CEO Roland Busch telling Marc Benioff at a Dreamforce fireside chat that students should study engineering or physics, not software, to judge AI outputs.
post_text:
Was sollten junge Leute im Zeitalter der KI eigentlich noch studieren?

Die Frage wird mir in letzter Zeit oft gestellt, sowohl von deutschen als auch amerikanischen Bekannten und Freunden. "Du beschäftigst dich doch damit, was meinst Du?" Und ich muss gestehen, dass ich mich mit einer Antwort schwer tue.

Siemens-Chef Roland Busch gab darauf heute auf der Dreamforce im Fireside Chat mit Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff eine überraschend konkrete Antwort. Wenn ihn Eltern oder junge Leute fragten, was sie studieren sollten, sei seine Antwort nicht unbedingt Software oder Informatik.

„Ich weiß es natürlich nicht genau. Was ich aber weiß, ist, dass die Nachfrage in Zukunft mit Kreativität zusammenhängen wird, mit der Art, wie man mit Menschen umgeht, also mit dem sozialen Aspekt. Und sie wird mit der Physik, mit der realen Welt verbunden sein.“

Deshalb, so Busch weiter: „Ich rate sehr häufig dazu, Maschinenbau oder Elektrotechnik zu studieren, also etwas, bei dem man wirklich lernt, welche Physik dahintersteckt. Solides Maschinenbauwissen gibt einem eine völlig andere Möglichkeit, KI-Werkzeuge zu nutzen, als wenn man dieses Wissen nicht hat. Denn dann kann man sich selbst ein Urteil bilden.“

Busch selbst ist ausgebildeter Physiker. Physiker hätten eine besondere Art, Probleme zu betrachten, meint er: Sie versuchten, die Welt so weit zu vereinfachen, dass sie sich mathematisch beschreiben lasse. Diese Fähigkeit helfe dabei, beurteilen zu können, ob eine von einer KI vorgeschlagene Lösung „in der konkreten Realität wirklich funktioniert“ oder falsch sei.

Aber es muss nicht unbedingt Physik sein. „Manche sagen: Beschäftigt euch mit den Künsten, denn diese erlauben eine völlig andere Art, auf Dinge zu schauen. Wenn man das noch mit richtig fundiertem Ingenieurwissen verbindet, kommt man vielleicht auf neue Ideen.“
Und schließlich der klassische Rat: „Am besten ist es, wenn man liebt, was man tut."

Gleichzeitig, mahnt Busch,  müsse man neue Technologien annehmen. Sich ihnen zu verweigern, sei keine gute Idee.
„KI wird die Welt in den kommenden Jahren verändern. Das ist sicher. Also sollte man sie besser annehmen.“

Interessant ist, dass Siemens daraus bereits Konsequenzen zieht. Busch erzählte von einem Besuch bei den Softwareentwicklern seines Konzerns in Los Angeles. „Sie erzählten mir, dass sie wieder Maschinenbau- und Elektroingenieure einstellen und nicht spezifisch Leute für reine Softwaregeschäft.“

Der Grund laut Busch: „Unsere Leute müssen künftig vor allem festlegen, was die Software leisten soll. Das ist entscheidend. Den eigentlichen Code kann dann die KI schreiben. Aber in den Anforderungen stecken das Fachwissen und das Verständnis dafür, wie die reale Welt funktioniert.“

Stop your ego-flation. 

You're not quite Agentic AI guru you think you see in the mirror.  You're as much a neophytes as the rest of us. 

Today's question for anyone at Dreamforce or purchasing an Agentic platform is simple. 

Ask anyone who sells something agentic to explain what Agentic AI means in simple terms

If they cannot answer this question, which I bet they can't, then you're at risk of purchasing the brake pads that Tommy Boy talked about that just slapped a sticker on the box.

Now, if you aren't quite sure what Agentic AI means, here is what you're looking for in the answer.

First, most AI is lyjng to you and simply telling you want you want to hear. They're not straight up lying, they are simply agreeing with a single transactinal approach to your question and the answer. 

Which is very dangerous one if you're the rep trusting it with a forecast. 

Now for the cool part, I was interviewing Outreach's CEO, Abhijit Mitra and he answered the question, "What is Agentic AI?"  in the simplest way to understand.

This was my take away and falls under the buzzword umbrella of content might be king, but context is the kingdom. 

Agentic AI is not about doing one or two different tasks and simply answering your prompt. That's transactional. 

Agentic AI is about the understanding the larger context and strategy based on the data. 

What it really means is about focusing on the revenue architecture so the agent understands "the why" of the task in addition to the workflow relations, as well as bigger picture goals in addition to relevant smaller information. 

Example: 

An agent that flags a stalled deal isn't agentic.  An agent that flags the deal as stalled is simply content related. 

An agent knowing why the workflow and why the workflow is stalled, what happens next in the process and variety outcomes if nobody acts.,hat's the kingdom. 

Knowing why the workflow stalled, knows what happens next in the process and variable outcomes if nobody acts.  That's the kingdom.

But across Dreamforce and UNBOUND, I think Salesforce and HubSpot are confronting the same problem:

AI could make our CRM more valuable while making per-seat pricing harder to justify.
  - Salesforce’s AIforce brings CRM data and workflows into Claude Code and Slack.
  - AIforce could drive more work through CRM while leaving fewer human seats to bill for.
  - HubSpot’s Smart CRM updates itself. Breeze assigns work to agents. 
 
Ahead of UNBOUND, Stifel Bank maintained Hold, worried about when AI would generate meaningful revenue.

“AI is creating an interface revolution,” Marc Benioff said. "Our customer history, permissions, and workflows still matter. Agents need them."

But if agents handle more prospecting, follow-up, and service, we could buy fewer human seats and more AI usage.

A higher software bill could still be a great deal if our total cost of winning and serving customers falls.

This all becomes a renewal conversation, ... cost per closed deal and resolved case, including the people, the platform, and the agents.

That standard applies to stand alone AI Employees like ours at Atonom, too.

If we’re paying for AI productivity, the savings need to show up in our P&L in growth and savings.

while the work happens. For example, a PM flags a bug, the agent proposes a fix, the engineer reviews and ships it, and everyone can see it happening. People who have never written code can be part of building it, and that opens up a kind of creativity teams haven’t had access to before!

But this is part of something even bigger. Salesforce also announced AIforce: for 25 years you went to Salesforce. Now, Salesforce comes to you. Inside Slack, inside Claude, wherever you already spend your day, with the same data and the same permissions you have today. When the tool you’re already in knows your business, the answer shows up in the conversation instead of multiple tabs away.

I also got to sit down with Rob Seaman, EVP and GM of Slack, to talk about where team
collaboration goes from here. That interview is coming next week and I can’t wait to share it.

author_headline: I redesign how work gets done, using AI agents instead of headcount growth · $25M Delivery P&L · 40% value & productivity target · Delivery Leader - Life science and Healthcare @ Genpact
summary: Delivery leader details Salesforce's Air India Agentforce pilot for refunds under 4 hours and name changes under 30 minutes, quoting CEO Arundhati Bhattacharya on compliance and auditability.
post_text:
Enterprise agents are leaving the demo booth. The first test is a refund desk. At Dreamforce 2026, Salesforce announced that Air India will use Agentforce-powered AI agents for refund requests, baggage and loyalty claims, eligibility checks, and ticket reissues. The test is operational.

Two numbers make this concrete. Refunds in under 4 hours, and requested name changes in under 30 minutes.

That is where enterprise AI becomes real.

Not in a keynote.
Not in a model leaderboard.
At the counter where a customer is waiting and the process has to close.

Salesforce South Asia CEO Arundhati Bhattacharya also said Indian enterprises have moved faster than they were 12 months ago, from experiments toward serious deployments. But she added the important bit: security, compliance and auditability are now part of the buying decision. Audit matters.

The plain reading is useful.

The agent is not the product by itself. The operating wrapper is the product: data access, workflow permissions, audit trail, human-in-the-loop decision points, and a clear recovery path when the answer is wrong. The wrapper decides.

I read the Air India example as a service-level agreement story, not an automation story. The SLA is the story.

It is like adding a new ticket clerk at a busy station. The question is not whether the clerk can speak quickly. The real question is whether the clerk can issue the right ticket, follow the fare rules, and leave a receipt the supervisor can inspect. The receipt matters.

For Indian enterprises, start with one queue.

Pick a queue with volume.
Define the turnaround time.
Define the exception path.
Measure whether the human supervisor gets fewer messy cases, not just more generated replies.

Start where the queue hurts. Which customer queue would you automate first: refunds, claims, onboarding, or internal helpdesk?

Today I skipped the gym, which I usually go to 5 days a week, and went for a long morning walk instead. I listened to the Day 1 keynote of Salesforce Dreamforce 2026 (held in San Francisco, USA on September 15, 2026) on YouTube. Thanks to my YouTube Premium account, I didn't get a single ad, so I got to listen to the whole thing non-stop! Sharing my summary below 👇
  
🔹 Marc Benioff used the word "karma" while welcoming Dario Amodei on stage, praising Anthropic's partnership with Salesforce as "good karma" and "karmic and kismet."
  
As someone from India, it genuinely warmed my heart to hear a Sanskrit word like "karma" used so naturally by a top tech leader on a global stage like this. Small moment, but it stayed with me. 🙏
  
🔹 Jensen Huang pushed back on AI job-loss fears, calling the idea that "AI is going to destroy jobs" completely nonsense — arguing AI is a new layer on top of software, not a replacement for people.
  
🔹 Dario Amodei compared the AI industry's safety approach to a car company responding to a rival's safety incident — review your own practices, invest more in safety, then work together on industry-wide standards. He also said that even if AI capabilities stopped improving today, we've only put 5–10% of what current AI can already do into real use — there's still a lot of untapped value in just applying what exists.
  
🔹 Salesforce showcased its "Marshall" agent learning to operate inside an SAP sandbox in ~90 minutes, then executing supplier onboarding autonomously in live SAP — addressing what they called the point "where the majority of AI projects hit a wall."

author_headline: Head of Product | Fintech, Digital Banking & Multi-Platform Ecosystems | Growth, Care & Omnichannel CX
summary: Product head Manuel M. shares Dreamforce 2026 takeaways from Benioff, Amodei, Altman, Huang and AlOlama, highlighting Salesforce's Aiforce interface strategy across Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and Slack.
post_text:
Estos días tuve la oportunidad de participar de Dreamforce 2026 en San Francisco, representando a ueno bank S.A. , itti y Grupo Vázquez SAE junto a Ursula Krochik , Melina Andrea Di Rosa y Juan Ignacio Olivares  

Más allá de los lanzamientos, me llevo varias ideas interesantes después de escuchar a Marc Benioff , CEO de Salesforce; Dario Amodei , CEO de Anthropic; Sam Altman, CEO de OpenAI; Jensen Huang , CEO de NVIDIA; y Omar Sultan AlOlama , Ministro de Estado de Inteligencia Artificial de Emiratos Árabes Unidos.

Algunos aprendizajes que me quedaron:

• La interfaz empieza a dejar de ser el producto. Con Aiforce, Salesforce plantea un modelo donde su plataforma, sus datos y sus procesos pueden vivir detrás de distintas interfaces como Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini o Slack. La UI empieza a construirse de manera mucho más dinámica alrededor de cada usuario y cada contexto.

• El desafío pasa de incorporar IA a integrarla con el negocio real. Los modelos probabilísticos necesitan convivir con procesos, permisos, datos y reglas determinísticas para poder operar dentro de una empresa.

• Los agentes empiezan a desafiar la ciberseguridad. Sam Altman habló de cómo agentes cada vez más capaces obligan a repensar los modelos tradicionales de seguridad, especialmente a partir de los incidentes recientes con sistemas autónomos (Huggingface)

• En ventas, el contexto en tiempo real pasa a ser parte central del CRM. Capturar actividad mientras sucede, detectar oportunidades en riesgo, resumir automáticamente el trabajo de los equipos y utilizar agentes para encontrar nuevos leads cambia bastante la lógica tradicional de carga y seguimiento comercial.

• En servicio, no alcanza con automatizar conversaciones. El foco empieza a estar en agentes que resuelven, aprenden de cada interacción y ayudan a optimizar continuamente los canales de atención.

• Y probablemente el aprendizaje que más me quedó fue de Omar Sultan Al Olama: la adopción de IA no es solamente un problema tecnológico. Es también un problema de educación, confianza, regulación y acceso.

Su planteo sobre acercar a quienes innovan con quienes regulan me pareció especialmente relevante. También la decisión de Emiratos de capacitar masivamente a su población y a empleados públicos en IA para que la transformación tecnológica no deje a las personas sin herramientas para adaptarse.

Una frase que resume bastante de lo que me llevo de Dreamforce: la discusión ya no parece ser si vamos a trabajar con agentes de IA, sino cómo construimos empresas e instituciones preparadas para hacerlo de manera útil, segura y responsable.

summary: Healthcare/product leader Andjela Azabagic recaps Siemens CEO Roland Busch and Marc Benioff discussing industrial AI, noting Siemens' shift from a 'fleet of ships' to one unified technology company.
post_text:
Another great Dreamforce conversation — Roland Busch , CEO of Siemens, with Marc Benioff, CEO of Salesforce, on industrial AI, transformation, and what it really takes to change a company at scale.

One point really stood out: AI does not respect silos. And you cannot scale AI if the organization itself is fragmented.

Siemens  has been moving from what Roland described as a “fleet of ships” toward one technology company — connecting automation, electrification, software, AI, manufacturing, and customer experience around the problems customers are actually trying to solve.

A few takeaways I found especially relevant:

• AI at scale is an operating model challenge, not just a technology challenge.
• Transformation is cultural. Leaders have to bring people with them, explain the “why,” and create room to learn, unlearn, and experiment.
• Innovation requires build + buy + partner. No company can develop every capability itself.
• Deep domain expertise may become even more valuable in the AI era. AI can increasingly help build software, but people still need to understand the physics, context, requirements, and real-world problem.
• Global scale doesn’t mean global sameness. Different regions bring different strengths — from deep tech and commercialization to engineering expertise and speed of innovation.

The last point really resonated with me.

As AI becomes more capable, the differentiator may be less about simply knowing how to use AI — and more about how well we combine it with domain expertise, creativity, judgment, and real-world understanding.

That’s where I think some of the most meaningful transformation will happen.

Sumeru Inc

summary: Executive search consultant Niall Cook argues Salesforce copied ServiceNow's Bill McDermott by launching an AI Control Plane, contrasting Benioff's economic-rents defense with McDermott's deterministic governance stance.
post_text:
Bill McDermott built the control tower. Marc Benioff copied it for Dreamforce. The crash happens anyway.

Salesforce just surrendered an argument it never admitted it was having.

Rivals only ever tell you three things. Mockery means you are winning. Silence means you have won. Copying means it is over. Last week Salesforce copied.

Not on stage. Benioff spent Tuesday defending Salesforce's economic rents. 

The confirmation came five days earlier in a press release most people skipped. An AI Control Plane. One place to govern every agent in the enterprise, including the ones Salesforce did not build.

McDermott shipped that in May 2025. The AI Control Tower. Any agent, any vendor. The ecosystem shrugged. Governance only looks boring until an agent does something nobody can undo.

Now count the arrivals.

May 2025, ServiceNow. May 2026, Microsoft, at fifteen dollars a seat. This quarter, SAP, and Christian Klein will govern rivals' agents for free. February at the earliest, Salesforce, same idea, new noun.

Four vendors. Four towers. One blueprint, and McDermott drew it.

Here is what four keynotes left out.

Nobody sends me a brief for someone who can pick a tower.

The brief arrives after the first agent goes wrong with a perfect record. Every permission granted. Every action logged. Every tower waved it through. The money still went to the wrong place. The agent trusted a record nobody owned.

Then the client wants the person who owns the record. That job barely exists yet.

The tower did its job. It was the wrong job.

McDermott set the bar at Knowledge:
"You can't have a probabilistic solution for an enterprise. It has to be deterministic, and it has to be right every time."

Benioff on Tuesday was defending the airline, not the flight:
"AI is not going to eliminate our software or impact our economic rents."

A control tower governs what an aircraft may do. It has never once corrected a chart. If the map is wrong, the tower clears a perfectly governed flight into a hillside.

Salesforce's own research says the average company runs twelve agents. Everyone believes whatever the data beneath it says. Not one tower checks whether that data is true.

A tower governs permission. What an agent may do.

Nobody yet governs belief. What an agent takes to be true before it moves.
Permission was the easy half, and three rivals just spent a year copying it.

Belief is the hard half. Either McDermott ships it first again, or Benioff learns to copy faster. Only one of them has ever been first.
