summary: Amit Asthana lists Dreamforce announcements—Hunter, long-horizon runtime, Multi-Agent Orchestration, AIforce, Agent Optimizer, Marshall, Agent Script—linking them to Salesforce's outage and resilience needs.
post_text:
One of my biggest takeaways from Dreamforce this week came from connecting the announcements with something Salesforce definitely didn’t plan….Yesterday’s outage!

Let’s look at what Salesforce  announced so far at Dreamforce 26:

→ Hunter, the new outbound sales agent, can work opportunities over weeks and months, not just complete a single prompt.

→ The new long-horizon Agentforce runtime adds memory, durable execution and dynamic steering so agents can keep working towards a goal across multiple sessions.

→ Multi-Agent Orchestration lets specialised agents hand work between each other when a process crosses teams or systems.

→ AIforce now lets Claude, Slack and other interfaces trigger Salesforce workflows and actions without users even opening Salesforce.

Simply put, we are now in a very different world from a chatbot answering a question!

Let’s imagine a sales agent has been working an opportunity for three days. It has researched the account, updated CRM records, triggered tasks and handed work to another agent. Then a dependency goes down….

Yesterday Salesforce reported severe delays, intermittent errors and inability to access some services across multiple regions after an internal login service became constrained.

So the questions I would now ask in every serious agent programme are:

-> Can it resume where it stopped?
-> Can it tell what already completed?
-> Can it retry without doing something twice?
-> Can a human see exactly what happened?
-> Can work move to a safe fallback?

Good news is that Salesforce is already moving in this direction.

Agent Optimizer will analyse session traces to identify where agents need improving. Marshall, the new supply-chain agent, provides an audit record of every action. Agent Script combines probabilistic AI reasoning with deterministic business rules.

So, my biggest Dreamforce lesson so far is : Enterprise AI isn’t just about making agents smarter, it’s about making failure boring. Once agents are doing real work for days rather than answering questions for seconds, resilience, observability and recovery become part of the AI product.

 3️⃣ Marc's fireside with H.E. Omar Sultan AlOlama, the world's first AI Minister, appointed in 2017, "the year 3 B.C." (before Covid!). An interesting conversation about how a state can have the vision and the eagerness to explore, experiment, and eventually embrace disruption. The Middle East's experience with banning the Gutenberg printing press for 200 years offers surprising parallels with regulating AI and how to make up for lost time in innovation and technology adoption. post_text:
Hundreds of booths. One afternoon. Most people walk the Dreamforce expo floor collecting swag and leave with nothing else. Here's how to actually use it.
The floor breaks down into 3 things 👇
🔹 Salesforce product booths Staffed by actual Salesforce PMs and engineers — hands-on demos of what's new and what's coming. Free to browse, no pitch involved.

🔹 ISV / partner booths (AppExchange) Third-party apps that extend Salesforce. This is the one place on the floor where you actually need a 
strategy, not just curiosity.

🔹 Community & Trailblazer zones Certification stations, user group meetups, career help. Also zero sales pitch — just people.
The middle one is where most of the value (and most of the risk) lives, so here's the read-a-booth-like-an-admin version:

Native or managed package? Native means it's built directly on the platform. A managed package is installed and upgraded on its own schedule, separate from your org
Security review status? Anything actually listed on AppExchange has to pass Salesforce's security review first — ask to see the listing. If they can't show you one, that's your answer
Pricing model & support SLA? Per user or per org? What's actually included in support, and what starts costing extra the moment you need it?
Fun fact: a booth can look genuinely impressive and still not be listed on AppExchange at all. That alone is worth asking about before a demo goes any further.
Bring this exact 5-question script with you, it takes about 90 seconds per booth and filters out booth theater fast:
"Is this native, or a managed package?" "Can I see your AppExchange security review?" "What's the pricing model?" "What's included in support, what costs extra?" "Got a reference customer my size I can talk to?"
That last one is the fastest filter of all. Most vendors who are just there for the pitch can't produce a reference on the spot.
🔹 3 habits for using the floor well
Bring a real problem, not just curiosity — you'll get a sharper demo, and a faster no if it's not a fit
Scan the badge, but take your own notes — booth staff talk to hundreds of people a day, your 2-line note is what you'll actually remember later
Follow up within a week — interest fades fast on both sides, and the vendors who follow up well are often the ones worth a second look

author_headline: GTM Engineer | RevOps Architect | Building the systems behind revenue
summary: João Coelho says Salesforce declared reps will stop logging into the CRM directly and outlines five gates—written definitions, field permissions, read-before-write access—before agents get write access.
post_text:
Salesforce Just Said Your Reps Won't Log In Anymore. Is Your CRM Ready For That?

This week at Dreamforce, Salesforce put an interface layer on top of the CRM and said the quiet part out loud: you won't need to log into Salesforce anymore. Work happens from Claude, from Slack, from whatever UI you build. The CRM becomes a database with agents on top.

My opinion? It's a good thing. That's where the stack is going, and it's where I already work: CLI over UI, the whole thing run through agents, and the last time I opened a CRM's interface to do actual work was to fix something the CLI and the agents couldn't reach.

But here's the part the keynote skips.

The interface was doing work nobody wrote down. A rep looking at a screen filled the empty field, ignored the wrong stage, corrected the record by hand and moved on. Take the screen away and the agent inherits every definition you never wrote, and acts on it, at scale, confidently. The data model stops being plumbing and becomes the product.

Five gates to check before any agent gets write access to your CRM:

1️⃣ Definitions, Written and Enforced
What a qualified lead is, what an open opportunity is, what counts as an activity, who owns what, what a next step means. In most CRMs I've walked into, "activity" has no definition at all, and that's the one the agent will act on first.

2️⃣ Field Permissions
What writes where, which fields are required, which values are allowed, who can overwrite whom. An agent updating a stage without a contract is a rep with no manager and infinite time to corrupt your data.

3️⃣ Read Before Write
Every agent runs read-only first. Write access is granted by object, never globally. A standard I enforce on every agent I build, and it saves a lot of course corrections, because the agent contextualizes itself before it acts.

4️⃣ Human Ladder
Approve every action at first. Once you've identified the common outcomes and patterns, build the list of actions it can run on its own and review it weekly. Once that's refined, set an alarm that notifies you when something looks off and let it run unattended. Each step earns the next with a number, and a bad number sends it back down. Nobody skips the first rung because a demo went well.

5️⃣ Kill Condition
Written before the first action. The data-quality drop, the forecast swing nobody can explain, the rep quietly overriding it. What stops the agent and who gets paged in the first hour.

A test you can run this afternoon: pick ten records your team touched this week and ask whether an agent, reading only what's in the fields, would have done what the rep did. If the answer is "it depends," your CRM isn't ready for an interface layer.

What the announcement gets right? The UI was never the product.

What it quietly assumes? That the model underneath was built for something other than humans looking at it. Most weren't.

post_text:
𝐓𝐡𝐞 "𝐖𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐃𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐦𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝟒𝟕 𝐈𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐬" 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 — 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐅𝐢𝐱 𝐨𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐞𝐞𝐤

This happens every year.

Teams come back from Dreamforce fired up. A list of sessions they attended, features they want to implement, and things they told their manager they were going to do.

By November, most of it hasn't moved.

Not because the ideas were bad. Because there was no process for deciding which ones were worth doing first.

Here's the framework I use with clients after any big Salesforce event.

Write everything down first. All 47 ideas. Get them out of your head and into one place before you lose them.

Then sort by two questions only. Does this solve a problem the team is feeling right now? And do we have the data foundation to support it?

Anything that scores yes on both moves to the top. Everything else goes on a backlog for later.

Then pick one. Not five. One. The thing that is most broken, most felt, and most fixable in the next 30 days.

Build that. Measure it. Then go back to the list.

Dreamforce inspiration is only useful if it turns into something your team actually experiences on a Tuesday morning three months from now.

That's the standard worth holding.

#Salesforce demoed an Autonomous Agent breaking into #SAP during its Dreamforce keynote yesterday.
It is impressive, but last time I checked, not allowed by SAP in many angles.
If you watch the video, Marshall logs into a Sandbox SAP , spent 85 minutes clicking through 51 S/4HANA transactions (vendor master, purchase orders, deliveries, maintenance orders, and SE16N), recorded every field and branch, and packaged them as MCPs.
That's an impressive demo, where no OData, no BAPI, no API Hub, just an autonomous agent wearing a user badge.

- The problem is in SAP's API Policy; there are specific sections that forbid "impersonation techniques"
- The problem is in the policy: any Autonomous AI must go through SAP "endorsed architectures".
- The "problem" is Mark Benioff knows 100% that this is the most polished ungoverned integration to SAP that he could show on stage, yet he did it. 
Not only did they connect to the SAP API to update a Supplier, which would have been simple but no WOW effect required for a keynote. They connected to an SAP system, captured SAP application logic, ME21N required fields, how the BP role model works, MRKO's settlement steps... the complete SAP's product behavior.

If this is not part of a new partnership between SAP and Salesforce (which I am not aware of), it might not even be a problem for Salesforce because that Marshall Agent is "custom made", meaning, its not an Agentforce feature; they just built it, so the problem lies in its usage. That means, if any customer thinks, "This is great, can I do that?" the answer comes from SAP.

For that, you must have someone who really understands SAP by your side; it can be done, but differently. Mark knows; probably that's why he brought this demo to the keynote.
Now, if Salesforce has a "partner VIP pass" which I am not aware of, let me know.

post_text:
It's events season. In the GTM world, nothing demonstrates that more clearly than UNBOUND and Dreamforce which both kicked off this week. 

Event marketing is usually one of the biggest line items in the budget. It's also the one nobody can defend with a number.
 
I don't think that's a measurement problem. I think it's a decision problem.
 
Ask a team why they're going to a show and you'll get one of three answers.
1) We go every year. 
2) Our competitors will be there. 
3) We scanned 400 badges last year.

None of those are business cases, and none of them produces a target you could measure the event against later.
 
So the measurement never fails. It never starts. There's nothing to measure against, so the debrief becomes a story about booth traffic and how the dinners went.
 
The fix isn't a better post-event report. It's deciding at kickoff what the event is supposed to produce, and how to definitively measure ROI. Better to do that up front than to argue about it after the event.
 
I built a calculator that helps marketers set objectives the whole team agrees on and produces a measurement scorecard that ties the investment to outcomes. You'll find the calculator on my Resources page. Link in the first comment.

summary: Justin Panzer argues event ROI measurement fails because teams lack upfront objectives, and promotes his free calculator for setting measurable Dreamforce/UNBOUND event goals.
post_text:
It's events season. In the GTM world, nothing demonstrates that more clearly than UNBOUND and Dreamforce which both kicked off this week.
Event marketing is usually one of the biggest line items in the budget. It's also the one nobody can defend with a number.

I don't think that's a measurement problem. I think it's a decision problem.

Ask a team why they're going to a show and you'll get one of three answers.
1) We go every year.
2) Our competitors will be there.
3) We scanned 400 badges last year.
None of those are business cases, and none of them produces a target you could measure the event against later.

So the measurement never fails. It never starts. There's nothing to measure against, so the debrief becomes a story about booth traffic and how the dinners went.

The fix isn't a better post-event report. It's deciding at kickoff what the event is supposed to produce, and how to definitively measure ROI. Better to do that up front than to argue about it after the event.

I built a calculator that helps marketers set objectives the whole team agrees on and produces a measurement scorecard that ties the investment to outcomes. You'll find the calculator on my Resources page. Link in the first comment.

summary: Mike Coutts, a commercial operations consultant, reports Dreamforce felt "thin," citing 30,000 live Agentforce customers, 1,300 sessions, and four recurring themes: messy data, rep admin burden, change management, and pace of change.
post_text:
This Dreamforce felt thin.

It was my tenth or so. Over nearly two decades I have watched Salesforce pioneer innovation, mostly from inside industrial companies using the platform to run commercial operations.

The thinness was not the production. AIforce, Claudeforce, Slackforce, and Agentforce were everywhere, and Salesforce says 30,000 customers are live on Agentforce. It was the hallway conversations. Enterprises have had about twelve months to live with the AI mandate, and the people carrying it are tired.

Four themes repeated across roundtables, customer conversations, and first-time attendees, about as reliably as the safe-harbor statement that opened every one of the more than 1,300 sessions:
1. The data is still messy. What is new is a layer that will be confidently wrong about it. AI now has to clear the same trust barrier CRM never fully cleared.

2. Reps still spend too much time on administration. We were fighting that in 2014. We are fighting it in 2026 with a larger budget.

3. Change management is the line item most often cut, and it is about to get harder. We are moving from structured systems, where the workflow is defined for the user, to unstructured ones, where the user decides what to ask. Most companies never won adoption on the structured version.

4. Pace of change is now its own problem. No one masters a craft that is redesigned every quarter.

A year ago, executives funded AI, handed it to their teams, and said go. Some teams disliked what they got. More have not found the value. The phrase I kept hearing behind closed doors: "we can taste it, but we haven't captured it."

What has held for me over the past 18 months: the first use case has to be small, measurable, and it is usually not the one on the slide. Many companies in 2026 still lack a conditioned muscle around lead management or case handling. 

That gap is the Manual Tax, and it is where the revenue is. An agent placed on top of it does not remove the tax. It automates it.

If you were there, which of the four did you hear most?

summary: Salesforce SVP Martin Kihn details the newly announced Campaign Agent, explaining its Coworking and Decisioning phases, Content Personalization, Review Gates and Send Prioritization features.
post_text:
💥 💥 Dreamforce continues to dazzle this week and today's Marketing keynote features big news ...  💥 💥 

... in the form of CAMPAIGN AGENT

This is an acceleration of the Marketing Goals Agent bruited at Connections incorporating also Content Personalization and CMS

 👉 So what does Campaign Agent do for you?

Well marketing is more complicated than other functions IMO because it has so many moments-of-decision both for machines and for the people involved

So think of this Campaign Agent as a "campaign-coworker" rather than a self-driving marketing operation

There's 2 PHASES:

 👉  👉 (1) Coworking - (I told you) - which is the very human-mediated process of defining a campaign, pulling together the right audience, elements and assets, setting up the right channels ...

... all of this human-gated so you can get those approvals and sign-offs from legal

👉  👉 (2) Decisioning - where machines take the lead - the mathematical and iterative exercises of prioriting different campaigns for the individual, pulling the right elements together in real-time ...

... and of course optimizing, assessing, learning from what's actually coming out of the campaign, shifting course

Each of the PHASES has its ELEMENTS or STEPS:

(1) COWORKING elements are:

👉 (1) Campaign Assembly - marketer provides their business goals, brand guidelines, etc. and Campaign Agent pulls together an audience, appropriate content assets and channel connectors (email, SMS, ads) to reach these goals

👉 (2) Content Personalization - this element puts together a library of assets pulled from brand-approved pieces that are adapted to different channels reaching customers, like Email, RCS, MMS, SMS at first (then WhatApp etc)

👉 (3) Review Gates - user-defined approvals as needed to change and progress the components

(2) DECISIONING elements are:

👉 (1) Send Prioritization - this is the real-time element that looks at each customer's intent and context in the moment and makes a decision among campaigns; this moves up or suppresses campaigns to improve response

👉 (2) Assembly - this elements generates content variations that are matched to the channel, language (English, French and Spanish at launch), variations; and these are importantly grounded in the brand guidelines you provide, CMS asset context etc

👉 (3) Optimization - pure Agentforce here, with a larngin loop that looks for patterns across customers and LLMs reasoning about what customers need (hybrid ML/LLM interestingly)

You will notice BRAND CENTER in the diagram on top of Agentforce, and this is a filter GA'd last summer: it is a kind of "brand kit" that lets you set standards for identity, voice, tone, styles (verbal and visual), no-nos, must-haves etc.

Campaign Agent is GA in Marketing Cloud Next (MC on Core) by 10/26 aka in a few weeks

What a blast!!!! Day 2 at Dreamforce was packed, and I walked away with a much clearer picture of where enterprise AI is actually heading. #sponsored #salesforcepartner

We started the day at the Campground on the Agentic Enterprise City Tour. Seeing agents work across sales, service and operations in 1 connected flow makes it feel real. Building 1 agent is easy. Getting 10 of them to share context without stepping on each other is the real challenge. 

Then came the panel on how Slack turns AI into a team sport. What stuck with me is that AI rarely fails because of the model. It fails when it sits in a separate tab nobody opens. Put agents where people already work and they pick up the context of the conversation, while humans stay in the loop. Ryan Gavin and Slack Team are nonstop!!!!

The highlight for me was sitting down with Savinay Berry EVP & GM, Data Management at Salesforce. We talked about why every enterprise needs an AI infrastructure layer, and why AI-ready data is what separates a cool demo from something that works at scale. Can't wait to release that, stay tuned.

The way I see it, AI-ready data comes down to 3 things. It is unified across systems. It is governed, with permissions that travel with the data. And it carries enough metadata that an agent knows what a field actually means. Full conversation coming soon.

After lunch, we went back to the Campground for hands-on demos. Watching agents get built and tested live shows you quickly where grounding and guardrails make or break the experience.

The Boardroom session on the “Trust Imperative” tied it all together. If an agent can act on your data, you need to know what it can see, what it did and why. That is no longer optional.

And to close out the afternoon, I got to meet chess grandmaster Sam Shankland at the FIDE and FIFA exhibition on Howard Street. A fun reminder that good strategy, on the board or in AI, is about thinking a few moves ahead.

If I had to sum up the day: agents are only as good as the data behind them and the trust around them.

post_text:
The smarter AI becomes, the more valuable human judgment becomes. #Sponsored 

That thought stayed with me at Dreamforce after a conversation with Adam Forrest and chess Grandmaster Maurice Ashley and Sam Shankland. Chess may be the clearest analogy I have found for the agentic enterprise.

A Grandmaster does not win by calculating every possible move. There are too many. They win by knowing which moves deserve attention, what matters right now, when to attack, when to wait, and when the position has changed enough to require a new plan.

AI is creating the same challenge for business. Agents can analyze more information, generate more options, recommend more actions, and increasingly execute those actions themselves.

And Salesforce is connecting those agents to the things that make enterprise decisions meaningful: business context, permissions, workflows and governance.

That creates a paradox: the more intelligence AI gives us, the more judgment we need. Someone still has to decide what we are optimizing for and which recommendation actually matters. Someone still has to decide what level of risk is acceptable, and when the agent should act alone versus when a human should step back in.

👉 This is the Human+AI equation in practice. AI keeps expanding what can be done. Human judgment decides what should be done.

The hardest part is neither the human nor the AI. It is the "+": who decides, who acts, who checks, and when control changes hands.

When intelligence becomes abundant, judgment becomes the scarce resource.

🤔 Where in your organization is AI already moving faster than your ability to judge its decisions?

A marriage and family therapist, an AI Partnerships leader Atlassian, a Sales wonder woman at ElevenLabs, a small business owner, a VP Salesforce, a CMO at Qualified (Acquired by Salesforce), and a million other lives and careers that none of us could have predicted back then. And somehow, all these years later, the group chats are still going strong.
We talk a lot about the importance of having a “network,” especially when it comes to our careers. But really, this is what a network looks like to me. It’s how we stay sane, find jobs, make connections, and feel supported through all of it.

Never underestimate the power of a really good group chat and simply showing up for each other any way you know how.

post_text:
Si el primer día de Dreamforce 2026 presentó una nueva visión para el futuro del CRM, el segundo planteó una pregunta más práctica: ¿cómo funciona esta visión cuando llega a la operación?

El foco pasó de los grandes anuncios a la ejecución. Sesiones técnicas, demostraciones, casos reales y conversaciones sobre ROI y gobernanza mostraron cómo las empresas están poniendo a trabajar a los agentes de IA en procesos reales.

En el keynote “The Enterprise AI Harness for the Agentic Enterprise”, la conversación giró en torno a la infraestructura necesaria para convertir la IA en una capacidad empresarial, conectando datos, aplicaciones, agentes y gobernanza.

La agenda también incluyó conversaciones de Marc Benioff con Roland Busch, CEO de Siemens, sobre IA en la industria, y con H.E. Omar Sultan Al Olama, ministro de IA de los Emiratos Árabes Unidos, sobre la adopción de esta tecnología por el gobierno.

Uno de los temas centrales fue la evolución de Agentforce más allá de la experimentación: poner agentes en producción, medir resultados y crear agentes especializados. Entre los ejemplos están Casey, para atención al cliente; Piper, para pipeline inbound; y Hunter, para ventas outbound.

La evolución también incluye agentes capaces de perseguir objetivos durante días o semanas, dando seguimiento a los procesos en lugar de responder a una solicitud puntual.

Otro destaque fue Data 360. Para tomar decisiones y ejecutar acciones con contexto, los agentes necesitan datos confiables y entender qué significan dentro del negocio. Esta combinación permite que la IA actúe en procesos específicos.

El ROI también estuvo en el centro del Executive Spotlight “ROI or It Didn't Happen”, sobre cómo CFOs, COOs y CIOs evalúan sus inversiones en IA. La necesidad de demostrar valor en plazos más cortos fue recurrente, con foco en flujos centrales e impacto medible.

A medida que los agentes ganan escala, también crece la necesidad de gobernar este ecosistema: saber cuáles existen, qué hacen, a qué datos acceden y cómo se miden sus resultados. ADT compartió planes con MuleSoft Agent Fabric en este contexto.

En cuanto a clientes, AT&T mostró experiencias agénticas con Data 360, A2A y arquitectura headless, incluida una demostración de AT&T Retail Mobile App en Agentic City. En América Latina, Banco Agibank destacó el uso de Agentforce Service y agentes de IA para escalar operaciones sin aumentar proporcionalmente los costos.

Brasil también estuvo presente: hubo 27 sesiones de LATAM con clientes y socios, de las cuales alrededor de 13 contaron con empresas brasileñas.

Después de un primer día marcado por grandes anuncios, el segundo trajo una perspectiva complementaria: para las empresas, la IA no se trata solo de entender lo que puede hacer, sino de ponerla a trabajar, medir su impacto y establecer una gobernanza que permita escalar.

Convertir la visión de una Empresa Agéntica en una operación real. Esa es una de las principales conversaciones de Dreamforce.

Solo apto para valientes: rediseñar los procesos de principio a fin, con la IA en el centro, para acelerar un proceso de 48 horas a 48 segundos, y que un humano solo intervenga en el 2% de excepciones.

post_text:
Salesforce had a global outage yesterday in the middle of Dreamforce.

As their leaders were on stage selling the future of autonomous business, all of their customer's automation and AI completely stopped.

During the downtime:
  - Most customers couldn’t even log in.
  - Some couldn’t submit support cases to get help.
  - Many scheduled jobs still weren’t running after access returned.

We get excited about AI doing more of our selling, follow-up, and customer service.

But AI employees have the same vulnerability human do.

If systems like Salesforce, HubSpot, ServiceNow and Atlassian go down, we lose access to the customer history, data and workflows, and we can service our customers.

Building a more autonomous business means decoupling our AI agents, models, and core business systems.

Putting every layer with one vendor may simplify buying but clearly concentrates risk.

This next phase of building needs redundancy at every layer.

Yesterday is a reminder that AI can't replace good business strategy.

summary: Ravit Jain recaps Slack's Dreamforce keynote with CEO Rob Seaman, CMO Ryan Gavin and CRO Zach Ciliotta-Young, detailing Slackforce Surfaces, Slack Code, and Slackbot's 1.5 million monthly users.
post_text:
I just came out of the Slack Keynote at Dreamforce, and I got to spend time with Rob Seaman, CEO of Slack, Ryan Gavin, CMO Slack, Zach Ciliotta-Young CRO, talking through the announcements. Thank you both for the time and the candid conversation. It helped me see the bigger picture behind the product news. #ad #salesforcepartner
 
First, what Slack announced:
 
- Slackforce Surfaces. Ask Slackbot in plain language for a dashboard, report, deck, or calculator, and it builds a live, interactive one inside Slack. Built on Salesforce and your connected data, under your own permissions, and shared with your team right in the channel. Live data refresh rolls out in October.
 
- Slackbot in channels. Tag it in and the whole team works from the same answer. Now in early pilot.
 
- Slackbot in Salesforce Lightning. Your AI teammate sits right next to the record, so you never leave the page.
 
- Big mode. A full-screen AI workspace in Slack for deep research, writing, and analysis.
 
- Two-way voice and video generation. Talk to Slackbot, hear it respond, and have it take action. Coming later this year.
 
- Slack Code. Code channels where people and agents write, review, and ship together, with 11 new agents including Snowflake, Datadog, Replit, and Lovable.
 
- Slack Frontline. A mobile-first preview for the people who do not sit at a desk.
And Slackbot has crossed 1.5 million monthly active users, up 145% quarter over quarter.
 
Now, my thoughts.
 
Slack is where companies communicate. So it was always going to become the place where the systems show up. This week, that stopped being a theory.
 
The second thing I keep coming back to. Every dashboard ever built has had the same flaw. It is a photograph. The moment you export it, it starts aging. And the decision it was built for usually happens somewhere else, in a conversation, using a number that was true last Tuesday. Surfaces flips that. The decision and the data finally sit in the same room, and the data stays alive while people debate it. The real win is not faster reports. It is fewer stale decisions.
 
The third shift is quieter, and it may matter most. AI at work has mostly been a solo activity. One person, one chat window, one private answer nobody else learns from. Bringing Slackbot into channels makes AI social. You see how a colleague asked the question. You build on their answer. The team gets smarter together.
 
This is outstanding work by the Slack and Salesforce teams. Shipping this much at once is hard. Making it all feel like one coherent idea is much harder. They did both.
 
After the keynote and my conversation with Rob and Ryan, one thing is clear to me: Slack is just getting started. Voice, video, frontline teams, agents shipping code next to engineers. The conversation is becoming the layer the whole company runs on, and we are only reading the first chapter.
 
Loved all the announcements!!!!
 
#dreamforce #slack #salesforce #slackbot #ai #futureofwork #leadership #theravitshow

summary: Fintech GTM Advisors analyzes Salesforce's new Koa reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, arguing enterprise AI's real moat lies in solving specific workflow problems.
post_text:
NVIDIA + Salesforce : The Next AI Battleground Isn't the Model. It's the Workflow.

NVIDIA and Salesforce made an important announcement at Dreamforce and we think there is a much bigger GTM lesson behind it.

Jensen Huang’s message was powerful:

“Know everything. Do anything.”

Salesforce's new Koa reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron, points to where enterprise AI is heading: from answering → reasoning → recommending → acting.

And importantly, doing it inside real enterprise workflows.

That matters enormously for capital markets.

Our journey from fixed-income trading, through 16 years at Bloomberg and subsequently across capital-markets fintech has taught us one consistent lesson:

Great technology doesn't automatically create a great business.

Technology must solve an expensive problem inside a workflow somebody actually cares about.

A trader doesn't want an LLM.

They want to know:

What changed? What matters to my book? Where's the liquidity? Which clients matter? What's my risk? What should I do next?

Imagine AI connecting those decisions across market data, positions, trades, liquidity, client interactions and risk - then recommending or initiating controlled actions.

That's where things become interesting.

And it's why we believe the competitive moat is shifting.

Foundation models will become increasingly accessible.

Domain expertise, proprietary context, trusted workflows and distribution won't.

For fintechs, that changes the GTM conversation.

Don't start with:

“How do we add AI to our product?”

Start with:

“Which expensive customer problem can we solve materially better using AI?”

Then establish the data, permissions, governance and human oversight required to make that outcome trusted.

The GTM journey becomes:

Domain Expertise → Proprietary Context → Workflow → Trusted Action → Measurable Outcome → Repeatable GTM

AI isn't the GTM strategy. Solving an expensive customer problem is.

The winners won't necessarily have the most impressive model.

They'll understand the customer's workflow, know where intelligence creates value, prove that value quickly and make the outcome repeatable across the market.

Great technology opens the door. Great GTM builds the business.

author_headline: Customer Experience, Growth Marketing, Business Transformation, and Human-Centered Design at LTM
summary: Brandon Gerena of LTM lists seven Dreamforce takeaways, citing Sam Altman on AI security, Jensen Huang's Marc Benioff interview, and agent-outcome measurement frameworks.
post_text:
Leaving Dreamforce excited, exhausted, and fueled with ideas I’m ready to put into practice. A few things I’m still thinking about before my ✈️:

1. Sam Altman’s surprisingly calm discussion of AI security risks, along with his call for companies to do their part to protect people as the technology advances. The interview felt surreal as everyone was on the edge of their seats.

2. Jensen Huang turned his interview with Marc Benioff into a roaming conversation around the theater. As an improv performer myself, I felt every unscripted moment. Equal parts anxiety-inducing and hysterical.

3. Brands are (finally!) putting a human-centered north star, better collaboration, and redesigned processes at the heart of sales transformation. Music to my ears! The technology needs that foundation to deliver measurable results.

4. Salesforce local developer communities were a reminder of how much belonging matters. People learning, building, and having fun together. This amazing energy is showing up around the globe.

5. The static interface is getting a serious rethink. Despite their catchy t-shirt slogans, the UI isn't dead. But watching AI generate dashboards and surface insights from a prompt raises some interesting questions about how we’ll design experiences going forward.

6. Salesforce’s value framework felt familiar to what we use in our LTM consulting practice. What stood out was the explicit connection between business goals and agent objectives. Every agent needs a clear job and a measurable contribution to the business. That should shape what we build from day one.

7. The scorecard needs to follow the work across people and agents. An agent can look great on its own while creating more work downstream. Measure the handoffs, human review time, and customer outcome together—and keep improving after launch.

Plenty to bring back to the LTM team. First, some sleep…

author_headline: CRO @TrustLayer · Founder @majorGTM · I find and fix the GTM collisions costing your pipeline.
summary: TrustLayer CRO Jason Reichl argues Salesloft, Outreach, Gong, Clari and Drift exist because Salesforce left gaps open, and warns vendors' incentives favor lock-in over solving problems.
post_text:
Dreamforce week. Every booth on that floor is a company that exists because Salesforce left a gap open. Salesloft, Outreach, Gong, Clari, Drift is an entire ecosystem built on top of problems the platform never fixed.

Not because Salesforce couldn't build them. Because the wedge stayed profitable longer as a problem than as a feature.

I watched this pattern for a decade running GTM teams. The gap doesn't close until a startup proves the market, gets acquired, or gets big enough to force Salesforce's hand. Then Agentforce ships at the keynote and the industry acts surprised.

Here's what I actually think about when the "AI-first" slide hits: I don't trust a roadmap that's built on my captivity. Salesforce isn't rewarded for solving my problem fast. They're rewarded for owning my data long enough that leaving costs more than staying.

Trust isn't what a vendor says on stage. It's what their incentive structure forces them to prioritize when nobody's watching.

The SaaS era ran on lock-in, so a wedge economy grew up around every gap they left standing on purpose. AI-native vendors don't have that legacy to protect yet. That's not a promise they'll behave better. It's a different incentive worth checking before you sign a five-year dependency on top of them.

Ask what a vendor is optimized to protect before you ask what they're optimized to solve.

They are working towards a locked in future, put that on the keynote slide.

summary: CMO Eric Eden analyzes Dreamforce and HubSpot UNBOUND announcements, arguing Salesforce makes CRM headless via Claude/Slack/Lightning while HubSpot makes it self-updating, requiring five AI-fluency skills.
post_text:
Salesforce and HubSpot announced dozens of new AI capabilities at their big conferences this week that make AI Fluency the most important skill for GTM teams.

Dreamforce and HubSpot UNBOUND happened simultaneously this week.

Your CRM is about to become less visible and far more powerful.

It was a fundamental change in what a CRM is becoming.

For decades, CRM has been a system people open, search, update, and maintain.

Now it is becoming the context and execution layer underneath the work.
Salesforce is making CRM headless and ambient.

Its data, permissions, business logic, and actions can increasingly appear inside Claude, Slack, Lightning, and other work surfaces.

HubSpot is making CRM self-updating and outcome-oriented.

Hubspot's platform can capture more customer context automatically, expose gaps in that context, and coordinate specialized agents around goals.

Different strategies by Salesforce and Hubspot but the same destination.

CRM is moving from a system of record to a system of action.
That will transform how B2B teams:
- Build and optimize campaigns
- Research accounts and buying groups
- Capture meetings and update opportunities
- Monitor buyer signals
- Coordinate prospecting
- Create quotes and manage revenue
- Measure visibility inside AI answers
- Govern agents that can change live customer data

It also creates an urgent new requirement.
Sales, marketing, and RevOps teams must become AI fluent.

Modern GTM teams need five capabilities:
1. Context fluency: Giving agents accurate customer, product, brand, and process knowledge.

2. Workflow fluency: Designing the path from an objective to a completed outcome.

3. Evaluation fluency: Measuring quality, corrections, cost, and business impact.

4. Governance fluency: Controlling what agents can see, change, send, or spend.

5.  Human judgment: Knowing when relationships, creativity, ambiguity, or consequences require a person.

The companies that deploy the most agents will not automatically win.

The winners will build the strongest partnership between humans, trusted context, and controlled AI execution.

I unpacked the most important announcements from Dreamforce and UNBOUND, what they mean for B2B revenue teams.

If you work in sales, marketing, RevOps, growth, or revenue leadership, I would love to hear your perspective:

Which GTM workflow are you redesigning first?

Share this with your coworkers and send it to the GTM leaders deciding how your technology stack will work

author_headline: VP Global Partnerships & Data Solutions, G2
summary: G2's Christine Li lists takeaways from Dreamforce and UNBOUND: agents becoming interfaces, data provenance, reimagined reviews, and G2's new "G2 Everywhere" strategy.
post_text:
Dreamforce + UNBOUND in one week. My feet hurt, my voice is questionable, but my brain is very full. 😅

The biggest takeaway from a week of conversations with builders, marketers, data leaders, and partners?

AI is moving fast. Trust has to move with it.

A few themes I’m taking home:

🤖 Agents are becoming the interface. We’re moving beyond AI that simply answers questions toward agents that take action — launching campaigns, updating systems, connecting data, and executing workflows.

🔗 Data provenance matters more than ever. As AI consumes more third-party data, knowing where that data came from — and being able to trust it — becomes incredibly important.

🗣️ Customer voice needs a rethink. The future of reviews probably looks a lot less like filling out a form. Voice, AI-guided experiences, and agentic workflows can make sharing authentic customer experiences dramatically easier.

📍 The best AI disappears into the workflow. Buyers shouldn’t have to go somewhere new to find trusted information. The opportunity is to bring intelligence and customer voice into the places where people are already researching, building, and making decisions.

That last one especially reinforced something we’ve been working toward at G2 :

G2 Everywhere.

The next chapter of B2B isn’t about creating more destinations. It’s about making trusted data and authentic customer voice available everywhere buyers — and increasingly their AI agents — make decisions.

Lots to build. 🚀

Thanks to everyone who made #DF26 + #UNBOUND such an energizing week. ❤️

Dreamforce is proving it: Enterprise AI just got serious.

Salesforce isn't just talking models and copilots anymore. They introduced an Enterprise AI Harness — context, agents, actions, governance, security, models, unified.
That's a huge shift.

But it exposes the next problem: companies are about to have more AI capability than they know what to do with.
"Can we build an agent?" is no longer the hard question. Increasingly, the answer is yes.

The hard questions are:
→ What should the agent actually do?
→ Which process is worth redesigning around AI?
→ Where does a human need to stay in the loop?
→ Is this real value — or just a good demo?
That last one is the question I keep coming back to.

author_headline: Brand Experiences, Exhibits, Events, Digital Engagement, Activations @ Elevation3D
summary: Elevation3D's Atida Bakst recounts producing Own Company's multi-building "Data Independence" Dreamforce activation—a statehouse-themed booth, wrapped building, and VIP yacht—that won Bronze at the ExSys Awards.
post_text:
We wrapped an entire building in vinyl for a software conference. That's not even the interesting part.

A few years ago I was the client. I was at Own Company, and we brought a theme called Data Independence to Dreamforce. Here is what that turned into.

A 30x30 booth on the show floor built to feel like a statehouse, with a rotunda and a demo alley cutting through it. A 10x10 right beside it. An off-site building wrapped completely in vinyl, illuminated logos hanging off the outside, a Liberty Bell replica sitting in the window. An executive briefing center running in there all week. A private premiere next door for 1,000 clients and prospects, live music, themed menus, the works. A lit up box truck circling the city to pull people to it. And the same look carried all the way out to a VIP yacht and two suites at a Giants game.

One week. Multiple buildings. And you could not tell where one piece ended and the next began.

It won Bronze for Best Event Design at this year's ExSys Awards. A judge said the Revolutionary-era details made an abstract software idea feel real. That is exactly how it felt to stand in it. But the award is not what I think about.

What I think about is what my job was that week, and what it wasn't.

When you are the client, you are usually the glue. Booth vendor here, graphics vendor there, venue, AV, production. Every one of them sees their own piece and only their piece. You are the only person who sees the whole week. So you explain your brand over and over, you check whether the sign at the off-site matches the wall on the show floor, and when something slips at 11pm, it is still your name on it.

I did not have that job. One team did the design, the graphics, the production, the digital engagement layer and the logistics, in house, and they carried the idea everywhere it had to go. It never got handed off nine times, so it never got watered down nine times.

I got my week back. I spent it on our guests, our execs, and our message instead of babysitting my own brand across five invoices.

That is a big part of why I work at Elevation3D now.

And here is the part I really want event marketers to hear. The size of that week was a budget decision. The seamlessness was not. That came from how the work was set up, not from how much it cost. A 10x10 and one dinner can feel just as whole as a wrapped building and a premiere, if it all comes from one place.

So if your show week has more than one thing in it, the expensive part probably is not the booth. It is you, being the glue. And that cost never shows up on an invoice.

If you are client side right now, how many partners are you holding together for one week?

post_text:
AI adoption isn't a procurement decision, it's a culture decision. Most orgs start with “which platform do we buy” and work backwards to a use case. The ones who get it right start with “what are we actually trying to solve.”

And it's bigger than productivity. It's about power, who gets visibility, who decides, at what speed, and whether the systems running underneath are something people can actually explain.

Which also means every AI decision is a decision about what stays human. Let agents handle research, triggers, signals, sure. But the moments that call for real judgment, the human inflection points? Those should be protected, not left to default.

Feels especially relevant with Dreamforce happening this week, the agentic enterprise conversation is everywhere right now. But the real question isn't which agent you deploy, it's what you're deploying it for.

#Dreamforce #DF26

author_headline: Regional Sales Director | Mid Market Germany
summary: Sales director Andy Ryll details Benioff's keynote with Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Roland Busch, plus new products Koa, Claudeforce, Piper, Hunter and Casey.
post_text:
Four days in San Francisco. I'm still buzzing.

I've been to a lot of conferences. I have never seen a stage like this one.
Marc Benioff opened Dreamforce '26 and then brought out, one after another: Jensen Huang (NVIDIA), Dario Amodei(Anthropic), Sam Altman (OpenAI) and Roland Busch (Siemens). Four of the most consequential leaders in technology, in one room, disagreeing openly about pace, safety and regulation. That honesty was the best part.

The moment that stayed with me came from Roland Busch. He said the hard part isn't the model, it's "bringing a probabilistic technology into a deterministic world." Because hallucination doesn't work on the shop floor. Every third manufacturing line on this planet runs on Siemens technology, so he would know. Working with mid-market customers in Eastern Germany every day, that sentence landed harder than any product slide.

And the products did show up as well:
→ Koa, our first CRM reasoning model, built with NVIDIA
→ Claudeforce, built with Anthropic, now in open beta. AI replaces the UI, and I mean that literally
→ Piper qualifying inbound, Hunter on outbound (GA in November), Casey handling service including voice resolving complex customer conversations end to end
→ Deeper partnerships with Google Cloud and AWS, so this works where our customers already are

One takeaway for every Mittelstand leader I spoke to: nobody has to build this from scratch anymore.
Dario Amodei said we're using maybe 5 to 10% of what this technology can already do today. That's not a gap. That's the opportunity of the decade.

post_text:
For the first time in a decade, I was not onsite for Dreamforce.
 
And that got me thinking: when you leave a career you spent nearly 20 years building, what comes with you? What gets left behind?
 
My life in events taught me how to translate. Not languages, but what a client or business partner said they wanted, into what they were actually trying to accomplish, into what needed to be configured and operationalized.
 
I used to think the valuable part was moving fluently between those three layers: business need, technical solution, onsite execution.
 
What I’ve come to realize is the deeper skill is listening closely enough to hear what isn't being said, asking the right questions to crack that open, and helping identify what actually needs to happen next.
 
I didn't leave that when I left events. It’s at the center of my work now at Stillpoint Studios — just without a big blue cloud in the background.
 
Different application. Same skill.
 
As Dreamforce wraps today, I'm feeling a lot of gratitude for the people and experiences that helped hone that skill in me. To those of you rounding out Day 3, congratulations!

summary: Sohil G. of Two Circles reports that Dreamforce attendees focused heavily on building agents while largely ignoring underlying data and semantic-layer definitions.
post_text:
Back from Dreamforce. Findings, in order of importance:
1. Can't wait for Harry Breedon to share what he took away from it, his notes will be better than mine.
2. Everyone was building agents
3. Almost nobody was talking about the data and semantic layer underneath them

Number 3 is the whole game. An agent can only answer a question if it knows what the question means and in sport, "fan", "attendance" and "engaged" mean six different things depending on which system you ask. Get the definitions right and the agent is useful on day one. Skip that step and you've built something that gives you confidently wrong answers very quickly.

Lots to bring back to our clients at Two Circles.

Your sales channel has 47 messages about the deal.

The deal still needs updating.

That’s the Slackforce opportunity that actually interests us.

Slackforce Surfaces let teams build live, interactive views from their data inside Slack—something people can explore and act on together.

Think about a deal review:

→ Pull up the current pipeline.
→ Look into a stalled opportunity.
→ Review the context together.
→ Take the next action.

That’s a more useful ambition than having a bot summarize the 47 messages.

Our test: pick one recurring deal review. Measure how many follow-up messages and manual updates it takes to finish the work.

Then try the new experience.

Slack lists Surfaces as available now, depending on licensing and rollout. Slackbot joining channels is still in early pilot—different capabilities, different availability.

We’re interested in fewer tabs.

We’re much more interested in retiring “Can someone update Salesforce?”

🌁 Bryd on the Ground | Dreamforce 2026 Day 2 Highlights

Five Bryd sessions in one day. Day two was the biggest day of our week at #DF26, and the theme running through all of it was the same one Salesforce spent the day making from the main stage.

🔑 Keynotes: Proof Over Promises

 The Agentforce keynote was deliberately demo led, built around customers already running agents and the returns they are seeing. The afternoon went deeper on AIforce and Headless 360, and on what it takes for people and agents to work across interfaces without adding one more disconnected tool.

🎤 Bryd on Stage

📊 Laurence Fitch started us at 8:30 with Ditch the Dashboard: Tableau Data in Slack. Tableau Next brings richer, interactive analytics into Slack's conversational interface, so teams act on data in the flow of work instead of going looking for it. A few hours later, Slackforce Surfaces made much the same case from the keynote stage.

🧩 Ali Waguespack and Gigi Chan ran Rethinking Interfaces in a Headless Data Architecture, on Slack as the system of engagement: one surface to connect external systems, surface insights and take action without switching tabs. Objective one was simply understanding AIforce, on the morning Salesforce was making the headless case itself.

💥 Then Mythbusting Hour: Slack, Microsoft and Enterprise AI, with Laurence Fitch, Ali Waguespack and Gigi Chan together on the panel. Real numbers from a 50 million message enterprise migration, playbook included, and why headless is the real unlock inside a Microsoft heavy stack.

🚀 Gigi Chan closed a three session day with Become a Salesforce Developer Without a Technical Background, on Apex, Trailhead and the transferable skills people underestimate, then Design and Build Beautiful Slack Apps in the Learning Lab.

🤝 Bryd in the Ecosystem
 Learning Lab shifts, Partner Lounge conversations, and Dreamfest to close the night.

author_headline: Director of Engineering | Technology Leader | AI, SaaS & Platform Architect | Passionate About Games & Scalable Systems
summary: Engineering director Michael Evans details having his AI 'chief of staff' bot autonomously complete a Salesforce Security Challenge, earning gold in 45 minutes among 601 total participants, only 454 finishing.
post_text:
2 bots vs. a Salesforce security challenge. Human written, to the point and with pictures... because no one wants to read 10 paragraphs of Opus output.

It's the last day of Dreamforce 2026 and I ran into a Security Challenge Booth I hadn't noticed before. 6 challenges on a scratch org and the promise of prizes. While I think the expectation was for humans to be completing the challenges, where's the fun in that? 

I pointed my right hand AI Agent at the URL and said 'Go. Play.'

For context, I run a fleet of 20+ agents that manage our systems. Different bots, different jobs. One of them acts as a chief of staff for the operation, maintaining and overseeing the other bots and keeping an eye on the overall system health. He's who I pointed at the challenge via a Discord message on my phone.

And he crushed it! Read each of the challenges, came up with a plan and went to work. Meta Data API deploys, permissions set completions, etc. 4 of the tasks he completed fully on his own while I walked the floor of Moscone West. Two of them he needed human hands to complete the MFA confirmation.

45 minutes, gold medal on the score board and he earned himself a cool keychain that's going on his MacMini when I get home.

I forwarded the challenge to my team. Our Technical Product Manager in charge of Salesforce is competitive, and so he started our SF Admin agent on the challenge. Different bot, different training, upgraded model. Like I said, the TPM is competitive, so he set the bot to use Fable. It decided to use a virtual authenticator to complete the tasks that the Chief of Staff bot needed human hands for. It tests Salesforce stuff all day long, of course it came up with that solution. Neat.

Two agents, different methodologies. One defaulted to human in the loop, one defaulted to full automation. I think it's a good picture of where an Agentic Enterprise can be right now, but a lot of leaders still have a fear based mindset about what can be done. Like Benioff said in his keynote: "The door's open, people just aren't walking through."

I think that's a shame, because of the 601 people who attempted the challenge, only 454 completed all 6 challenges. 147 walked away. Neither of our team's agents did.

I talked to the Salesforce Director running the challenge booth about how the agents did and he said something important: "I don't care how you do it, as long as you're thinking about security."

I think that's the right mindset for all of this.

post_text:
I signed up for this event about an hour before it started. Thanks to Kaushik for letting me know.

A few hours later, I was standing in front of the room demoing something I had just built. 😅 Today I joined Prompt to Pipeline, a Dreamforce build lab hosted by WingRep × Lovable in San Francisco.

The idea was simple: bring a laptop, identify a real problem, and use Lovable to actually build something around it.

One thing the Lovable team said stuck with me: "The people closest to the problem should be the ones solving it."

So I built around a problem I know very well right now: networking at tech events while job searching and I called it ConnectWise.

You give it a Luma event link, and the idea is that it can:
• understand the event, speakers and attendees
• look at your resume/background
• prioritize who might actually be useful for you to meet
• explain why you should talk to them
• generate a personalized elevator pitch or LinkedIn opener
• surface relevant opportunities at the companies represented in the room  

I also started thinking about the other half of attending events: what happens afterward? So I added the idea of connecting event notes/transcripts so the tool could help turn what you actually learned into a useful recap or LinkedIn post instead of letting everything disappear into another forgotten notes folder. 😂

The coolest part was getting to demo it in front of the room. It’s definitely not a finished product. I built the first version incredibly fast, and there’s a lot I’d want to improve.

But that was probably my biggest takeaway from today. You don’t always need to start with a giant startup idea. Sometimes you start with:
“This annoys me. Can I build something that makes it better?”
And now, apparently, you can get surprisingly far with that question.

Thanks to the WingRep and Lovable teams for creating a space where we could actually build instead of just listening to another AI panel.

Lovely meeting you all - Amit Bakshi, Alan Tai, Fizz Ahmed, Luke Arno, Dan O'Leary Gobind Brar, Patty L.

summary: Mollie Golden lists five Dreamforce blind spots: fundamentals over tools, manager-led enablement, behavior change over training scores, completion versus impact, and win/loss debriefs.
post_text:
Dreamforce is genuinely great for a lot of things. Learning what actually makes your reps better isn't really one of them (and by the way, I get it, that's not the point of Dreamforce but wouldn't it be nice if it was?) 

Five things you won't pick up on the mainstage or the expo floor:

1. AI won't fix broken fundamentals.
The whole floor is AI right now. But a tool can't teach a rep to sell — it can only make a good seller faster. Foundations first. Tools second. Always that order.

2. Enablement scales through managers, not tools.
Nobody's selling you this one, because you can't put it in a shopping cart. The best training in the world dies by Wednesday if the frontline manager doesn't reinforce it. Enablement is a team sport.

3. Knowing isn't doing.
A packed training with great feedback scores isn't changed behavior. Enablement is a behavior-change problem wearing an information-transfer costume — and behavior change is the hard, slow, unglamorous work.

4. Completion isn't impact.
Attendance and certification rates are the easiest things to game and the least worth measuring. "They showed up" has never been the same as "they got better." If you don't already know this one, we need to have a serious chat.

5. Your best training is the deals you already ran.
No framework from the keynote, your CRO, or the best leader in the industry beats an honest win/loss debrief of a real deal, in your market, this quarter. The curriculum is closing and dying around you all the time — most of it just gets filed as "closed lost."

post_text:
Day one at Dreamforce old friends, familiar faces, and a lot to think about.

Seeing Dario Amodei, Jensen Huang, and Sam Altman all in one day was a highlight. Reconnecting with friends and former Salesforce colleagues made it feel like a reunion.

A few perspectives that stayed with me:

Marc Benioff emphasized that models alone cannot run an enterprise. Business context, data, workflows, and trust are essential.

Dario Amodei highlighted shared safety standards and companies learning from one another. He also suggested we’re only realizing around 5–10% of the potential value of today’s AI. There’s enormous opportunity in applying capabilities that already exist.

Jensen Huang framed AI safety as an engineering priority and argued that safety and progress can advance together. His encouragement to businesses was to keep experimenting and deploying, even when the first attempt doesn’t work. Keynote coverage

Sam acknowledged concerns about AI’s growing capabilities and the concentration of power, while remaining optimistic about its potential for creativity, entrepreneurship, and improving lives. Stronger safeguards become increasingly important as these systems gain the ability to take action. Sam’s conversation with Marc

Salesforce’s direction with AIforce and Claudeforce brings those ideas into everyday work: connecting AI to business data, workflows, and permissions. Salesforce’s announcements

At skysync, our perspective on AI ROI starts with a simple question: what business outcome are we improving, and how will we measure it?

Faster lead follow-up. Better conversion. Lower cost per resolved support case. Fewer hours spent on manual work.

Establish the baseline, connect the right data, deploy into the actual workflow, and measure the change. Include implementation, usage, oversight, and maintenance in the economics.

Safety belongs in that calculation. Incorrect actions and constant rework can erase productivity gains. Clear permissions, testing, monitoring, and human escalation help make those gains sustainable.

My takeaway: the opportunity is to turn increasingly capable AI into measurable results that businesses and their customers can trust.

After years at Salesforce, being back as the founder of SkySync feels especially meaningful. Grateful for the friendships and conversations that make this community special.

post_text:
Dreamforce is supposed to blow Salesforce fatigue away every year, at least a little bit. At least during the concert on Wednesday night :)

This year it delivered the biggest outage alongside yet another AI rebranding..

We went from Einstein to Einstein GPT to Copilot, Agentforce everywhere and now AIForce, with each “AI” replaced before enterprise teams could even adopt the previous one letting alone the UI.. This year, the keynote declared the UI dead.

Declaring the interface dead is convenient when your own UI is unusable. But when an incumbent rebrands its AI strategy every year, suffers a massive outage on its biggest stage, and asks customers to trust autonomous agents while they are still drowning in basic adoption debt, you are watching a giant run out of road.

RevOps inherits capabilities announced on stage that nobody can adopt, while the underlying architecture stays untouched and just rebranded every year with the increasing check to pay.

Indeed, SaaSpocalypse is real..

The enterprise model was simple: charge massive seat licenses, layer more complexity into rigid databases, and force users to click through endless screens developed by SIs. Now, the same incumbents are telling customers software is dead and agents will run everything, while still billing them like crazy for the privilege of navigating legacy sprawl.

When AI shifts the paradigm, legacy software cannot simply slap an agentic narrative over architectural debt. The complexity collapses under its own weight. The new AI-native CRM with Unlimited offering will conquer the market. Guess who is that company? :)

author_headline: Salesforce MVP | Salesforce Architect & Advisor | Salesforce Marketing Champion
summary: Lukas Lunow recaps Eric Zenz's keynote, covering Contentful-Palmata integration, a new campaign agent, and SDR agents Piper (GA) and Hunter (pilot, GA November).
post_text:
If there is one Salesforce SVP who knows how to enter a keynote stage, it is Eric Zenz.
 
Once he got there, he thanked two people. His fiancé, for letting him be in San Francisco days before their wedding. And a groomsman named Claude, who had picked the wine: a Washington red, matched to the menu, inside budget. I have been to weddings where the human groomsmen did worse.
 
The point he drew out of it: AI did not return a list of links but returned an answer. So the question is no longer whether you show up, but how. We now market to a human audience as well as an AI audience, and that's why our tactics need to change.
 
Cue Contentful, now part of the Marketing Cloud suite, and it embraces this new reality. The website used to be the front door. Now every answer engine is. Palmata measures how you show up there, and the uncomfortable part is the gap between being mentioned and being cited. Then we saw Contentful and Palmata being wired together, and one prompt pulled the recommendation, found the content, updated it and published it. One minute. This one will be interesting to follow.
 
Next came the campaign agent: grounded in a marketing plan and a brief carrying a goal, rather than a canvas you draw. A segment now defines eligibility, not recipients, and the agent decides which campaign each person receives. It can also decide not to send at all. After a decade of building declarative journeys designed to always send something, this one is new.
 
The third chapter turned intent into pipeline, and this is the part some recaps keep getting wrong. Piper and Hunter are not two SDR agents.
 
Piper is the front door. It talks to the buyer, in real time, in any language, and books the meeting. Hunter never speaks to a prospect but reads the intent signal, fills the gaps in the buying committee from third party data, and hands the seller a brief, a follow-up mail and an opportunity record. Its output goes to your sellers and to other agents, not to your customer. One is a conversation, the other runs in the background for weeks.
 
Piper is generally available. Hunter is in pilot, with GA stated for November. If you read the Connections coverage in June, you were told Hunter initiates outreach and runs nurture sequences. That description has been quietly re-scoped since.
 
What I would have wanted more of: close to two thirds of the keynote went to capabilities that arrived by acquisition. Contentful took one chapter, Qualified another, and both were genuinely good. That leaves roughly a quarter of the stage for Marketing Cloud Next itself, which, for those of us rebuilding on Next, is the part we came for.
 
And the best moment had nothing to do with product. Erin Duncan was called down and given the golden hoodie. As a fellow Marketing Champion: congratulations, Erin, thoroughly deserved.

After attending Dreamforce 2026 in San Francisco, I’m leaving with one thought:

Salesforce is no longer talking about AI as a feature inside CRM. It is positioning CRM, data, agents, workflows and governance as the enterprise layer powering AI wherever work happens.

That shift was visible across the keynotes, sessions, demos and conversations at #DF26.

Here are some announcements and themes that caught my attention:

🔹 AIforce — Salesforce beyond the CRM screen

Salesforce intelligence is increasingly available wherever employees already work—not necessarily inside Salesforce. 

Claudeforce, Slackforce and the broader AIforce vision bring Salesforce data, business context, permissions, workflows and actions into other AI interfaces and collaboration environments.

🔹 Claudeforce — Salesforce + Claude + MCP

This particularly caught my attention from a technology perspective. Cook Salesforce is bringing its data, context and capabilities directly into Claude through a prebuilt MCP approach.

Salesforce says Salesforce in Claude launches with 37 prebuilt sales skills, while developers can use the Salesforce Development plugin for Claude Code with 40+ skills.

🔹 Slackforce — CRM where the conversation happens

Slack is evolving into an operational interface.

Teams can interact with Salesforce context, records, workflows and actions directly from conversations.

Imagine asking:

“Which accounts are going quiet?”

…and having AI reason across CRM data, support cases and conversations to identify the issue and initiate the next action.

🔹 Agentforce Coworker — AI teammate, not just a chatbot

Agentforce Coworker is designed to work alongside employees—understanding business context, surfacing insights and taking action while respecting permissions and business rules.

🔹 Koa — reasoning built around CRM

Salesforce and NVIDIA announced Koa, described by Salesforce as its first CRM reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron. 

What stands out is its focus on reasoning around CRM-specific business scenarios and enterprise context.

🔹 Guardian — trust is part of the architecture

As enterprises move toward autonomous agents, the question isn’t only:

“What can the agent do?”

It becomes:

“What SHOULD the agent be allowed to do?”

🔹 Agent Fabric — the multi-agent world

Another fascinating direction is the move from a single AI agent to an ecosystem of agents.
Different agents may specialize in sales, service, finance, supply chain, employee support and more.

The future isn’t about building more chatbots. It is about creating trusted digital workers that understand enterprise context, reason over it, take action across systems, collaborate with other agents—and know when to involve a human.

That, for me, was the real story of Dreamforce 2026.

We talked openly about topics that don’t always make it onto the leadership agenda: imposter syndrome, mentorship vs. sponsorship, visibility, finding your voice, and what we want the next chapter of our leadership journey to look like.

post_text:
🚀 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗿𝗲𝗲 𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲𝘀. 𝗔𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗱𝗿𝗮𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆.

For the 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗱 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿 𝗶𝗻 𝗮 𝗿𝗼𝘄, I had the privilege of attending and presenting at 𝗗𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗺𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲.

And this year, my focus was on a question that is becoming increasingly important for every enterprise:

🤖 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗱𝗼 𝘄𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝘀𝘄𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗾𝘂𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗴𝗲𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗱𝗼𝗻𝗲?

I had the opportunity to present on:

𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗲𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮 + 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝗲𝗦𝗼𝗳𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜.

One thing stood out to me.

𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗰 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹.

The real enterprise challenge is everything that surrounds the model.

🔹 𝗜𝗻𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮 — bringing trusted, governed data and context into the picture.

🔹 𝗠𝘂𝗹𝗲𝗦𝗼𝗳𝘁 — connecting agents to APIs, applications, and the systems where business actually happens.

🔹 𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲 — enabling AI agents to reason and take action within business workflows.

The architecture becomes incredibly powerful when you think about it as:

𝗧𝗿𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗗𝗮𝘁𝗮 → 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗲𝘅𝘁 → 𝗥𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴 → 𝗔𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 → 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲

And that changed the way I approached the rest of the week. Over the next three days at Dreamforce, I found myself looking at AI through a slightly different lens.

The interesting question is no longer just "What can AI do?" 
It is becoming: What work should we actually delegate to AI?

How do we give agents the right context and data? Where should an agent reason and act independently and where should a human remain in the loop? And most importantly, how do we move from impressive demos to AI that creates measurable business value?
That made learning more about Agentforce and Agentforce Coworker particularly interesting. The idea of AI is evolving from something we simply ask questions to something that can increasingly work alongside us - grounded in business context, data, workflows, and actions.

For someone working at the intersection of CRM, data, digital engagement, and life sciences, that opens up some very interesting possibilities. I also spent quite a bit of time learning about Life Sciences Cloud and thinking about how these capabilities could eventually come together across commercial operations and customer engagement.

Of course, Dreamforce is never only about technology. Some of the most valuable moments were conversations with peers, partners, Salesforce experts, and people trying to solve similar problems from completely different perspectives.

And after a week of learning, experimenting, conversations, and lots of walking around San Francisco, I wanted to finish with one more challenge - Salesforce Certified Agentforce Specialist ✅

Certification is a nice milestone. But learning a technology is only the beginning. The real value comes when you take what you learned, identify the right problems to solve, experiment thoughtfully, measure what works, and turn the technology into something useful.

author_headline: Real-time & Event-driven Architectures | SAP Integration | AI Ambassador & Business AI Enablement
summary: Raphael Heinrich, an SAP integration specialist, analyzes Salesforce's Marshall agent autonomously creating SAP suppliers, arguing Kafka/Flink event monitoring matters more than the demoed action.
post_text:
Do you know Marshall and Piper? They might be your new colleagues soon.

Salesforce demoed them this week at the Dreamforce keynote. Marshall is the interesting one: no API, no connector, no integration. The agent looked at the transactions in an SAP sandbox and learned where to click and which fields are mandatory in 90 minutes. After that he creates suppliers fully autonomously.

Mario de Felipe has written up the governance questions very well, so I won't repeat those here.

Something else caught my attention. Marshall only works when someone tells him to work. In the demo a human types in a supplier name, then off he goes. But what about all the events that often aren't actively monitored by anyone? 

SAP events tell you what your company is already committed to. A goods receipt that never arrived is a commitment breaking, with a contract, a quantity and a date attached to it. A pricing condition that changed overnight means last month's margin calculation is wrong. Those things happen at 3am, and nobody is sitting in front of a screen to notice them. 

Having people approve is right and in most cases wanted. Using people as sensors is expensive.

The other half of the architecture is not exotic. SAP pushes business events out as they occur, Kafka carries them, and Flink starts the agent when a pattern over time warrants it rather than on every field change. 

Two things decide whether that survives production: The events have to be real business objects, assembled where the semantics already live, because a changed table row is not a delivery date slipping. And there has to be a schema contract between SAP and Flink, declared and versioned. Without it you learn about a change the way Marshall does in the demo, by going back to the classroom and relearning after something broke.

My takeaway: this week we saw an agent move its hands inside SAP. acting inside SAP is the half that gets demoed, and the half everyone is nervous about. Knowing when to act is the half that is ready today and hardly anyone uses.

*) I really wanted to illustrate this with Marshall from PAW Patrol sitting in front of an SAP screen. Then I remembered who owns him. You will have to imagine it.

post_text:
[드림포스(Dreamforce) 참관기] 

지난 3일 동안 센프란시스코, 드림포스 현장에서 머물며 세일즈포스가 혁신하고 있는 기업의 오늘과 미래를 온몸으로 체험하였습니다.
3일간의 여정 속에서 개인적으로 느낀 가장 강렬했던 3가지를 정리해 봅니다.

1. 'Unlock the Trapped Value': 갇힌 데이터 가치의 해제와 시장의 증명 현장에서 가장 상징적이었던 순간은 엔비디아, 오픈AI, 앤트로픽이라는 AI 시대를 이끄는 3대 거인이 세일즈포스와 한 자리에 모여 'AI 에이전틱 엔터프라이즈'의 미래를 논의한 것이었습니다. 지난 수년간 에이전트포스(Agentforce) 비전에 대한 시장의 우려도 있었지만, 세일즈포스의 본질은 명확했습니다. 바로 'Unlock the Trapped Value' 기업 내부 사일로(Silo)에 갇혀 있던 데이터의 가치를 풀어 AI가 안전하게 실질적 '액션'을 수행하도록 만드는 역량입니다. 
압도적인 성과와 앤트로픽 협업 기반의 클라우드포스(Claudeforce) 발표는 이 가치를 완벽히 입증해 냈습니다.

2. 맨파워 중심 성장의 종말: SMB와 스타트업의 새로운 방정식 기업의 매출 성장이 필연적으로 '인력(Manpower) 증가'를 동반하던 시대는 끝났습니다. 현장에서 다뤄진 SaaStr의 사례처럼, 소수 정예 조직이 수많은 AI 에이전트를 가동해 24시간 세일즈와 마케팅을 전담케 하며 수천억 원대 가치를 입증하는 시대입니다. AI 에이전트를 잘 활용한다면 소규모 기업도 폭발적인 스케일업이 가능해졌으며, 저 역시 이 변화의 흐름 속에서 시장에 기여할 명확한 이정표를 찾았습니다.

post_text:
My biggest takeaway from Dreamforce 2026:

The question is no longer “Which AI should we use?”
It’s “Which AI should we use for which type of work?”

Three experiences stood out to me — Slackbot, Agentforce and Claudeforce — and I see each playing a different role.

💬 Slackbot → Help me work.
Your AI teammate where conversations and collaboration are already happening. Summarize discussions, find context, surface Salesforce information and help you move from conversation to action.

⚙️ Agentforce → Help my business processes run.
This is where AI becomes operational. Specialized agents can follow business rules, work with enterprise data, execute workflows and take governed actions across systems.

🧠 Claudeforce → Help me think, connect, create and act.
What excites me here goes beyond reasoning. Claude can bring together context from Salesforce and multiple enterprise systems, reason across that information, and create dynamic UI experiences around the problem you’re trying to solve.

For me, that’s the bigger shift:

AI isn’t just becoming better at answering questions.
It’s becoming part of how work gets done.

And we’re already putting that idea into practice at Cloud Maven.

For our lending platform, we’re building 10+ specialized AI agents focused on automating different parts of the loan origination and servicing lifecycle — from intake and verification to underwriting, document processing, servicing and ongoing operations.

The objective isn’t to add AI everywhere.

It’s to identify where an agent can remove manual work, make better use of enterprise data, and help people get to an outcome faster.

That’s what made Dreamforce 2026 particularly exciting for me.

Different AI experiences. Different strengths. One increasingly connected enterprise.

If you’re exploring Agentforce or trying to determine where AI agents can create meaningful value in your business, I’d be happy to compare notes and share what we’re learning as we build and implement these solutions.

That's the exact shape of the agentic enterprise. AI expands what's possible. Judgment decides what's worth doing. And the more intelligence you hand your business, the more valuable — not less — human judgment becomes.

Every company adopting AI agents right now is really solving a governance problem, not a technology one: who decides, who acts, who checks.
