The SaaSpocalypse was supposed to be Salesforce's reckoning. #ad

Instead they've had their biggest quarter ever, and the AI labs now need them to reach customers.

Dario Amodei, Jensen Huang and Sam Altman all showed up at Dreamforce to stand next to Marc Benioff on day one.

Salesforce invited me to see it for myself, and Marc's keynote is the clearest picture I've had of where SaaS goes from here.

He laid it out across four layers:

1. The data - rich context about your business (Data 360)
2. The apps - the business logic and rules (Customer 360)
3. The agents - the AI that does the work for you (Agentforce)
4. The interface - where your people already hang out (AIforce)

It's the fourth layer I keep thinking about.

For twenty years you had to go into Salesforce to get work done. 

Now Salesforce comes to you, in Slack, Teams, ChatGPT, or Claude.

Then I sat down with three people running this at scale.

→ Corinne Sklar, VP & Managing Director of the Salesforce practice at IBM
→ Christophe Coenraets, SVP of Technical Audience Relations at Salesforce
→ Rob Seaman, EVP & GM of Slack

What became clear from our conversations is that an AI agent on its own has nothing to work with. 

It needs the data, the rules and the place your team already talks, and Salesforce has spent decades collecting all three.

No enterprise is ripping out the system that holds twenty years of its customer data. They want more out of it.

Large software companies and systems of record simply won’t go out of style.

The AI labs understood this first and that's why they're building on top of Salesforce this week rather than trying to replace it.

Dreamforce ’26 is over — and after connecting the announcements, I think the biggest story is much larger than any single product.

Salesforce  is attempting to rewrite the architecture of enterprise software.

For decades, CRM worked like this:

Login → Navigate → Search → Click → Update → Save

Dreamforce ’26 points toward:

Intent → Context → Reasoning → Action

A few announcements make that shift very real:

🚀 AIforce — Salesforce data, logic, workflows and governance become available across AI interfaces.

🧠 Claudeforce — Anthropic Claude + Salesforce context + governed enterprise actions.

⚡ Koa — Salesforce  + NVIDIA  building specialized CRM reasoning rather than relying only on general-purpose AI.

🤖 Agentforce + Coworker — moving from AI that answers questions toward agents that reason, act and work toward outcomes.

💬 Slackforce — bringing agents, CRM context and actions directly into Slack .

🗄️ Data 360 — because the real enterprise AI advantage may not be the model. It may be the trusted context surrounding the model.

🔌 Headless 360 + MCP + Skills + APIs — opening Salesforce capabilities to entirely new AI experiences.

Put everything together and the architecture starts looking very different:

AI Interfaces
↓
Agents & Reasoning
↓
Trusted Enterprise Context
↓
Skills, APIs & Business Logic
↓
Security + Governance

That may be the real #Dreamforce26 story.

Salesforce isn’t simply putting AI inside CRM.

It is turning CRM into infrastructure for AI.

Cloud changed where software runs.

Mobile changed where we access it.

AI changed how we interact with it.

Agents are changing who — or what — performs the work.

And perhaps the future of Salesforce isn’t Salesforce on every screen.

Maybe it’s Salesforce behind every intelligent action.

post_text:
Legal and finance are now on nearly 100% of deal desk calls.

Eighteen months ago that was closer to 40%.

I went to Salesforce's Dreamforce '26 to understand one thing, how AI is changing the way revenue actually gets handled. 

Not just quote to cash, but all of it. 

When the SKU is being built, when the deal is being negotiated, when the forecast is being analyzed, when performance is being reviewed, and when the numbers are being disclosed. 

So I spent two days talking to finance pros on the floor.

That jump from 40 to nearly 100 was the theme I heard again and again. 

The deals are more complex, the obligations messier, and recognizing revenue on all of it is exponentially harder.

Salesforce's revenue roadmap leans straight into this. It was packed with AI to mine and improve the value across your entire quote to cash process. For example, there was a clean demo of using claude to rapidly build a deal from a massive product catalog and optimizing for pricing within the sellers constraints. It was natural, rapid, and delivered a real tangible and immediately impactful result. AI Force, especially where revenue is concerned, will help companies grow faster. 

It will also drag the job of managing all of it to the front of the line.

Is this a new business logic?

Yes and no. 

No, because handling complexity has always been the work. 

Yes, because we have never operated in a world where exceptions and complexity are the norm and the volume climbs nearly every single day.

Benioff put it well in the general session. "It's not the end of software. It's the end of software that makes humans do all the work." The death of SaaS is not coming any time soon.

Business logic is hard, especially at scale, and someone has to own it.

So of all the business logic you choose to prioritize, put the logic that lets you operationally handle revenue at the top. It is the one you cannot afford to get wrong.

That is what the two days affirmed for me about what we are building at RightRev. The derived revenue truth you need to move forward, and the agents that mine the value of that truth.

Have a plan of attack for revenue truth. 

Now.

author_headline: Senior Industry Advisor (TMT) | Helping organizations make clear decisions during moments of real transformation
summary: Paul Wilson, a senior industry advisor, argues Salesforce's new Guardian tool separates agent identity from users, making org data models and sharing rules the real asset.
post_text:
The Salesforce Renaissance: Your Org Was the Asset
 
Agents have identities now.
 
That was the announcement that mattered this week, not the one on the highlight reel.
 
Guardian shipped as an evolution of Shield and trusted services, and its center is agent identity held separately from the user who invoked it. An agent acting on behalf of one of your reps is not that rep acting.
 
Everyone watched AIforce. The story was the locks.
 
Sam Taylor on our team at Coastal calls this the Salesforce Renaissance. A renaissance is not an invention. It is a rediscovery of foundations that were already there, suddenly worth more than anyone thought.
 
That is what happened to your org this year.
 
For twenty years we walked into rooms with people, process, technology. That does not hold anymore. It is people and agents, process, and the governed core.
 
Your objects, sharing model, validation rules and the data they protect are one artifact now, and an agent reads it directly. Nothing interprets for you.
 
Which changes what your configuration is worth.
 
The shallow layer gets cheap. Screens, guided flows, the automation built to walk a human through a process one field at a time. An agent needs none of it.
 
The deep layer becomes load-bearing. Data model, sharing rules, entitlements, validation. Agents inherit all of it and act faster than anyone reviewed it.
 
Now the part that will hurt.
 
Structure is the asset. Accumulated complexity is the tax.
 
An agent cannot navigate a workaround. It has no memory of why the third picklist exists, or that the real approval rule lives in a screen someone built in 2019 and left. A person routes around that without noticing. An agent walks into it and acts, confidently, at speed.
 
Decustomization is not cleanup. It is how you stay eligible for whatever ships next.
 
Here's the part I had wrong last year after Dreamforce '25: "All new still has to live inside all real. And all real is messy with overlapping systems, outdated data, and workflows that no one has touched since 2018."
 
I wrote that as a warning. Half of it was the advantage.
 
Every year your team spent modeling entitlements and arguing about sharing rules is why an agent can be trusted in your org. The overlapping systems and the untouched workflows are still the problem. Telling those two apart is the work.
 
So, what to tell your team on Monday: We can start this month without a budget cycle. Salesforce in Claude is in open beta, Agentforce Coworker is live. Our deep configuration makes agents trustworthy. That work already happened.
 
Before we build anything, we find out what our org tells an agent that we never meant to tell it.
 
And ask what it costs before building the dependency. AIforce arrived with no published price, same as Headless 360 in April.
 
Last year was about what we had to rebuild.
 
This year is about telling apart what we built from what we accumulated.
 
The renaissance isn't Salesforce's. It's your org's.

summary: Sebastian Hardung details Informatica's Dreamforce presence, citing MDM sessions, Agentic PIM announcements, and Savinay Berry's customer anecdotes on trusted data context.
post_text:
For me day three at Dreamforce came down to one company. Every session I sat in was about the role of Informatica in the wider Salesforce ecosystem, from the morning through to the closing keynote of the whole show, and it was packed.

I saw much the same team in May in Las Vegas, at Informatica World. Much of the argument was familiar. What changed is where it sits now: in Vegas a data company made its own case to its own audience, here it arrived as one layer inside a much bigger stack, in front of a Salesforce crowd.

▪️ Trusted context. The clearest version of it came off the keynote stage: a model will know what an order is, but it will not know that the order belongs to that customer, that the customer has called three times because they still don't have it, or that the inventory is stuck in Italy right now. From the MDM session: the hallucinations created by bad data are worse than the ones created by the model itself.

▪️ Data quality as a cost line. Three sessions argued it as spend rather than as correctness. "Nowadays we measure money in tokens." The mechanism is simple: an agent that does not know which data to look at will reason, search and discover over and over, and you pay for every lap.

▪️ Product data, from the stage instead of from me, for the first time this week. Agentic PIM was named in the MDM announcement set, with product onboarding and product narratives as agent work. Informatica has carried that positioning on its Product 360 pages since last year, so the label isn't news. The room it was said in is. The guest from Workday put the business end of it in one line: the faster you get a product on the shelves, the faster that SKU is money ready to be made.

▪️ Two anecdotes, which is how the closing keynote opened. Savinay Berry had been EVP & GM, Data Management for 72 hours when Informatica World opened in May. He picked two of the 50-plus customer conversations he has had since, as the two ends of one spectrum. A CIO at a aerospace company: agents built all over the company and he isn't sure where they are or what they do, while a separate team has run data management for more than ten years, and the two are not really talking. Then a CIO at a manufacturer buying up distributors: forget agents, forget AI, how do I just master my data.

Dreamforce closed with a comedy hour. Jim Gaffigan, mostly on family and on the joy of doing nothing, with one line about loving his family more when he is away from them, a fondness that grows right up until he walks through the door. Fair timing, the evening before I fly home.

Three days in, the strongest impression is the community. Ohana is the word Marc Benioff uses for it, and on day one Steve Molis said the same thing on the main stage about people he has never met face to face. After this week I understand why it sticks. The whole trip was worth it, and I'm looking forward to the flight home and to letting all of it sink in.

author_headline: CEO Oomnitza | Investor | Board Member | Advisor | Mental Health Advocate
summary: Oomnitza CEO Robert Potter argues after Dreamforce that CMDBs aren't broken but need an independent system establishing trusted enterprise technology state for AI agents.
post_text:
I was wrong about the CMDB.

I’ve been focused on what was wrong with the traditional CMDB.

But after two days at Dreamforce, I think I had the symptoms right, but the diagnosis wrong.

The CMDB isn’t broken. It was designed for a different era, with fewer systems, fewer sources of IT data, and far less autonomous action.

Modeling operational context and relationships is still important.

The challenge is ensuring the technology state reaching the CMDB and every other system relying on it is complete, reconciled and trustworthy.

As the Agentic Enterprise expands, that raises a different architectural question:

Who establishes whether the underlying enterprise technology state can actually be trusted?

I increasingly think that’s a different job. And there’s a structural reason why.

Enterprise technology truth doesn’t live in one system.

ServiceNow knows operational state. Salesforce knows customer and service context. CrowdStrike security. Okta identity. Workday people. Procurement what was purchased. Finance what it costs. Cloud and SaaS platforms what is being consumed.

Each knows part of the truth.

If trusted enterprise IT state must serve multiple Systems of Work, security, HR and financial platforms, and AI agents, can the function that establishes that trust logically belong to any one of them❓

Other consequential systems have confronted versions of this problem.

Cybersecurity moved from implicit trust toward continuously verified trust. Financial systems separate execution from authorization, reconciliation and audit.

As the consequence of an incorrect decision increases, independently establishing trust becomes more important.

AI raises those consequences. An inaccurate record that once produced a bad report or ticket can now cause an agent to make a bad decision or execute a costly action.

That makes provenance, completeness, reconciliation, lifecycle state and governance more important, not less.

Here is how I now think of the Agentic Enterprise:

➡️Systems of Work + AI Agents
Reason, decide and act.

➡️CMDB / Service Graph / Discovery
Provide operational context and relationships using trusted technology state.

➡️Independent System of Trust
Establish complete, reconciled and governed technology state across the systems that collectively know the truth.

We do not need a replacement for the CMDB. We need a trust layer to improve the accuracy of every system consuming enterprise IT state.

The more agentic the enterprise becomes, the more important one question becomes:

❓Who establishes the truth before agents act?

author_headline: CEO, Chestnut Compute Corp
summary: Marc Etherington reports Salesforce suffered a 3.5-hour global outage during Dreamforce, caused by a legacy login server dependency failure, questioning CRM reliance.
post_text:
Salesforce went down globally during its own Dreamforce keynote last week.
The outage ran roughly 3.5 hours (12:50am–4:19am PDT, Sept 16), hitting "hundreds of instances" across every region — logins, APIs, even the ability to open a support case. The stated cause: a legacy login server had an external dependency failure, and the resulting stalled requests backed up until they overloaded core platform components.
The timing is what makes it worth sitting with. This is the company that just spent its flagship conference telling the market to hand AI agents deeper, more autonomous access to their CRM data and workflows. Hours later, a single authentication component took the whole platform down — for every customer, everywhere, all at once.
Info-Tech Research Group's take on it is the sharper point: "cloud does not eliminate architectural dependencies — it can sometimes make them less visible." A component's age isn't the risk. Its position in the dependency graph, its blast radius, and the quality of its isolation are. When thousands of companies share one system of record, one hidden dependency becomes everyone's outage at once.
Worth asking before your next renewal: if your CRM vendor's login service has a bad night, what happens to your business that night?

author_headline: CEO & Founder @ Maven AGI
summary: Jonathan Corbin, Maven AGI CEO, questions Benioff's claim that agents return hours to employees, citing Tripadvisor's 90% and Mastermind's 93% autonomous resolution rates.
post_text:
Marc Benioff told Dreamforce this week that Salesforce is not seeing customers cut headcount because of agents. The hours, he said, are being given back to employees.

A year ago, same man: support went from 9,000 people to about 5,000, because he needed less heads.

The new sentence is the harder one to deliver.

Given back is not a number. It is a claim about where the time went, and I have yet to sit in the meeting where anyone audits it. Any team running agents in production can quote me their resolution rate from memory. Ask the same team what the recovered hours bought and you get a pause.

Tripadvisor does not pause. 90% of incoming queries handled autonomously, for a support team covering 30,000 hotels and restaurants across 43 countries, and Rahul Todkar's own line is that it put his agents on strategic work.

Mastermind.com does not pause. 93% of live chat answered autonomously six weeks in, and the team used it to carry more customers through peak rather than fewer people through the same volume.

That is what capacity looks like when somebody wrote down where it went.

Gartner said last week that 30% of the people cut in AI-driven layoffs will be rehired by 2029, and that customer service is the bellwether. That bill lands on the companies that cut first and counted later.

The hours are real. Someone has to say where they went.

Sources: Marc Benioff at Dreamforce 2026, reported by InformationWeek, September 15; the Logan Bartlett Show, September 2025; Gartner via CX Dive, September 11 2026; Tripadvisor and Mastermind results on mavenagi.com.

summary: AI advisor Liza Adams recaps keynotes by Dario Amodei, Marc Benioff and Jensen Huang, then details her CMO fireside chat with Leandro Perez and Erin Oles.
post_text:
Salesforce's Dreamforce gave me AI, CMOs, and Gwen Stefani singing “Don’t Speak” live during the keynote. That made for a pretty good Tuesday.

Dario Amodei (Anthropic) said companies may be capturing only 5 to 10% of the value AI can already provide. Marc Benioff (Salesforce) showed people, agents, data, and applications working together. Jensen Huang (NVIDIA) talked about AI moving from knowing to doing. That 5 to 10% estimate is consistent with what I’m seeing across marketing teams.

That afternoon, I joined Leandro Perez, SVP & CMO, ANZ at Salesforce, and Erin Oles, CMO of Salesforce, for a fireside chat and Q&A with CMOs from some of the world’s largest companies.

I love how openly people are sharing what they’re trying, learning, and still figuring out. In 25+ years in tech, I don’t remember another period with this much openness and generosity.

I shared what I’m seeing as a practitioner working with marketing teams through AI transformation. I’m hesitant to call any of this a “best practice” yet. We’re still writing them, and their shelf life may be short. What I can share is pattern recognition from the teams I work with.

A few things I shared:

► What teams use and build with AI is limited by what they believe it can do. Four mindset shifts can expand that view: use AI as a sparring partner; see faster as the starting point, then reimagine work so we can do things that weren’t possible before; move from tool to teammate to orchestrated workflow; and move from org charts to work charts so work can cross functions instead of getting trapped in silos.

► Assess existing workflows before applying AI. Sort them into five buckets: speed it up, sharpen it, rethink it, build something new, or stop doing it.

► We can’t drive AI transformation when people are stuck in a hamster wheel. Reprioritize work, give people time and a safe place to learn, show what’s possible, run hands-on keyboard workshops, and create ways for people to share what they’re learning.

► The leadership traits I see repeatedly are intellectual humility, intense curiosity, and the ability to meet people where they are with grace and compassion.

For me, that’s People First, AI Forward in practice.

BTW, if it’s true that Gwen is 56, then I must be 82. 😂 She looked and sounded fantastic.

author_headline: Founder & CEO at Sentire Tech | Co-Lead Scotland Salesforce Admin Group | Driving Innovation & High-Performing Teams
summary: Sameer W details Salesforce's AIforce umbrella covering Claudeforce, Slackforce and Agentforce Coworker, plus the Enterprise AI Harness, Koa model, seven prebuilt agents, and Google/AWS partnerships.
post_text:
Dreamforce 2026 is a wrap. There was a lot more here than just keynotes — so here's the fuller picture, for anyone who couldn't watch it all.

The big idea: Salesforce is betting its future isn't the screen you log into, it's the data, logic and permissions underneath, available wherever you already work.

AIforce is the umbrella for that. Underneath it: Claudeforce (Salesforce inside Claude, now in open beta via AppExchange), Slackforce (Slackbot with new "Surfaces" — live, interactive Salesforce data inside a Slack conversation), and Agentforce Coworker for teams staying in Lightning. Same underlying idea, three different front doors.

Holding it all together is what Salesforce is calling the Enterprise AI Harness — six products working as one stack: Informatica gets your data AI-ready, Data 360 turns it into real customer context, Tableau defines what your business terms actually mean, Guardian (the old Trust Layer) handles security and agent identity, MuleSoft's Agent Fabric governs and costs-out every agent you run, and Agentforce Studio is where it all gets built. Unglamorous, but it's the part that decides whether any of this actually works at scale.

On the model side: Koa, a CRM-specific reasoning model built with NVIDIA on Nemotron, purpose-built for sales/service/marketing actions — not trying to be a general frontier model, just very good at CRM.

And rather than asking every customer to build their own agents, Salesforce shipped seven ready-made ones: Casey and Fin for service, Paige for HR/IT, Carter for shopping, Piper for inbound leads, Marshall for supply chain, Hunter for outbound sales. Turn on, configure, go — no IT project required.

Two partnership expansions worth knowing: Google Cloud (Hyperforce running natively on Google infrastructure, Salesforce data surfacing inside Gemini Enterprise, Commerce checkout inside Google Search) and AWS (Salesforce data in Amazon Quick, AWS agents inside Slack, full Bedrock model access including Anthropic and NVIDIA, and live agent-to-agent handoff between Amazon Connect and Agentforce Voice).

One small but telling detail: "Agentforce Sales," "Agentforce Service" etc. have quietly reverted to Sales Cloud, Service Cloud, Marketing Cloud. Agentforce is the AI layer now, not a rebrand of every product.

Zoom out and it's one architecture, not a dozen separate announcements: open up the interface, harden the data and governance underneath it, and let AI meet you wherever you're already working.

That's the theory. Now the real test starts — off the show floor and into the field. I'll be going coast to coast over the coming weeks meeting customers and partners across the US, and I want it straight from you: what's actually working, what's still more demo than reality, and where you need help closing that gap.

author_headline: Delivering data integration and intelligence market insights to software vendors and best practices to enterprises.
summary: Stewart Bond compares Dreamforce and Alation's revAlation, citing IDC survey data showing 39% rank data quality and 38% rank AI-readiness as top priorities.
post_text:
Two very different conferences, one very consistent message.
This week took me from Dreamforce #DF26 (Salesforce) in San Francisco to #revAlation (Alation) in Chicago. The throughline: agents are only as good as the data and context underneath them, and that capability is forcing a serious governance conversation.
At Dreamforce, the story was Salesforce's stack coming together around business context: Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, and AIforce. All oriented around giving agents the business-function context they need within familiar workflows like sales, service, and marketing.
At revAlation, Alation told a complementary story from the data layer up. Its new AIOS is built to deliver governed data products and enterprise knowledge to agents, paired with agent governance, so organizations can trust the outcomes agents produce.
IDC research data backs up what I heard on both stages. In our most recent Worldwide Data Management Survey (n=715), data quality and trustworthiness (39%) and data readiness for generative and agentic AI (38%) are now the top two data management priorities, well ahead of readiness for traditional AI/ML (28%). A separate IDC QuickPoll found that 56% of organizations named data quality improvement as their top data readiness priority for AI, with 43% citing data intelligence work, such as cataloging and lineage, close behind.
That is the pattern I heard echoed at both conferences. Metadata and the intelligence built on top of it keep surfacing as the foundational layer that makes agentic AI trustworthy. Without it, "context" for an agent is just a guess, and last year's IDC FutureScape predicts that organizations that do not prioritize high-quality, AI-ready data will face a 20% loss in productivity as they try to scale agentic solutions.
A comment from a CISO at a major systems integrator stuck with me, too. "The mean time to exploit has now outpaced the mean time to patch." That is not only a security statistic. It is a signal of the pace at which the whole AI and data stack is now moving.
Innovation is arriving fast this fall conference season. The real question is not whether these capabilities are real. It is about how quickly and responsibly organizations can adopt them, backed by data.

post_text:
Dreamforce dropped about a dozen announcements this week. If you're on an integration team, only three of them actually matter.

1. AIforce - and the Headless Toolkit underneath it
Salesforce's headline announcement lets people work entirely inside Claude, Slack, or wherever they already are, without ever opening the Salesforce UI. The interface is the part getting attention. The part worth actually paying attention to is what's underneath it: the Headless Toolkit - MCP servers, APIs, plug-ins, and developer tooling that make that interface possible at all. No integration layer, no AIforce.

2. Claudeforce - governance was the real pitch
Salesforce's expanded partnership with Anthropic ships as a plugin with 37 prebuilt sales skills, powered by that same MCP-based harness. "Zero data retention" was repeated on stage more than any single product name. That's telling - Salesforce isn't selling trust on the model. It's selling trust on the governance layer wrapped around it.

3. Koa - Salesforce's first CRM reasoning model
Worth knowing it exists. Less structurally important than the two above, since a reasoning model still depends entirely on the same context and governance layer to be useful on real enterprise data.

The pattern across all of it - AIforce, Claudeforce, and the Google Cloud and Amazon Web Services (AWS) expansions from earlier this week - is the same bet: agents are only as good as the integration and governance layer connecting them to real data. That's the actual story of this Dreamforce, even though it wasn't the one on stage.

post_text:
Salesforce’s AI lineup now needs its own onboarding session. 😂

Our cheat sheet:

Einstein = the established CRM AI feature family: predictions, scoring, recommendations and generative features.

Agentforce = build and run agents with context, tools and actions. Named job agents include Hunter for outbound, Casey for service and Paige for employee support.

AIforce = the interface strategy. Claudeforce brings Salesforce into Claude; Slackforce brings Salesforce context, actions and interactive views into Slack; Agentforce Coworker works in Lightning and calls specialized agents.

Koa = a NVIDIA Nemotron-based CRM reasoning model for Agentforce. It isn’t a separate finished workflow.

Enterprise AI Harness = architecture connecting context, actions, governance, security and model access across Salesforce and other systems. Foundations exist; its unified experience and new capabilities are planned from early FY28.

Keep availability separate from the names: Salesforce in Claude is in beta; Hunter is in pilot with a November 2026 GA target; Koa has selected pilots and a winter 2026 U.S. GA target.

Start with one workflow. Identify the interface, agent, systems and exception owner. Then add three columns:

Available today | Included in our contract | Someone owns it

The naming quiz is optional. Those three columns aren’t.

🚨 Salesforce Wants AI Agents Running Your Business. Then Its Own Platform Went Down

Salesforce spent this week's Dreamforce keynote telling every customer that AI agents are ready to run their business operations. Then Salesforce's own systems went down for hours, mid-event, with login failures and delays hitting customers across multiple regions. 😅

And honestly, I think there’s a bigger lesson here than “Salesforce had an outage.”

It’s the gap between the AI pitch and the plumbing underneath it. 🔧

Every major platform wants us to believe AI agents can handle:
→ Sales operations
→ Support tickets
→ Internal workflows
→ Production decisions

But before we hand agents more responsibility, I want to know something much more boring:
Will the system still be there when I need it?

My take: reliability is becoming an AI moat.

Models will keep getting better.
Agent demos will keep getting flashier.
But uptime, incident response, failover, observability, and recovery?
Those are what determine whether AI actually works in production.

The real AI question isn't just:
“What can your agent do?”
It's:
“What happens when everything goes wrong?” 🚨
Infrastructure may be boring.
Until it isn't.

Les données, les règles métier et la gouvernance, elles, resteront l’actif le plus précieux de l’entreprise. L’avantage stratégique de l’IA agentique se construit sur une plateforme qui relie l'intelligence des modèles à la réalité des métiers tout en permettant la liberté de choix.

D'où une responsabilité nouvelle. Mesurer ce que les agents produisent. Encadrer ce qu'ils font. Maîtriser ce qu'ils coûtent. Et surtout, organiser une collaboration fructueuse entre les équipes et ces nouveaux coéquipiers. La gouvernance humaine doit avancer au rythme des capacités des agents.

summary: Piyush Chandra argues AI agents need clean account hierarchies and deduplication, warning messy records let agents act wrongly at machine speed.
post_text:
I saw a lot of excitement about AI agents at Dreamforce. Understandably — there's real substance behind it.
 
But I keep coming back to two things that get less airtime, and that I think will quietly decide how trustworthy those agents actually are: Account hierarchies and duplicates.
 
It makes sense that they're not front and center. Nobody builds a keynote around entity resolution. There's no reasoning trace to show, no action to demo. "We figured out that Acme Corp, Acme Inc, and the ACME your SDR created last Tuesday are the same company" doesn't make the highlight reel.
 
So demos tend to start after that part is already handled. The customer is resolved, the hierarchy is clean, identity is assumed. And in a lot of real orgs, that's the part that's still a work in progress.
 
Here's why I think it matters more now than it used to.
 
A person reading a dashboard sees "Acme — $2M" and "ACME — $1.4M" and pauses. Their gut says: those are probably the same, let me check.
 
An agent is less likely to pause.
 
It reasons over both records, rolls the numbers up to whatever it reads as the parent, and can act on that at machine speed.
 
Duplicates and messy hierarchies used to be mostly a reporting-accuracy problem — something you'd catch at review time. As agents start taking action, they become more of an operational one, because the action can happen before anyone reviews it.
 
And "which account is the parent" isn't always a clean question to begin with. Legal, sales, billing, and the territory view can be four different structures over the same entities — and they don't always agree. M&A keeps them moving.
 
The exciting part of AI is the agent. The part that decides whether it works is the account record underneath it.

The honest number at Dreamforce was not in the main keynote.

It was in the manufacturing keynote on Wednesday. Salesforce thanked the room for its honesty and read the result back. Only 10% of you use AI to do real work. Same company, the day after the keynote that opened with agents everywhere.

Then they brought up a customer who had made it work. PPG's chief digital officer, on what came before the agents. Fifty acquisitions in ten years. About 32 ERP systems. Almost no product catalog built out. Two years of mapping all of it with two integrators, eight of nine business units, on time and on budget. Nineteen straight quarters of flat or falling organic volume before that work, six quarters of growth after it.

The line from the stage was that AI without context is a fast guesser, and that all of this is digital Jenga, where a messy bottom makes anything you build on top wobbly. Salesforce is right about both. Its own customers had just told it that 90% of them are still down there.

So the 10% is not an adoption gap. It is the group that already did the estate work, and that work took years.

Nobody gets PPG's two years before the board asks for agents. What you can do is read the estate before you fund anything on top of it. Four weeks, read only, a written answer on whether it supports what you are about to build and what has to be fixed first.

author_headline: Practical Data and AI Perspectives
summary: Data/AI analyst Kevin Petrie describes Salesforce's Agent Context Engine (GA December), citing demos by Muralidhar Krishnaprasad and April M. on race-ticket and Lowe's customer-inquiry use cases.
post_text:
Phase 1 of context engineering will focus on familiar application tasks like customer inquiries and product purchases. Good - this is the safe way to start. 

This became clear to me at Dreamforce this week as Salesforce showcased use cases for its Agent Context Engine, slated for GA in December.

During Phase 2, enterprises will customize their approach, tap more unstructured data, and federate across more diverse sources.

Let's start with a definition.

Context engineering is the tricky discipline of preparing and delivering context - i.e., selected data and metadata - to AI agents.

Done right, this requires:

- A semantic layer that translates source data into consistent, business-friendly context

- Conceptual models such as glossaries, ontologies, and taxonomies that describe how concepts and entities inter-relate 

- Reusable prompts for GenAI models 

- Search and retrieval mechanisms for multi-structured data

- Memory that stores context for reuse

- Security and governance controls that enforce policies, rules, and standards

That's a daunting list.

And I think that's why Phase 1 of context engineering will leverage and expand existing logical workflows and business processes.

Enterprise application vendors can help a lot here.

Muralidhar Krishnaprasad (MK) and April M. of Salesforce showed how this can work for race ticket purchases and Lowe's customer inquiries.

Their excellent demos showed how Salesforce integrates data, learns, and intelligently helps users get what they need faster.

They even engage third-party sources and applications.

All this delivers incremental results without complex data engineering.

I think that Context Engineering Phase 2, yet to come, will have higher rewards... and risks.

During this phase, data engineers, data scientists, ML engineers and developers will build custom workflows to create competitive advantage based on their proprietary knowledge.

This will involve deep analysis of enterprise documents, carefully classified, tagged, and cataloged.

It will empower smart employees to discover new value and build new revenue streams.

It will require teams to govern inputs, scrutinize outputs, and fix hallucinations. The governance guardrails will not be so clear.

Phase 2 will also be more complex. While agentic vibe-coding will help, innovation here will require some expert developers.

What do you think? Are you in Phase 1 or 2 of context engineering?

post_text:
Este año estoy viviendo Dreamforce de Salesforce desde otra óptica 😉. Y me ha impresionado cómo Marc Benioff y su equipo trasladan una visión clara: la IA y los servicios tradicionales no compiten, coexisten. Y cuando la IA está en el centro, el ecosistema crece de formas que hace un año ni imaginábamos. Estos son mis 5 hot topics:

1. AIforce:  La IA reemplaza la interfaz: SF deja de ser la “App” y pasa a ser una capa invisible que vive detrás de Claude, Slack, Teams. Los equipos accederán a Salesforce sin tocar la interfaz tradicional. Adiós curvas de aprendizaje interminables. Adopción inmediata. Así es el futuro del CRM empresarial.

2. Koa: modelo de razonamiento nativo para CRM: Primer modelo de Salesforce entrenado en 27 años de datos reales de clientes. Dicen supera o iguala el rendimiento de los modelos líderes en acciones CRM con 3 veces menos errores. Esto no es un modelo genérico adaptado. Es un CRM optimizado desde cero. Eso importa cuando la precisión es tu margen.

3. Claudeforce: Salesforce como servidor integrado en Claude Esto ya lo venia leyendo en varios medios especializados y desde ayer ya es oficial. 37 skills de ventas preconstruidas. Los comerciales trabajan en Claude, acceden a datos de Salesforce sin cambiar de contexto. Anthropic + Salesforce alineadas en la estrategia empresarial.

4. Slackforce: contexto de Salesforce vive en tus conversaciones. El contexto de clientes, oportunidades, cuentas aparece en Slack. Slackforce Surfaces genera interfaces dinámicas dentro del chat, sin salir de la herramienta. Menos cambios de ventana. Más fluidez operativa.

5. 7 agentes listos para producción: Casey, Fin, Agentforce Coworker. De lo más llamativo y también más fácil y rápido en términos de adopción, 7 agentes configurables por administradores que resuelven consultas de clientes, atienden en voz y digital, funcionan sobre sistemas terceros. Implementación en semanas, no meses. Automatización que realmente llega a producción.

Salesforce ya no apuesta por ser el más completo. Apuesta por ser la capa de inteligencia invisible detrás de donde tú ya trabajas: Claude, Slack, Teams, Lightning. ¡Eso es un gamechanger total!

author_headline: Founder & Principal Analyst, InFlow Analysis | The Architect of Flow | Digital Workplace, AI & CX Strategy | Guiding the Shift from Static Tools to Intelligent Orchestration
summary: Analyst David Smith argues Dreamforce showed democratized agent-building alongside a new governance control plane, crediting Marc Benioff's honesty about data and human-in-the-loop limits.
post_text:
Great week at Dreamforce 2026 and lots to discuss! So, two things went on the same stage at Dreamforce this week. First, democratization. Everyone can build now. Headless architecture, an interface that assembles itself, agents you can hire off the shelf with first names on them. Second, a control plane. One registry for every agent wherever it runs. Security for the data they reach. Governance for what they're allowed to touch.

Now, you don't build the second thing for a problem you haven't already had. And that's the useful part, because it describes a sequence most of us are about to live through. You remove a constraint at one layer, and it shows up at the next one. Building got easy. Now the hard part is knowing what got built, what it costs, and who said yes. The constraint didn't disappear. It moved.

I watched it move three times this week. Deployment moved from the vendor into the customer, where a new kind of team now sits between IT and the business. Review moved downstream, because when agents produce more, somebody reads more. And judgment moved to whoever is still checking, which gets harder once the agent has a name and starts to feel like a colleague.

Credit where it's due though, as Marc Benioff especially and the speakers were very deliberate in tone and pace. They were honest about the data problem, they earned their terminology before using it, and someone said out loud that human-in-the-loop doesn't survive contact with agents. That's a more mature position than most of this industry holds.

But here's the habit I'm taking home. When somebody tells you a thing got faster, don't ask whether the work went away. Ask where it went.

Huge shoutout to the Salesforce Market Strategy team, you guys rock!!! 
#DF26

Adecco said this week it is rolling Salesforce's Agentforce Coworker out to 27,000 of its own employees across more than 40 countries, after pilots in the UK and France. Recruiters there launch pre-screening and onboarding agents from inside the platform. Agentic AI is already live in recruitment in ten countries that make up half of Adecco's revenue, and the company says candidates have had more than 2.5 million interactions with these agents since April 2025. Adecco's CEO told the Dreamforce keynote that recruiters are saving 35% to 40% of their time. Those are Adecco's figures, offered from a stage, not an auditor's.

Now open your own AI policy with a staffing agreement next to it. The policy governs your employees and the tools your company bought. It does not govern a recruiter in Adecco's UK operation running a pre-screening agent across a pool of your applicants, on a model nobody at your company selected, and it never will.

You are still the employer. If that agent quietly sorts out the people who took eighteen months away from work, that lands on your req, not on Adecco's Salesforce license.

So go pull the master services agreement with your largest staffing supplier and look for language on automated screening, candidate data retention, audit rights, and who carries the liability when a tool sorts someone out. Most of those agreements were signed before any of this existed. They say nothing, which is its own kind of answer.

What share of your hires last year came through an agency, and do you know what screened them before you saw them?

post_text:
When I joined Salesforce, Rahul Auradkar asked me to look into a problem that sounded deceptively simple:

What are we going to do about unstructured data?

At the time, so much of the enterprise's most valuable knowledge was sitting outside traditional databases: PDFs, contracts, presentations, support documents, emails, call transcripts, images, and countless other fragmented sources.

The challenge wasn't simply ingesting that data. 
The real challenge was turning it into trusted, usable context for AI.

That started a journey that has taken us from connecting fragmented unstructured data sources to building an end-to-end data and AI pipeline — including:
 → Document ingestion and processing
 → Intelligent parsing and extraction
 → Semantic chunking
 → Enrichment and metadata
 → Embedding generation
 → Semantic indexing and retrieval
 → RAG
 → GraphRAG and relationship-aware retrieval
 → Accuracy evaluation and tuning
 → Governance, observability and trust

And every layer mattered because the model can only be as good as the context we give it.

We weren't building "unstructured data support."

We were building the context layer that allows Agentforce to understand the enterprise.

That work evolved into Intelligent Context and the broader Data 360 unstructured data capabilities powering Agentforce.

And recently, at the Data 360 keynote, seeing +800% growth in unstructured data processed was a pretty incredible moment.

Because behind that number isn't just technology.

It's months of solving hard problems with an incredible team led by Raveendrnathan Loganathan, Anil Nori,, Adithya Nittor Vishwanath, Palaniappa Ramanathan figuring out how to make enterprise data usable, searchable, connected, governed and ultimately trustworthy for AI. Great job by our architects, engineers, designers, content, PM, TPM, and my excellent PM team led by Hannan Saltzman, Kartik Muktinutalapati

We've also been sharing more of the technical journey publicly.

Looking back, Rahul's original question — "What are we going to do about unstructured data?" — turned into something much bigger.

We didn't just solve for unstructured data.

We built a foundation for turning the enterprise's fragmented knowledge into trusted context for AI.

And I think we're still just getting started.

author_headline: Principal, US Health & Human Services Lead
summary: Amiran Gelashvili, a KPMG health/human-services lead, argues Dreamforce showed deterministic, auditable, caseworker-in-the-loop AI must precede speed for Medicaid and SNAP eligibility decisions.
post_text:
The LLMs we're marveling at today will be the SLOWEST models we ever use again. 
And maybe— speed isn't the story. Trust is.

As I wrap up an incredible week at #Dreamforce, one truth kept surfacing across every keynote, demo, and hallway conversation: the organizations that will lead the next decade of AI aren't the ones chasing the biggest model — they're the ones building the most responsible, effective, and auditable systems.

Nowhere is this more critical than in Health & Human Services. 🏛️❤️

When we're determining Medicaid eligibility, processing SNAP benefits, or supporting a family in crisis, "move fast and break things" isn't a strategy — it's a liability. Real people. Real benefits. Real consequences.

Here's what I'm taking home from Dreamforce for HHS leaders:
-Deterministic > Probabilistic for policy decisions. Eligibility rules aren't a guessing game. Policy-as-code ensures 100% auditability and zero hallucinations where it matters most.
-Agents belong in the flow of work, not on the decision seat. Let agentic AI handle verification triage, document synthesis, and notice drafting — so caseworkers can focus on people.
-Caseworker-in-the-loop is non-negotiable. The future frontline worker isn't replaced by AI — they're amplified by it. Faster case cycles. Less burnout. Better outcomes for families.
-The winners will be the ones who build for compliance FIRST, then layer in speed and scale. Responsible AI isn't a brake pedal — it's the foundation.

The LLMs of tomorrow will be exponentially faster, cheaper, and more capable. But the organizations that win will be the ones who never confused fast with right.

For HHS, responsible AI isn't a feature. It's the mission.

Day 3 of Dreamforce, and Slack was the headline.

Salesforce called it the front door to the Agentic Enterprise, no longer just a messaging app, but an entry point into the broader Salesforce ecosystem.

Benioff also shared that Slack is now Salesforce’s fastest-growing product. The idea is simple: the intelligence and context inside Salesforce should show up wherever teams are already working, without constantly switching systems.

If you rewind to Day 1, this is exactly where the week was heading. #AIforce made the case for business data and logic moving beyond the boundaries of one application and becoming accessible wherever work happens.

Day 2 showed what that can look like in practice. Fulton Bank went from zero to 20+ live use cases in a few weeks and saved 80,000 hours.
And then… day 3 brought that same principle into Slack.

The Marketing Cloud keynote extended it into marketing, with agents now able to understand customer and brand signals, execute against goals, and continuously adapt campaigns.

PalMATA, Campaign Agent, and the broader move toward agentic marketing, all point in the same direction.

Three days of Dreamforce, and here's what I keep coming back to: It's easy to walk out of a keynote impressed by a demo. It's harder to ask whether your own business is actually ready for it.

That’s why I ask every business leader I speak with: “Would your company’s data hold up if you added an agent tomorrow?”
For many, the answer is still no.

Not because the tools aren't good enough, but because the foundation underneath them isn't ready yet.

That’s why showing ChargeOn live at Booth #540 mattered to me.

ChargeOn already runs on Agentforce and Headless 360, so we could show what this looks like in practice rather than just talk about it.

The conversations were specific: features, payment setups, and integrations. And the reaction often changed the moment people saw it running live.

That’s my biggest takeaway from Dreamforce 2026:
The real value of this next wave of AI won't come from the flashiest agent. It will come from having the data and foundation ready to support it.

If this week left you excited but unsure where your own setup stands, that’s a conversation worth having.

author_headline: Forward Deployed Engineer | Agentforce Champion | Bridging the Gap Between Technology & Strategy
summary: Victor Noe, a Forward Deployed Engineer, reflects on his first Dreamforce as an official Salesforce resource, thanking mentors John Bates, Ken Taylor and Rebecca O Gargis.
post_text:
Change sure seems fast when you're just scrolling through a camera roll. But the reality is that most of the breakneck changes you see are a direct result of a ton of failures, iterations, and one or two life-defining "AH-HA" moments.

If you had told the guy (and the other guy who was apparently living inside of him) that in a little over a decade he would be a healthy and vaguely handsome bald dude manning "Ask an Agentforce Expert" booths and conducting demos in SICs, he would have said, "What the hell is an Agentforce?" Then he would have been very excited for the future. But he still wouldn't have known about all of the hard work, all of the failures, and all of the joys that were prevalent on the journey. If he jumped to the current day and started living life in my (our?) body, he would be much worse off because of it.

This is an incredibly important concept to keep in mind when thinking about the amazing functionality you want to bring to your organization. Not having enough distance between Start and Finish robs you of everything that comes between. Those gigantic failures and low-key successes are foundational to understanding how to scale even further once you reach your end state. Don't try to press an easy button and skip over them altogether. It won't be as glamorous as you think.

As I reflect on my first Dreamforce as an official Salesforce resource, I am overcome with gratitude. Gratitude for leaders and friends who helped shape my career into what it is, like John Bates  and Rebecca O Gargis . Gratitude for teachers along the way, like Ken Taylor , who taught me what it was to be a responsible IT professional. Gratitude for current colleagues and leaders like Applonia C. , Chris McKrill , and Mackenzie Coats , who are providing support and setting a seemingly unattainable bar to match (but that won't stop me from trying). But ultimately, I have gratitude for me. As egotistical as that sounds, I think it's important that we all express gratitude for ourselves, because we're the ones who got us to where we are at the end of the day. 

Go us. Keep on keeping on. I can't wait to scroll through the camera roll in a few years, see how much has changed, and reflect on how much I have learned.

summary: CMO Van Diamandakis reports Gil Allouche's Metadata agentic GTM produced ~30 meetings from 400 accounts using a ledger, deterministic gates and 99% confidence bar, contrasting it with Salesforce's new AIforce control plane.
post_text:
Gil Allouche runs Metadata's go-to-market with agents. Three weeks in, by his count, the motion had produced about 30 meetings from a target list of roughly 400 accounts.

He showed how at Hard Skill Exchange on September 8. Before any agent acts, three things exist. A ledger records every action before it happens. Deterministic gates return the same answer to the same question, so the rules can be verified. A confidence bar shows the agent at 99%; below that, the agent asks.

He built all three himself, in code, around seven tools from four vendors. He is a software engineer with a decade of ad-platform patents.

Two days later, Salesforce announced a harness for the enterprise, with a control plane it says will govern agents "across Salesforce and third-party AI." Then it spent #Dreamforce building around it: AIforce, a CRM reasoning model, and agent partnerships with Google Cloud and AWS.

78% of executives lack strong confidence they could pass an AI governance audit. Nearly 3 in 4 are giving agents access to their data anyway. Most of them can't write what Gil wrote, and now two very different vendors are offering to sell it to them.

That is the piece I published today. The ledger, the gates, and the confidence bar are the operating system. The buying question is who controls it.

What stood out to me was how vulnerable each of the leaders was in sharing their lived experience. The power of authenticity and connection will only grow as we continue to delegate work to agents.

summary: Reej Consulting recaps Dreamforce 2026 keynote announcements: AIforce interface across Claude, Slack and Lightning; the Koa reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron; Salesforce Guardian security suite; and expanded Marshall agent capabilities.
post_text:
Lors de la keynote Dreamforce 2026, plusieurs annonces ont été présentées sur scène :

- AIforce
Une nouvelle couche d'interface IA qui rend les données, les processus et les règles de Salesforce exploitables là où les équipes travaillent. Elle se décline dans Claude, dans Slack et dans Lightning.
Concrètement : un dirigeant retrouve en un clic l'état de son pipeline, repère une opportunité bloquée par une revue de sécurité, puis envoie directement un message à son équipe sur Slack, sans quitter l'interface.

-Koa
Le premier modèle de raisonnement CRM de Salesforce, construit en étendant le modèle Nemotron de NVIDIA et entraîné sur des données synthétiques, sans aucune donnée client. Il est conçu pour les agents qui mènent des tâches longues et complexes.
Concrètement : c'est le modèle qui permet à un agent commercial de déterminer seul la meilleure action sur une négociation complexe, ou à un agent de support de trouver la bonne marche à suivre sur un dossier client difficile.

- Salesforce Guardian
Une suite de sécurité, évolution de Shield et des Trusted Services, centrée sur l'identité des agents, la détection des agents qui dérapent, la classification et la protection des données.
Concrètement : elle affiche la liste des agents jugés à risque selon leurs actions, et repère les données de l'entreprise qui ne sont ni classées ni protégées.

- De nouvelles capacités pour l'agent Marshall
Il apprend un processus dans un environnement de test, comme l'onboarding fournisseur dans SAP, puis l'exécute à partir d'une bibliothèque d'actions validées.
Concrètement : Marshall apprend rapidement ce qu'il faudrait des jours à un nouvel employé pour maîtriser, puis met à jour seul, sans intervention humaine, chaque champ du dossier fournisseur dans SAP.

C'est justement sur ces sujets de données, d'intégration et de gouvernance de l'IA que nos experts vous accompagnent.

author_headline: BDR Director at Salesforce | Ex LinkedIn, Intercom, PayPal, Corsearch, Lokalise
summary: Salesforce BDR Director Karl Connon claims AI assistants like Piper, Casey, Fin, Paige and Hunter will replace manual CRM logins by connecting to company databases via Slack, Claude, Teams.
post_text:
Software isn't dying, the boring, manual parts of it are. 

As I'm getting ready to head home after an epic experience at Dreamforce in San Francisco, i took some time to reflect on key messages and takeaways. 

3 keys points:
1. You might never log into your CRM again (edgey i know!): Instead of opening up complex software to manually log data, click around dashboards, or update statuses, you will just talk to the communication tools you already use daily (like Slack, Claude, Teams, and more)
The software will handle the backend work quietly by itself. 

2. AI needs a brain transplant to be useful: 
A generic AI chatbot (like standard ChatGPT) doesn't know anything about your business or your specific customers. It only becomes truly powerful when it is securely hooked up to your company's actual database (the CRM), giving it the facts it needs to make smart decisions.

3. Ready-made AI assistants are winning:
Companies do not want to always have to build complex AI tech from scratch. Often, they want simple, "plug-and-play" digital assistants that can start solving customer issues or automating tasks immediately right out of the box (Check out Piper, Casey, Fin, Paige, Hunter, and more)

Here's one example of this that was shared during the week that the entire audience had an ah-ha moment.

Imagine you run a busy customer support team.

The Old Way: A frustrated customer messages your team asking for an emergency refund. Your agent has to log out of their chat tool, open up a giant CRM database, search for the customer's account number, look up their payment history, check company policy, manually approve the refund, and then navigate back to reply to the customer. It takes 15 minutes of pure manual clicking.

The New Way: The customer messages your team. A pre-built AI assistant automatically recognizes the problem. Because it is safely plugged straight into your company database, it instantly reads the customer's history, verifies they qualify for a refund under company rules, processes it in the background, and drops a draft reply inside Slack for your agent to review.The agent clicks "send" without ever opening the CRM database. The software did all the heavy lifting, while the human just handled the final relationship check. That is the shift happening right now.

post_text:
My Reflections on Dreamforce 26:
Dreamforce impressed me this year with its sheer scale and star power — with 54,000 attendees watching Marc Benioff opening the Main Keynote in conversations with Dario Amodei, Jensen Huang, Roland Busch. Benioff unveiled AIforce as the next chapter of the AI revolution, alongside new Agentforce digital workers (Piper, Hunter, Casey, Fin) and Koa, a new CRM reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron. For me, the real highlight was the calibre of voices on AI's future, while I will always chuckle at Huang's energetic humour ("Bigger is not always better") , while staying sober with Amodei's grounded call for responsible, well-paced, transparently governed AI progress.

My theatre session : 6 Guiding Principles to maximise CRM adoption
This year I had the pleasure of co-presenting the theater session "6 Principles That Help Drive Faster CRM Adoption" alongside my brilliant colleague Matthew Shilvock. The session was fully booked out on both days, with standing attendance and excellent feedback.

We walked customers through our team's best practices for maximising CRM adoption — Know Your End Users, Lead with Data, Build an Adoption Committee, Plan for Change Management, Train-Learn-Repeat, and Commit to Simplicity — drawing on real examples from our work with our largest customers. It was a great opportunity to showcase the calibre of work our Customer Success teams do every day to drive real, lasting adoption for our customers, and to connect directly with attendees eager to apply these principles in their own organisations. A proud moment for the team, and a strong reflection of the value CS brings to the table.

Slack Keynote
This was such an inspiring keynote, with a simple but bold statement : Slack is the “Front Door” control centre for the agentic enterprise. With Slackbot acting as a superagent to orchestrate AI agents like Slackforce, Claudeforce, and Agentforce Coworker in channels and DMs, Slack is the company-wide human-AI interface layer—making AI a "team sport".

Agentic Commerce Keynote
I was not able to join the keynote live as it clashed with my own theatre speaker session, but was excited to read about the future of transactions, showcasing Salesforce agents that shop, negotiate, and transact on a customer's behalf. Driven by intent-focused search on Commerce Cloud and headless B2B commerce, it reframed commerce as a space where agents actively participate, signalling a future where checkout requires no human clicks.

Marketing Cloud Keynote
The Marketing Cloud keynote continued the same thread I saw across the week — AI moving from "helping marketers work faster" to "working alongside marketers as a teammate." The focus was on agents that can plan, personalise and execute campaigns end-to-end, grounded in real-time customer context from Data 360 so messaging stays relevant rather than generic at scale.

post_text:
🚀 Dreamforce 2026: 5 things Salesforce architects and developers should be watching

After this week’s announcements, one thing feels increasingly clear:

Salesforce is no longer positioning the CRM as the place where work happens. It’s positioning Salesforce as the intelligence and business-logic layer underneath where work happens.

Here are my top 5 things to watch:

1️⃣ AIforce — Salesforce beyond the UI

AIforce brings Salesforce capabilities into the interfaces where users and agents already work.

The architectural implication?

👉 CRM capabilities increasingly become services that can be consumed by humans, agents, and other applications — not just screens inside Salesforce.

2️⃣ Claudeforce + model choice

The partnership with Anthropic, combined with broader model-choice initiatives, reinforces an important direction:

Salesforce doesn’t necessarily need to own the model to own the enterprise context.

The competitive advantage increasingly shifts toward:
• Trusted enterprise data
• Business context
• Permissions
• Actions
• Governance

3️⃣ Headless 360 becomes much more important

Headless Salesforce isn’t just about building a custom UI anymore.

It becomes the foundation for exposing Salesforce capabilities to:

• AI agents
• External applications
• Digital experiences
• MCP-based integrations
• Other enterprise platforms

For architects, this means API and capability design becomes as important as UI design.

4️⃣ Agentforce Coworker

The evolution from “AI assistant” to digital coworker is significant.

The question for architects changes from:

“What can we automate?”

to:

“What work can an agent actually own?”

That introduces new architecture questions around permissions, orchestration, exception handling, human escalation, observability, and governance.

5️⃣ The Trusted Enterprise AI Harness

This may be one of the most important announcements for enterprise architects.

As agents gain the ability to take action, organizations need more than a good LLM.

They need guardrails around:

🔐 Identity
🔐 Data access
🔐 Permissions
🔐 Deterministic business rules
🔐 Monitoring
🔐 Governance

The agentic enterprise will be built on trust + intelligence + action.

My biggest takeaway

Dreamforce 2026 wasn’t simply about adding AI to Salesforce.

It was about changing where Salesforce lives in the enterprise architecture.

Salesforce is increasingly becoming the business context + data + action layer for humans AND agents.

And that creates a very different job for architects.

author_headline: Founder @Katalyz | Future 40
summary: Charles Merlet, Katalyz's founder, argues Dreamforce's 1,600 sessions focused on seller agents while ignoring buyers, citing Gartner's five-to-sixteen-person buying groups and 153% stat.
post_text:
Dreamforce is over. Three days, more than 1,600 sessions, over fifty keynotes.
 
But the buyer wasn't in the room.
 
One word was in nearly all of them: agent. Agents for reps. Agents for service. Agents for marketers. Agents that prep the call, score the deal, update the record, draft the follow-up, route the lead.
 
I went looking for the sessions about what the buyer receives at the other end of all that. There aren't many.
 
This isn't a complaint about Dreamforce. It describes where the industry's attention has sat for a decade. Call recording, conversation intelligence, forecasting, sequencers, enablement, coaching. Every one of them points at the same person: the seller.
 
Meanwhile the difficulty moved. It is on the buyer's side now. Gartner puts today's buying group at five to sixteen people across as many as four functions. A CFO who vetoes deals that were already approved. A security review that adds a quarter. A champion running a project they were never trained for.
 
Give a rep an agent and they produce more, faster. Give a buying committee nothing, and they still cannot agree.
 
Here is the uncomfortable version. Gartner measured buyers hit with too much good information, and information that contradicts itself, as 153% more likely to settle for a course of action smaller and less disruptive than the one they originally planned.
 
So we are about to get very good at producing more of the exact thing that makes buyers retreat.
 
Faster output into an unchanged coordination problem isn't a solution. It's volume.
 
Worth declaring my interest: this is the problem we build for at Katalyz. One room the buying committee actually works in, so the people who have to agree are at least looking at the same thing.
 
Not another tool for the seller. The first one designed for your buyer.
 
Does that sound familiar? I'd like to hear how it looks from your side 🙂
 
--
 
Hey, I'm Charles, co-founder and CEO at Katalyz — an AI-built dealroom for every deal, so you sell like you're always in the room.

post_text:
5 Key Takeaways from Dreamforce 2026 🚀
 
I tuned into Dreamforce 2026 virtually this year, and even from behind a screen, the message from Salesforce came through loud and clear: the future isn't about logging into a CRM — it's about meeting people where they already work.
 
Here's what stood out to me:
 
1. AIforce — CRM without the CRM screen
 Salesforce doesn't want workers logging into a CRM, digging through records and dashboards, and manually stitching together context before they can get anything done. AIforce is a live interface layer that pulls Salesforce's underlying intelligence into other AI and workplace tools — Slack, Claude, Amazon Q, Google's Gemini Enterprise, and Salesforce's own Agentforce Coworker.
 
2. Deep AI partnerships took center stage
 Watching the keynote stream, it was hard to miss how much airtime AI leaders got: Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei had ten minutes on stage, as did Nvidia's Jensen Huang, who's developed an AI agent with Salesforce — while Benioff spent 45 minutes with OpenAI's Sam Altman discussing slowing down AI development in the name of safety. Claudeforce also moved into open beta, and Slack got its own AI-focused refresh with Slackforce.
 
3. Seven "job-ready" AI agents launched
 Salesforce introduced Casey for customer service across voice, SMS, WhatsApp and chat; Paige for IT and HR requests; Carter for e-commerce; Marshall for supply chain and back-office orchestration; Piper for inbound sales qualification; Fin for complex customer experience workflows; and Hunter for outbound sales — all available now except Hunter, which stays in pilot until GA in November 2026.
 
4. It's all one architecture, not scattered features
 Salesforce named it the Enterprise AI Harness, spanning context, agency, action, governance, security and models — with deliberate cloud and model neutrality across Google Cloud, AWS, and Koa (running on Nvidia).
 
5. The ROI conversation is finally front and center — with some grumbling
 Rather than another big product reveal, Salesforce used much of its Agentforce keynote showcasing customers already getting measurable value from Agentforce. That said, even watching remotely, the chatter I saw echoed what attendees on the ground were saying: the extra fees for this AI future aren't sitting well with everyone.
 
My takeaway: Salesforce is betting its value doesn't live in its own UI anymore — it lives in the workflows, agents, and platforms people already use daily. Curious to see how fast that vision actually lands in day-to-day CRM work.

author_headline: 6x Salesforce Certified || Salesforce Developer || Omnistudio|| B2B ||Salesforce Developer at Cloud Analogy
summary: Salesforce developer Shubham Kumar details Salesforce's Sept 10 launch of MuleSoft Agent Fabric inside the Trusted Enterprise AI Harness, outlining integration patterns for External Services, Apex, MuleSoft and MCP tools.
post_text:
Agent sprawl is the new API sprawl.

That is the integration story Dreamforce 2026 almost buried under AIforce and Koa.

Salesforce did not just ship more agents. On 10 Sep 2026 it put MuleSoft Agent Fabric inside the Trusted Enterprise AI Harness as the control plane: one place to register, orchestrate, govern, and observe agents across Salesforce and third-party AI.

The architect problem is older than Agentforce. Every useful agent still has to call something. Salesforce's own Agentic Integration Patterns are blunt about which tool to pick.

Here is the stack I would put on a whiteboard this week.

🔐 TRUST FIRST
Wrap every callout in Named Credentials + External Credentials. Never hardcode a URL or a secret in Apex or Flow. The Winter '23 credential model is the one to use. Legacy named credentials are deprecated and will be discontinued.

🔌 WHEN THE AGENT IS THE CALLER
• External Services — the system has an OpenAPI spec. Import it. Operations become typed agent actions. Spring '25 added External Service actions so you skip the Flow/Apex wrapper.
• Apex or Flow + Named Credentials — REST, but no OAS. You parse.
• MuleSoft connected actions — protocol translation, fan-out, or legacy. The agent makes one call. MuleSoft does the ugly work.
• MCP tools — the agent discovers capabilities, not your SOAP/REST schema. First-party Salesforce MCP servers currently use end-user credentials. Need a system user? Custom MuleSoft MCP server.

📡 WHEN YOU SHOULD NOT WAIT
Agents can publish Platform Events via Apex/Flow custom actions. Everything already on the Event Bus — Flow, Apex, LWC, Pub/Sub clients, Event Relay — just keeps working.
• Inside Salesforce → Platform Events
• External subscribers at scale → Pub/Sub API

And just like that, it’s over.

Three incredible days at Dreamforce connecting with colleagues and partners, exchanging ideas, and getting a firsthand look at the innovations shaping the next generation of the Salesforce ecosystem.

And this year’s message was clear:

The future belongs to the agentic enterprise.

For the contact center, that means moving beyond a traditional model where humans are the primary engine of every interaction, with technology largely serving as a system for routing, recording, and retrieving information.

An agentic contact center fundamentally changes that equation.

AI agents can handle routine interactions end-to-end, work across systems to find and synthesize information, take action on behalf of customers and employees, and proactively surface insights. Humans remain at the center for the moments that require judgment, empathy, expertise, and complex problem-solving, while AI becomes a force multiplier that expands what those humans can accomplish.

The goal isn’t AI replacing people.

It’s people empowered by AI to do more.

My other takeaways — and wishlist items — for the journey ahead:

🔹 Transform Legacy Channels with AI
Phone and email aren’t going away. But the experience behind them can fundamentally change. AI should make every interaction smarter, faster, more personalized, and more efficient — regardless of the channel.

E se o futuro da experiência digital tiver menos interfaces, e não mais?
Entre os anúncios do Dreamforce 2026, uma das mudanças mais relevantes está na forma como a Salesforce está redesenhando a interação entre pessoas, sistemas e inteligência artificial.

Com o AIforce e sua arquitetura headless, dados, regras de negócio, workflows, permissões e ações deixam de estar presos à interface tradicional do CRM e podem acompanhar o usuário em diferentes ambientes de trabalho, como Claude, Slack, Teams ou aplicações próprias.
Na prática, muda uma lógica que acompanhou o software corporativo durante décadas.
Em vez de levar as pessoas até os sistemas, os sistemas começam a levar suas capacidades até onde as pessoas já estão.

A mesma discussão apareceu, por outro ângulo, na conversa entre Marc Benioff e Omar Sultan Al Olama, Ministro de Estado para Inteligência Artificial dos Emirados Árabes. Ao falar sobre aplicações de IA em serviços públicos, Omar colocou o foco menos na tecnologia e mais em como ela pode retirar atrito da experiência das pessoas.

Aplicar IA não deveria significar simplesmente adicionar uma nova camada de interação. Pode significar eliminar etapas que nunca deveriam ter existido para o cliente.
Em CRM, isso muda bastante a discussão.
Não basta conectar um modelo de IA. É preciso conectar contexto, dados, regras, jornadas e capacidade de ação. E, quanto mais invisível e autônoma essa tecnologia se torna, mais importantes ficam governança, identidade, segurança e controle.

summary: Product head Naren Chawla highlights Salesforce's prepackaged agents (Piper, Marshall, Casey, Fin, Carter, Hunter), the Koa fine-tuned model, and the Data 360 foundation built on MuleSoft and Informatica.
post_text:
I spent a day at Dreamforce this year, mostly exploring the exhibit halls. The Salesforce ecosystem remains incredibly vibrant.
Three things stood out to me:

Prepackaged agents

I saw a demo of Piper, Salesforce’s BDR agent, and found it intriguing.
Salesforce is proposing that customers shouldn’t have to build every agent from scratch. Instead, it is introducing configurable, persona-based agents—including Piper, Marshall, Casey, Fin, Carter, and Hunter—that give business users significantly more agency.
Equally important, these agents support a long-horizon runtime. They can pursue objectives over days or weeks using persistent memory, durable execution, and dynamic steering—not merely respond within a single conversation.

KOA

Koa is a refreshing idea and a strong example of using fine-tuning, including SFT and reinforcement learning, with open-weight models and synthetic data to create a highly domain-specific model.
I will be watching Koa closely because this is the direction I believe the industry should take: use specialized “small-brain” models for well-defined domains and tasks instead of relying on a frontier “big-brain” model for everything.

Data 360
I also saw a Data 360 demo and was impressed by both the product design and the breadth of its scope.
I believe Data 360 is the core data foundation that can enable the broader Agentforce vision. The progression from source data to Data Lake Objects (DLOs) and Data Model Objects (DMOs), combined with the MuleSoft and Informatica foundation, gives Salesforce the ability to support a broad spectrum of enterprise data sources.

That trusted, harmonized, and governed data can then provide the context needed to power agents across the enterprise.

My overall takeaway: Salesforce is moving beyond an agent-building platform toward a more complete agentic architecture—prebuilt agents, specialized models, and a unified enterprise data foundation.

post_text:
I wrote this article because of a conversation between Marc Benioff and Sam Altman at Dreamforce.

Benioff asked Altman about legacy. His answer was not about models:

“Maybe our first decade was thinking about the machine...now I think this has got to be about what it’s going to be for people.”

People first. Then companies.

This gave me a different perspective on AI transformation that I normally discuss about operationalizing with AI.

A few weeks ago, I was in the sauna at my gym talking to a guy who turned out to be a former 49ers running back.

He was using AI to navigate his recovery: translating what specialists told him and asking the follow-up questions there is rarely time for in a 15-minute appointment.

He does not work in tech. Nobody handed him a tool or a training plan. He simply found a way to use AI to understand more, ask better questions and take a more active role in his recovery.

We have spent the past few years talking about AI transformation operationally.

But a company cannot transform faster than the people inside it.

So instead of asking, “What is your AI strategy?” try this:

Can you point to one thing you can now do, create, understand or attempt that you could not three years ago?

If the answer is yes, that is transformation. It is the kind that compounds.

None of this means ignoring the risks. I am still an apocaloptimist: clear-eyed about what could go wrong and optimistic about what people can build.

Those positions have never been in conflict.

Be curious. Not judgmental.

🔗 The full article is linked below.

What has AI made possible for you that was not possible three years ago? At work and in life. I’m curious.

summary: Kat Goessl recaps a Dreamforce session with UAE AI Minister Omar Sultan AlOlama on balancing innovator and regulator roles to build better AI governance.
post_text:
Another fascinating session at Salesforce Dreamforce and one I am still digesting: A conversation with Omar Sultan AlOlama, UAE Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence. 

He was the world's first Minister of State for AI ever, was named TIME's most important people in AI and sits on World Economic Forum's AI Governance Council. 

The UAE has been an early mover in AI governance. He described the innovator and regulator dilemma that slows progress, and why bringing both to the same table matters. Heavily simplified:  when government writes laws alone, the tendency is to over-regulate. When the private sector writes laws alone, the tendency is to under-regulate. Bring both in, then have government and society pick it apart and fix it, and you end up with better rules and a shared understanding of why they exist.

His view of the near future was optimistic: more time, better health. He also warned that unequal access to the technology could fuel unrest. Who gets AI, and how soon, is a policy question as much as a tech one.

My biggest takeaway, (easier said than done, but we must): The best guardrails for building AI in this era comes from collaboration --> not working in silos. Judge AI by whether it improves the lives of the people it serves, and be clear about the lines you won't cross.
