author_headline: Senior Manager | Head of Digital Transformation and Customer & Corporate Solutions
summary: Renato Suplicy Lacerda Neto analyzes Salesforce's Headless 360 and AIforce announcements, describing Claude/ChatGPT-driven CRM actions and Agentforce's shift to long-horizon, memory-based agents.
post_text:
Dreamforce 2026: talvez a maior mudança não esteja no CRM. Está em deixar de precisar entrar nele.

Acompanhando os anúncios deste ano, uma coisa me chamou muito a atenção: a Salesforce não está só enfiando mais IA no CRM. Ela está mudando o papel do próprio sistema.

Com o conceito de Headless 360 e o AIforce, a ideia é clara: levar dados, processos, regras e segurança da Salesforce direto para onde o trabalho de fato acontece.

Na prática, você pode usar o Claude para analisar uma oportunidade, atualizar o pipeline e executar ações no Salesforce sem abrir a ferramenta. Ou usar o ChatGPT como interface para acessar processos corporativos, misturando Salesforce com Gemini ou modelos via AWS/Bedrock.

O ponto não é mais descobrir qual IA vai vencer, mas sim garantir que diferentes IAs operem com o mesmo contexto e as mesmas regras de negócio.

A segunda grande virada diz respeito aos agentes, que deixaram de ser reativos. O Agentforce agora aposta em agentes especializados e de longo prazo (long-horizon agents), capazes de perseguir objetivos por dias ou semanas, mantendo memória e ajustando o plano no meio do caminho.

Estamos falando de recuperar carteiras de clientes em risco, gerenciar ciclos comerciais inteiros ou antecipar problemas antes que o cliente perceba. É a transição definitiva da "IA que responde" para a "IA que trabalha".
Isso muda a forma como pensamos a arquitetura corporativa. Menos sobre "a plataforma onde todo mundo trabalha" e mais sobre criar uma camada confiável de dados, regras e governança para humanos e agentes.

No fim, a interface muda, mas o contexto continua sendo o principal ativo do negócio. Se o usuário não precisa mais entrar no sistema para operar, fica a provocação: estamos prontos para transformar nossos sistemas de registro em sistemas de execução?

Para mim, é aí que a TI deixa de ser o lugar onde os sistemas ficam e passa a ser a camada que faz o negócio acontecer.

Salesforce / Dreamforce / Marc Benioff

AI agents are moving from "help me" to "go do it."

-- AIforce: Salesforce is bringing its data, workflows, business logic and governance to AI interfaces beyond Salesforce itself

-- Koa: Salesforce and NVIDIA announced a new CRM reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron, designed for more complex, multi-step CRM work

-- Agentforce: Salesforce introduced more job-ready agents that can take on longer and more complex work across sales, service, commerce and employee workflows

-- Slackforce: Slack is becoming an even bigger part of the Salesforce ecosystem, bringing Salesforce context, data and actions directly into conversations

What I enjoyed most wasn't just seeing the product announcements. It was talking to the people actually building and using this stuff.

After covering Data and AI for years, it is interesting to see the conversation shift from "What can AI do?" to "What work should AI actually do?"

That shift was everywhere at Dreamforce this year.

quanto mais a IA assume a execução, mais importantes ficam estratégia, contexto e visão de negócio.

author_headline: Summer Intern - KiE Square Analytics || MBA BM 2025-27 || XIMB || Ex - CEPTES Software Pvt Ltd || CMRIT’23
summary: Abhishek Kumar, an MBA intern, details Benioff's AIforce interface layer, the Koa reasoning model with Nvidia, 30,000+ customers, 7 billion agent work units, and Sam Altman's appearance.
post_text:
Salesforce just redefined what "using software" means. My takeaways from Dreamforce 2026.

Having spent time in the Salesforce ecosystem earlier in my career, I've been watching this year's Dreamforce closely, and the shift on display is bigger than another feature drop. Here's what stood out:

🔹 AIforce is the headline. Marc Benioff introduced it as a new "live interface layer" sitting above Agentforce, Data 360, and Customer 360. The pitch: users no longer need to log into Salesforce at all. They can work through Claude, Slack, or any third party surface, and Salesforce "comes to them" instead. Benioff called it an "interface revolution," essentially saying AI replaces the UI.

🔹 Koa, a new CRM-specific reasoning model. Built with Nvidia on the Nemotron model family and trained on 27 years of CRM deployment data. Purpose built reasoning for CRM workflows rather than a general purpose model retrofitted for business use.

🔹 Agentforce 360 keeps scaling. Salesforce shared numbers that are hard to ignore: 30,000+ customers and 7 billion agent work units delivered. Sales Cloud is now available as a skill inside Claude, in open beta and free, a live demonstration of how deep the Anthropic partnership runs.

🔹 A nine part Customer 360 refresh. Updates spanned Sales, Service, Marketing, Commerce (including a shopper agent and agentic commerce search), Field Service, voice to form in multiple languages, IT Service Management, and Revenue Cloud with new MCP tooling.

🔹 Multi model, on purpose. Sam Altman joined Benioff on the main stage, confirming OpenAI's models sit alongside Claude inside Agentforce. Model choice is becoming a real architecture and governance decision, not a one time vendor pick.

The bigger story for anyone in sales, CRM, or GTM: the interface war is on. The platforms winning next aren't the ones with the most screens, they're the ones that disappear into the tools people already use.

Curious how others in the Salesforce and B2B SaaS space are reading the AIforce move. Are we ready to stop "logging in" to our CRM?

author_headline: Strategy & Transformation | Digital, AI & Product | Ex-McKinsey
summary: Alonso Perez Espinoza cites BCG research (26% embed AI in transformation, 14% track P&L) and analyzes Agentforce's evolution and Enterprise AI Harness.
post_text:
The next competitive advantage from AI may not come from having the smartest model. It may come from being the company most willing and☝🏻able to redesign how work actually gets done.

➡️ BCG’s recent CEO research captures the gap well: nearly 9 in 10 CEOs already see cost or revenue benefits from AI in targeted areas. Yet only 26% say AI is embedded in a broader business transformation, and just 14% clearly define the P&L impact of all AI initiatives.

That distinction matters.

After following the announcements from ☁️ Dreamforce 2026, three implications stand out:

1️⃣ From “AI use cases” to redesigning work end-to-end

The biggest opportunity is not adding an AI assistant to today’s process. It is asking whether the process, roles and decision rights should look the same at all.

BCG finds that higher-performing organizations are roughly 7x more likely to redesign workflows and reshape the business end-to-end with AI.

This is why the evolution of Agentforce is strategically interesting: agents are moving beyond discrete interactions toward long-horizon work, pursuing objectives over days or weeks, and multi-agent orchestration across specialized roles.

As agents move from completing tasks to executing workflows, AI transformation increasingly becomes operating-model transformation.

2️⃣ From “which model?” to “what proprietary context can the enterprise activate?”

Foundation models will keep improving and diffusing.

The more durable source of differentiation may therefore shift toward what competitors cannot easily replicate: ➡️ customer context, proprietary knowledge, business semantics, processes, permissions and institutional memory; and the ability to turn that context into action.

☁️ Salesforce’s Enterprise AI Harness points directly at this challenge: giving AI a shared understanding of the business while connecting context, actions, governance and multiple models.

The strategic asset is not AI in isolation. It is AI + differentiated enterprise context + redesigned workflows.

3️⃣ From experimentation to governed digital execution

Once agents can act, not just recommend, governance changes meaning.

Identity, permissions, guardrails, observability, economics and human escalation become part of the operating model itself.

☁️ Dreamforce’s AI Control Plane is notable because the ambition is broader than governing one application: managing agents and AI across an increasingly open, multi-model enterprise environment.

Success also cannot be measured simply by users, prompts or tasks automated. ➡️ The transformation needs an explicit path from AI-enabled workflow → operational KPI → P&L impact.

The technology is advancing remarkably fast.

But the harder question may now sit with leadership:
❓Are we using AI to make today’s organization more productive — or are we prepared to redesign the organization to capture what AI now makes possible?

#AI #BusinessTransformation #BCG #AgenticAI #Salesforce #Dreamforce2026

I came for AI. Somehow I left thinking about Elle Woods, the physical world, and why the best pitches include the ugly parts.

A few things I’m still thinking about:

1. Reese Witherspoon on the “Elle Woods feeling.”

That feeling of being underestimated, or thinking you have to choose between being feminine and being taken seriously.

Her point: you can care about the cute outfit (yuppp 🙂‍↕️) and have an incredible strong & ambitious career.

She also talked about seeing a gap in Hollywood, then deciding to do something about it herself. That eventually became Hello Sunshine and projects like Big Little Lies.

As someone who has definitely wondered whether I need to present a certain way to be taken seriously in tech… I felt this one.

2. Travis Kalanick on moving from bits → atoms.

After Uber and CloudKitchens, he’s now building Atoms around physical automation in food, mining and transportation. 

The idea is fascinating: we’ve gotten very good at using software to automate information. What happens when AI + robotics start doing the same thing to the physical world? 

He also shared 3 values he looks for in entrepreneurs: truth, trust, and passion.

My favorite was “valuable unknown truth.” What do you understand about the world that other people haven’t figured out yet?

3. And then I got to meet Allie K. Miller. 🥹

This one was personal.

Allie was one of the people who inspired me to start sharing what I was learning about AI in the first place. So getting to meet her, fangirl a little (okay, a lot), and tell her about what I’m building at Salesforce was a very full-circle moment.

One piece of her advice to founders stuck with me:

AI should make you reconsider the timeline.

If your vision was something you thought you could accomplish in 2050, what would it take to do it in 2030 now?

And when you pitch that vision, tell the real story. The friction. The grit. The parts that did NOT work.

Also, Reese casually dropped my favorite line of the day:

“Are you using AI, or is AI using you?”

Honestly… fair question. 🫪

Three veryyyy full days. A lot of ideas to process. And definitely a Dreamforce I’ll remember!

post_text:
Three days at San Francisco Moscone Center, and I'm still sorting my notes from Dreamforce '26.

What stayed with me wasn't a single product. It was who stood on that stage together. Anthropic, NVIDIA, Google Cloud, AWS, Siemens — same keynote, same platform. Claudeforce in open beta. Koa CRM reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron. Agentforce talking to Gemini Enterprise over MCP, model choice through Bedrock. That is what innovation power actually looks like — not one vendor's roadmap, but an ecosystem that compounds.

Siemens went a step further and wired Agentforce into Teamcenter, so engineering-grade answers land directly in sales and service.

For my world — Travel, Transport, Hospitality and Logistics — this matters more than in most industries. Our customers run on systems nobody is going to rip out: PSS, reservation hosts, TMS, warehouse and crew systems, decades of them. The question was never whether AI is useful. It was whether it can reach that data without an 18-month re-platforming project. Open protocols and real model choice change the answer.

And the proof is no longer hypothetical. 30,000 customers live on Agentforce. Siemens now qualifies 100% of inbound leads for 18,000 sellers. Southwest showed a genuinely grown-up architecture — an agent router with specialised subagents for intake, document validation and refunds. FedEx Freight talked openly about platform complexity as a newly independent company. And Engine's agent Eva handles more than half of their customer cases end to end.

summary: Chief Customer Officer Kim Keating shares four customer priorities from her AI Mindset Shift roundtable and announces Salesforce's $63B+ FY30 revenue target with AIforce and Enterprise AI Harness.
post_text:
#Dreamforce made one thing clear: Enterprise AI has moved from “Can it work?” to “How do we scale it?” And the questions customers are asking are getting sharper.

Thank you to every customer and partner who shared what’s working, where friction remains, and what you need from us next.

Between the AI Mindset Shift roundtable I led and meetings throughout the week, four priorities came through loud and clear and here are a few direct quotes:

1 | Meet people where they are on the agentic journey
Adoption requires role-specific skills, practical guidance, and AI embedded in familiar workflows. Customer quote: “Not everyone in my company is going to be ready to just start launching agents and building things with Claude.”

2 | Connect the work, not just the data
Customers want a contextual, guided experience across systems—not another swivel chair experience. Customer quote: “I have my files and emails and everything else. I want that context alongside my Salesforce data.”

3 | Make economics predictable—and outcomes measurable
Leaders need credible consumption forecasts, spending limits, and visibility by business unit. Customer quote: “I need a model to be able to project, anticipate costs.”

And productivity alone isn’t enough. Customer quote: “I can tell you we’re getting really productive. But I don’t know if we’re actually reusing those hours saved to do more things.”

4 | Scale autonomy with trust
Enterprises need visibility into what agents can access and do, what they cost, and where humans remain in control. Customer quote: “Do we choose to spend our very valuable engineering resources building more and more, or do we license … and work on different problems?”

This week’s Dreamforce announcements map directly to those needs:
→ Out-of-the-box agents for high-value work
→ AIforce, bringing trusted business context and action into the tools people already use
→ The Enterprise AI Harness and AI Control Plane, providing the observability, security, governance, and choice required to scale

We also announced our $63B+ FY30 revenue target, and the path is clear: earn it one measurable customer outcome at a time.

For leaders making this pivot now: Which question is most urgent—adoption, context, economics, or trust?

author_headline: AI & Cloud Leader | CRM, Salesforce & Integration Architect | Driving Enterprise AI/ML & Deep Learning Transformation
summary: AI/cloud architect Andrew Lawlor details Salesforce's AIforce layer, Salesforce in Claude, Headless360, MCP servers, Slackforce, Agentforce Coworker, and the new Koa model built on Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Super.
post_text:
This week's Dreamforce was busier and more consequential than most Dreamforce conferences in recent memory.
Salesforce is pushing further toward a world where the real value of its platform lives in the backend, the data, the workflows, the business logic, the validations, and the security model, not in the screens people click through to reach them. AIforce is the model-agnostic layer behind that shift, and Salesforce in Claude is its first expression. Instead of navigating Lightning, users describe what they need, and AI models, starting with Claude, render the interface on the fly instead of relying on custom, expensive Lightning Web Components.
None of this works without Headless360, released just six months ago, the piece that lets an AI bypass the web interface entirely. Claude and other models query Salesforce through MCP servers, pulling exactly the data needed. Salesforce in Claude runs through Claude Cowork Skills to deliver repeatable reports and dashboards, and customers, partners, and consultants will increasingly build their own Skills in place of writing custom Lightning components.
In a well timed coincidence, Anthropic announced yesterday that Claude Cowork and Claude chat are merging into one Claude, with Claude Design now built into ordinary conversations too. The line between chatting with Claude and handing it a real task is dissolving right as Salesforce bets its future on that same blurring.
Slackforce follows the same logic for Slack that AIforce follows for Lightning. Where one person can work an opportunity in natural language through Salesforce in Claude, Slackforce lets a whole team work that record together, with the interaction history preserved.
Agentforce Coworker, an agent living in Lightning that reasons over data and acts on it, is harder to read. Agentforce hype has outpaced its impact for two years, and I want more evidence before betting on adoption speed. My prediction is AIforce will see faster adoption than Agentforce has. It will be fun to watch which one wins the next twelve months.
Then there is Koa, Salesforce's first serious model release, built by fine-tuning Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Super, a 120-billion-parameter open-weight model competitive with Qwen3.5, but with known data provenance. Salesforce trained it purely on synthetic sales, service, and marketing data, no real customer data involved, and reports it matches or beats frontier models on CRM workloads with fewer tokens and a third of the errors. The platform will route CRM prompts to Koa and harder, non-CRM work to Claude. I'm eager to put Koa through its paces once it's available.
Taken together, Salesforce announced more at this Dreamforce than at any I can remember, which may say as much about the pressure they feel to stay relevant in an AI-first world as it does about any single announcement.

author_headline: 대표 Salesforce Customer Success Group Korea (컨설팅 서비스 사업부문 - Agentic Enterprise Consulting Services powered by Agentforce)
summary: Seongho Kim, head of Salesforce Korea's Customer Success Group, outlines a four-layer Agentic Enterprise stack—Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, AIforce—citing Claude/MCP integration and Zero Data Retention.
post_text:
올해 Dreamforce(9/15~17)는 Agentic Enterprise를 이루어줄 Salesforce의 모든 역량셋이 완성된 모습을 보여준 자리였다고 생각한다.
사실 지금까지 제가 경험한 모든 컨퍼런스 중 가장 임팩트가 컸다고 할 수 있다.

Agentic Enterprise를 지향하는 기업들에게 분명한 방향성과 구체적인 실행 로드맵, 그리고 이를 뒷받침할 Salesforce의 Readiness를 보여준 수많은 Wow Moment가 있었다.

한마디로 이번 Dreamforce가 가장 인상적이었던 이유는,
“실제 비즈니스 환경에서 기업이 보유한 Data와 Business Context, 즉 팩트에 기반한 결정론적 비즈니스 인프라 위에 확률론적 지능인 AI와 AI Agent를 어떻게 적용하여 실질적인 비즈니스 가치를 만들어낼 것인가?”

라는 질문에 Salesforce가 매우 구체적인 답을 제시했다는 점이다.
Salesforce가 보여준 구조를 네 가지 Layer로 정리해보면 다음과 같다.

1. Data 360
기업의 데이터를 통합하고 연결한다.

2. Customer 360
데이터를 실제 비즈니스 맥락과 고객 관계 속에서 활용할 수 있는 결정론적 Business Infrastructure를 만든다.

3. Agentforce
이러한 데이터와 비즈니스 맥락을 기반으로 역할과 업무가 명확하게 정의된 AI Agent가 실제 업무를 수행하도록 한다.

4. AIforce
AI가 Salesforce 안에만 존재하는 것이 아니라 Claude, Slack, Coworker 및 기업이 직접 개발한 다양한 Interface에서도 Salesforce의 Data, Workflow, Business Logic을 활용할 수 있도록 한다.

특히 이번 Dreamforce에서 가장 큰 Wow Moment 중 하나는 AIforce였다.

“AI가 UI를 대체한다.”

기존에는 사용자가 Salesforce UI에 들어와 데이터를 조회하고 업무를 수행했다면, 이제는 사용자가 원하는 AI Interface에서 Salesforce의 Data와 Workflow를 그대로 활용할 수 있다.

Salesforce UI를 한 번도 열지 않은 사용자도 AI를 통해 Record를 조회하고, 업데이트하고, Workflow를 실행하고, 필요한 질문을 할 수 있는 것이다.
그리고 Claudeforce는 이러한 변화가 실제로 어떻게 구현되는지를 보여주는 대표적인 사례였다.

Anthropic과의 파트너십을 확대하면서 Salesforce for Claude를 통해 MCP(Model Context Protocol)를 활용하고, Claude가 Salesforce의 Data와 Business Context 및 기능에 접근할 수 있도록 했다.
MCP는 쉽게 말하면 AI/LLM과 외부 시스템을 연결하는 표준적인 Interface Protocol이다.

또한 Zero Data Retention을 포함한 Trust 관련 메시지를 통해 기업 환경에서 AI를 활용할 때 가장 중요한 Data Security와 Trust에 대한 Salesforce의 방향성도 분명하게 제시했다.
결국 이번 Dreamforce의 메시지는 단순히

“AI를 도입하라”

가 아니었다.
오히려,
Data와 Business Context를 기반으로
→ AI Agent가 일을 하고

post_text:
Dreamforce 2026 is over. The theme that outlasted the keynotes: governance.

Two years ago, Dreamforce was about proving agents could work. This year, the question in almost every session was different: can you actually stand behind what you've already deployed?
The numbers explain why.

→ 53% of large US enterprises already have agents running in production (KPMG)

→ Just 21% rate their agentic governance as mature (Deloitte)

→ Gartner expects 40%+ of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by 2027 — not over model quality, but cost overruns, unclear ROI, and weak risk controls

That's the gap nobody talks about at the demo stage: most companies are further along deploying agents than governing them.

And agents fail differently than software does. No thrown error, no visible crash — just a wrong action, an escalation that shouldn't have happened, a different outcome from the same prompt on a different day. Silent failure is harder to catch and harder to explain to an auditor.

Salesforce has clearly been building for this — the Einstein Trust Layer, agent-level access controls, session tracing. But the tooling only matters if governance is treated as part of the architecture, not a compliance step bolted on after launch.

The rollouts that will hold up aren't the ones that moved fastest. They're the ones with:

A named owner who can actually shut the agent off
Tiered autonomy earned through demonstrated reliability
An audit trail that survives real scrutiny
A kill switch that's been tested, not just documented
Human checkpoints wherever being wrong is expensive

summary: Seongho Kim outlines Salesforce's four-layer Agentic Enterprise architecture—Data 360, Customer 360, Agentforce, AIforce—and highlights Claudeforce via the expanded Anthropic MCP partnership.
post_text:
I believe this year’s Dreamforce demonstrated that Salesforce now has the full set of capabilities needed to make the Agentic Enterprise a reality.
In fact, of all the conferences I have experienced so far, this was probably the most impactful.
For companies aspiring to become Agentic Enterprises, Salesforce presented a clear direction, a concrete execution, and the readiness to make it happen—with countless Wow Moments throughout the event.
In a nutshell, what impressed me most about this year’s Dreamforce was that Salesforce provided a very concrete answer to one fundamental question:
“In a real business environment, how can we apply AI and AI Agents—the probabilistic intelligence—on top of the deterministic business infrastructure built on a company’s Data and Business Context, in order to create tangible business value?”
I would summarize the architecture Salesforce demonstrated this year into four layers:
1. Data 360
Integrate and connect enterprise data.
2. Customer 360
Turn that data into a deterministic business infrastructure grounded in business context and customer relationships.
3. Agentforce
Enable clearly defined AI Agents to perform actual work based on that data and business context.
4. AIforce
Extend AI beyond Salesforce itself, allowing users to access Salesforce Data, Workflows, and Business Logic through the interfaces they choose—including Claude, Slack, Coworker, and custom-built interfaces.
One of the biggest Wow Moments at this year’s Dreamforce was AIforce.
“AI replaces the UI.”
Traditionally, users entered the Salesforce UI to access data and perform their work. Now, they can leverage Salesforce Data and Workflows through the AI interface of their choice.
Even someone who has never opened the Salesforce UI can use AI to retrieve and update records, execute workflows, and get answers to business questions.
Claudeforce was another great example of how this vision is becoming real.
Through an expanded partnership with Anthropic, Salesforce for Claude leverages MCP (Model Context Protocol), enabling Claude to access Salesforce Data, Business Context, and capabilities.
Salesforce also reinforced its commitment to Trust and Data Security, including Zero Data Retention, as a critical foundation for enterprise AI adoption.
Ultimately, the message of Dreamforce was not simply:
“Adopt AI.”
It was much more specific:
Build on Data and Business Context
→ Let AI Agents do the work
→ Give people the freedom to work through the interfaces they choose
→ Create real business outcomes.
That, to me, is what Salesforce is envisioning as the Agentic Enterprise.

“AI replaces the UI” is not a slogan. Its a real shift in how work gets done.
And the agents? They are no longer demos. They are becoming real digital coworkers; working pipeline, handling service, answering customers, and giving people time back to do the work only humans can do: build relationships, make judgment calls, and create :)
What moved me most was not the technology, it was the humanity in the room.
The conversations about trust, customer stories, the shared belief that the companies who win won’t have the most AI… they will be the ones who make humans and agents collaborate brilliantly.

I left more convinced than ever:
The next decade of CRM wont be about better dashboards. It will be about amplifying human potential at scale.

The future is not coming. Its already here, and its collaborative.

This week's learning...change management is now the bottleneck in RevOps/GTM systems work. Not build capacity.

That's my takeaway from Dreamforce week, reinforced by Augmented Collaboration: How Teams and AI Work as One to Drive Innovation, which I've been reading alongside it.

Here's the pattern. Agentic tools let a RevOps or GTM team stand up something real in days. We build as proxies for our stakeholders, because we're closest to the workflow and we can see what's broken. The tools are super efficient, and they work. So the results are frequently built without much detailed input from stakeholders.

Then the build lands, and the actual work starts: making users understand what changed, value the change, and shift their behavior. That's a human problem. No agent solves it. That's the "agentic conundrum" I heard all week.

If you've found something that works here, I want to hear it. How are you managing the change, not just the technology?

author_headline: Sales Manager LATAM en AI/R Everymind
summary: Gastón Apaza, LATAM sales manager at AI/R Everymind, describes Benioff's onstage interview pitting Dario Amodei's call for AI safety against Jensen Huang's 'run fast' market-driven stance.
post_text:
Escribo esto todavía con la adrenalina de estos días encima, desde el aeropuerto de San Francisco, volviendo a casa después de Dreamforce. ✈️
 
La verdad que me quedé pensando bastante estos días! No tanto por la cantidad de anuncios, que fueron un montón, sino por algo que pasó en el escenario principal. Benioff entrevistó a Dario Amodei (Anthropic) y a Jensen Huang (Nvidia), y sus posturas quedaron enfrentadas de una manera que no se ve todos los días. Dario, apoyado en un ensayo que había publicado días antes, planteó la necesidad de que la industria vaya más despacio y invierta más en seguridad y transparencia. Jensen, en cambio, sostuvo que no hacen falta nuevas leyes ni regulaciones, que las fuerzas del mercado ya alcanzan, y que hay que correr tan rápido como se pueda, aunque aclaró que si en algún momento el producto no está seguro, hay que frenar y arreglarlo bien. Nadie salió de ahí con una respuesta cerrada, y esa fue, posta, la charla que más siguió dando vueltas en los pasillos el resto del día, más que cualquier producto nuevo.
 
Y ahora mas tranquilo, poniendome a pensar no es un tema tan distinto del que vengo escribiendo todo este mes acá. A escala de industria, la pregunta es si se puede confiar en un sistema sin supervisar cada paso. A escala de una implementación real, es exactamente lo mismo: si un agente puede actuar sin que otro sepa qué decisión ya tomó. 
El problema de confianza no cambia de tamaño, cambia de escenario solamente!
 
Me subo al avión sin una respuesta concreta tampoco, y la verdad que está bien que sea así. Lo que sí me llevo es que la conversación que importa no es qué tan impresionante es el próximo agente. Es cuánto estamos dispuestos a confiar en él sin mirar por encima del hombro!
 
Gracias, Dreamforce. Gracias Salesforce. Gracias AI/R Everymind. Nos vemos el año que viene, con mucho más de esto funcionando de verdad!!!  🚀

summary: IBM's Bhaskar Menon highlights AIforce as his Dreamforce 2026 highlight, sharing three takeaways on AI moving beyond app boundaries, embedded ecosystems, and trust-driven adoption.
post_text:
🚀 What an amazing Dreamforce 2026!
The sheer size, scale, and organization of the event completely blew me away. It is truly something that needs to be experienced firsthand to appreciate the passion and energy of Trailblazers from across the globe.

Over the past few days, I had the privilege of connecting with account leaders, fellow IBMers, customers, Salesforce experts, partners, and industry peers. Whether discussing business transformation, managed services, customer success, or the future of enterprise technology, one theme consistently stood out:
AI is rapidly moving from experimentation to enterprise-scale execution.

For me, the highlight of the event was AIforce, which reimagines how organizations can harness the power of AI across enterprise platforms.
For decades, users have been trained to go to an application to access information and complete work. We are now entering a world where the intelligence, data, and business processes that power those applications can be made available wherever work is happening. 
My Three Key Takeaways
✅ 1. Enterprise capabilities are breaking free from traditional application boundaries. Business value is no longer confined to a browser tab or a specific enterprise application. Employees will increasingly interact with business processes through conversational and AI-driven experiences embedded within the tools they use every day. The experience layer is becoming more intelligent, personalized, and contextual.
✅ 2. AI can now be brought directly into our clients' ecosystems
One of the most exciting opportunities for organizations is the ability to extend enterprise intelligence beyond the core platform itself. Rather than requiring users to switch between systems, companies can infuse AI-powered insights, workflows, and actions directly into their own applications and business experiences.
✅ 3. Trust will determine the pace of AI adoption. As AI becomes more deeply embedded in business operations, governance, security, and transparency become increasingly critical. Organizations that establish a trusted foundation for AI will be best positioned to scale innovation while maintaining confidence among employees, customers, and stakeholders

author_headline: Chief Marketing & Ecosystem Officer @ Vena
summary: Vena's Allison Munro argues AI GTM demos assume a working data foundation, citing Gartner stats: 7.8% marketing budget, 54% of CMOs under-resourced.
post_text:
This week, Dreamforce and UNBOUND showed us an incredible vision of what AI can do for GTM.

Agents that find signals. Build audiences. Create campaigns. Personalize experiences. Take action.

I’m bought in.

But there’s a prerequisite hiding underneath almost every demo:

The foundation already works.

The data is usable. The systems connect. The workflows exist. The signals can be interpreted. The governance is there.

That’s not the reality inside a lot of GTM organizations today.

Sales needs more.

More pipeline. More leads. More content. More events. More signals. More intelligence.

Most of those asks eventually find their way to Marketing.

At exactly the same time, Marketing is being asked to spend less, hire less and use AI to produce more.

AI has created a dangerous assumption: that you can remove capacity before you build the leverage.

You can’t.

Especially in Marketing Ops.

One or two people are often being asked to connect CRM, automation, intent, web, paid, events, enrichment and analytics. Clean the data. Find the signals. Build the workflows. Automate the actions. And now, operationalize AI across all of it.

That isn’t less work.

It’s more work before it becomes less work.

And the data supports the tension.

Gartner reports marketing budgets at 7.8% of company revenue. 54% of CMOs say they lack sufficient resources to execute their strategy.

70% say becoming an AI leader is critical.

Only 30% say they’re ready to scale it.

So yes, AI can unlock enormous capacity.

But capacity isn’t magically created by adding AI to an operating model that isn’t ready for it.

You need capacity to build leverage before leverage gives you back capacity.

That’s the investment curve I think we’re missing.

Sales needs more.

Marketing can deliver dramatically more.

But if we’re serious about the AI-powered GTM organization we’re all talking about this week, we need to fund the foundation that makes “more with less” possible.

Not assume it already exists.

Sources: Gartner 2026 CMO Spend Survey; Salesforce Dreamforce 2026.

author_headline: Google ML AI Cert | Salesforce Architect (22x Certified) | AI (LLMs/RAG) | AWS CCP
summary: Orlando Agostinho argues Agentforce's multi-surface UI needs a shared action vocabulary (create, update, escalate, approve, cancel) rather than channel-specific verbs.
post_text:
Dreamforce made multi-surface agent UX a Salesforce design-system problem, not a skinning exercise.

Before you ship an Agentforce UI to five surfaces, standardize the verbs.

Surface-native experiences need shared interaction semantics even when the visual shell changes by channel. Five UIs with five different action names is still one brittle product — not five native experiences.

Define a small action vocabulary — create, update, escalate, approve, cancel — and contract tests every surface must pass: same verb → same intent, same parameters → same validation, same failure → same recovery path. If a surface invents a new verb without a shared contract, treat it as design-system debt — not a channel win.

HXL is a design-system problem in disguise.

Which verb is still unique to one channel in your stack?

author_headline: Software developer at fusionspan
summary: Shawn Lai says fusionSpan's fusionCore already runs Salesforce's new AIforce/Claudeforce layer, demoing order creation and payment processing via interactive Claude cards.
post_text:
Dreamforce is over. fusionCore already runs on what Salesforce announced there.

Salesforce introduced AIforce: one interface layer that brings Salesforce data, actions and permissions into Claude, Slack and Lightning, with Claudeforce as the Claude piece. Together with Salesforce's Headless Experience Layer, agents can show interactive cards instead of walls of text. We did not wait for the roadmap. fusionCore, our association management system on Salesforce, now works with it.

What it looks like for association staff, in the 60-second video below:

Membership services types "I want to place an order". An order form opens inside Claude. Account, contact, business unit and products are searched live in fusionCore, and the total updates as lines are added.

One click creates the order. The order card appears with the same labels and buttons as the fusionCore Order page: Pay Order, Create Invoice, Void Invoice, Refund. Create the invoice, pick the payment term, save and post.

Choose Pay Order. The card shows only the payment types allowed for that business unit, prefills the balance due, requires a check or reference number, and warns on a backdated date. Choose Check, enter the reference, pay. The payment lands in fusionCore with its Financial Event, under the staff member's own permissions.

The card never writes to Salesforce on its own. Each button hands one instruction to Claude, which calls a fusionCore action. Validation and the audit trail stay in fusionCore. Member and product search returns in under a second on large orgs.

The cards are built on an open standard. The same cards run in Claude today, and work in ChatGPT, in Salesforce Lightning with Agentforce, and in Slack.

We are bringing this to fusionCore first. The same approach applies to other customizations.

Want to see it on your own data? Reach out to the fusionSpan team.

Demo runs on a test org with sample data.

Most people are still using AI like it’s 2023.

They open a chatbot, ask a question, copy the answer, and close the tab.

That's single-player AI. Your team is nowhere in it.

At Dreamforce, I moderated a Slack panel on what comes next.
With Ryan Gavin, EVP & CMO of Slack.
Amy Bauer, Senior Director of Product Management at Slack.
And Lindsey Simon, VP of Engineering at Vercel.

The big idea: multiplayer AI.
One AI. The whole team. Same room.

Think about how work happens today.
You talk in Slack.
Your tickets live in Jira.
Your code lives in GitHub.

So you spend half your day copy-pasting context between tabs.

But now, with tools like Slack Code, it all sits in one place.

Your conversations, your data, your team's context.
So the AI knows what your team knows.

Say a customer reports a bug in a channel.
Support adds the account details.
The PM sets the priority.
An engineer asks the AI to fix it.
And ships it from the same thread.

Days of back-and-forth, done in one conversation.

AI gets a lot more useful when the whole team is in the room.

Thank you Slack and Salesforce for having me at Dreamforce.

So, the confession: I am a 2026 Agentblazer Champion and a Trailhead Mountaineer. For anyone outside the Salesforce world, Trailhead is Salesforce's learning platform, and Agentblazer is its programme for learning to build and deploy AI agents on Agentforce. Yes, a Genesys services leader has been quietly doing his Salesforce homework!

However, this isn't a hobby. Many of our customers run Genesys Cloud alongside Salesforce, with Genesys handling the voice, routing and orchestration, and Salesforce holding the customer record. When those two platforms are designed together, the agent sees the full picture of the customer the moment the call lands, and the AI has the context it needs to be useful, rather than confidently wrong. When they are designed apart, the customer feels the join.

Nobody buys an Experience Orchestration platform in isolation; it joins an estate that already has a CRM, a data platform, workforce tools, and, increasingly, AI agents. If you advise customers on CX transformation and only understand your own product, you are seeing half the architecture, and the half you can't see is where the engagement goes wrong. It's why we at Genesys put so much weight on knowing our partners' platforms as well as our own.

So, if you work in the Genesys world and have never looked at Salesforce, or in the Salesforce world and have never looked at how a contact centre actually routes a call, have a look at the other one and see how much of your customer's day you've been missing.

Just spent the week at Dreamforce discussing Outreach's agents and how they can complement what Salesforce is doing and releasing. (Watch the video in the link at the end)
 
A year ago at Dreamforce, most MCP conversations started with "what is it." This year they started with "which connectors do you have, and how do I wire them together." It was all about Agentforce and how teams are using MCP connectors like Outreach's to streamline their revenue cycles.
 
Build vs buy is really a build and buy conversation now, and MCP is what's forcing it. Salesforce leaned into the build side at Dreamforce with Agentforce Vibes, using natural language to generate agents. Vibes can get you to an agent, but you're still building and maintaining it yourself. MCP changes that equation, connecting you to agents that already exist so your team can spend its time on what makes your business different.
 
A RevOps team using Vibes could spend weeks or months building and deploying agents that research an account, draft a meeting brief, or flag a deal going quiet. That's before the real cost: hardening them, testing edge cases, security review, then maintaining them every time a data model changes. That upkeep rarely gets budgeted for, and it quietly eats the time the agent was supposed to save.
 
Or that team could connect Agentforce to Outreach's Research Agent, Meeting Prep Agent, and Deal Agent through MCP, and get all three on day one, already built and running in production, with someone else carrying the maintenance. Every month spent rebuilding what already exists is a month not spent on what differentiates your revenue motion, and that gap only grows as the ecosystem matures.
 
That's the shift MCP is enabling. Outreach's MCP setup works as both a server and a client, a two way exchange with the rest of your stack, not a one way feed. Agentforce can draw on Outreach's deal signals and account context, and Outreach can pull data in and act on it, updating records, prepping meetings, adjusting sequences, without a person moving data between the two. The client side reaches further too, connecting to Snowflake, Glean, ZoomInfo, and more, so an ops team can orchestrate pipeline signals, internal knowledge, and warehouse data through one connection.
 
Salesforce is building toward the same principle from its own side. AIforce, announced this week, is a new interface layer letting agents reach into Salesforce data without a person opening the app at all. It's a good sign for where this is headed, and it makes the case for Outreach's agents stronger, since they're already built for exactly that kind of headless, agent to agent model.
 
For ops teams, that's the real unlock. Less time building the plumbing, less risk in a custom build, more time on the parts of the workflow that actually make your revenue motion different.

author_headline: GTM Leadership @ Salesforce
summary: Jason Reid, Salesforce GTM leader, cites Anthropic, Google Cloud, AWS, OpenAI partnerships and Koa built on NVIDIA Nemotron, arguing enterprise data beats standalone AI models.
post_text:
One of my biggest takeaways from Dreamforce: nobody serious is trying to win AI alone.

Salesforce deepened its integration with Anthropic.

Expanded partnerships with Google Cloud  and Amazon Web Services (AWS).

Announced new work with OpenAI.

And built Koa, its new CRM reasoning model, on NVIDIA Nemotron.

That tells me something pretty clearly.

AI can only do so much by itself.

The model matters.

But the data matters more.

The permissions matter.

The workflows matter.

The business logic matters.

The infrastructure matters.

And when you can unlock all of that context safely, THAT’S where things start getting interesting.

So to the geniuses who continue to treat every strategic AI partnership as some kind of concession…

Why exactly would the companies you all love to glaze (learned that one from my team last week), keep choosing to partner with enterprise software companies?

Because this isn’t a race where one LLM eventually eats the entire technology stack.

It’s an AI marathon.

And everybody brings something different to the relay.

Anthropic brings frontier reasoning.

Google and AWS bring infrastructure, models and enterprise ecosystems.

NVIDIA brings accelerated compute and model foundations.

Salesforce brings decades of customer data, metadata, permissions, workflows and business context.

And acquisitions like Informatica, Qualified, Contentful and Fin keep filling in pieces around trusted data, marketing, content and service.

Now onto my favorite part: the receipts…

McKinsey & Company recently called data readiness a key constraint to scaling AI, specifically pointing to the need for governed, reusable foundations across structured and unstructured enterprise data.

Deloitte found the same operational gap: only 21% of enterprises surveyed said they currently have mature governance for autonomous AI agents.

So yes, the models are getting smarter incredibly fast.

Great.

Now give them something useful to reason over.

Clean data.

Connected context.

Defined semantics.

Permissions.

Actions.

That’s why Dreamforce felt less like “here’s our model, ours is better” and more like an acknowledgement of where enterprise AI is actually going.

The moat isn’t having every piece yourself.

It’s owning enough differentiated context that the best models, infrastructure and applications in the world become more valuable when they plug into you.

That’s partnership.

Not concession.

And frankly, if Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, AWS and NVIDIA all see enough strategic value to deepen their relationships with enterprise platforms…

maybe the LinkedIn comment section can survive putting the pitchforks down for five minutes.

summary: Preeti Lalwani, a Salesforce architect, warns that Quick Pages shown in Dreamforce's admin keynote lack clarity on deployment, versioning and backup, urging admins to restrict access now.
post_text:
Salesforce Quick Pages lets admins and permissioned users build React pages on live org data, and Salesforce hasn't said how those pages get deployed or backed up.

For release managers, that's a new kind of change with no process behind it. If a Quick Page sits outside your org metadata, it won't be in your source control or your backups, and the person who built it may be the only one who knows it exists. Decide who gets that permission now, before a page the business relies on turns up outside your pipeline.

Salesforce showed Quick Pages in the Dreamforce admin keynote. Its Admins blog calls them single-page React apps built on existing data without risking org metadata, and lists them as available now. Salesforce Ben reported a beta coming in October and little detail beyond one keynote slide. Nothing has been published on storage, versioning or deployment.

Slackforce does the same inside Slack. Agentforce Coworker sits inside Lightning. None ask you to "go to Salesforce." They bring Salesforce to wherever work is already happening.

That's a shift for how we think about digital experience. The old question: "how good is this platform's interface?" The new question: "how well does this platform function as infrastructure that other tools build on?" Tech debt, personalization, AI readiness — all of it starts to look different when the platform isn't trying to be the destination.

A general model reasons about a refund policy the same way it reasons about a physics problem. But governed, repeatable enterprise work requires a model that has learned the exact work to be done and applies that expertise consistently.

Silvio Savarese and I are excited to share our latest blog post on why we post-trained our own enterprise reasoning model, Koa launched at Dreamforce this week. Thank you to our partners Kari Ann Briski and the amazing team at NVIDIA.

Here are the key highlights:
1. Built for Enterprise Workflows: Instead of working every task out from scratch, Koa is optimized for complex, multi-turn, tool-using workflows and interactions that appear in the CRM domain.
2. Co-Engineered with NVIDIA: Post-trained on NVIDIA’s 120B-parameter Nemotron 3 Super model, giving us direct access to weights and transparent data provenance.
3. Simulated Workflow Training: Trained using reinforcement learning across simulated enterprise scenarios in 14+ industries to master real-world task resolution.
4. Knowing When Not to Act: Taught to recognize missing tools or permissions and safely halt or hand off to human teammates.
5. Trust & Data Control: Runs inside the Salesforce trust boundary, ensuring customer data and reasoning traces stay completely yours.

𝐀𝐈 𝐢𝐬 𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐚 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐧 𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐚𝐲𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐞, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡 𝐢𝐭: 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚, 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐬 𝐨𝐟 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝.

The question is shifting from 𝐰𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐡 𝐀𝐈 𝐦𝐨𝐝𝐞𝐥 to 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐈 𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰, 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐚𝐜𝐭? Salesforce's data and CRM foundation become even more important here.

3. 𝐀𝐈 𝐧𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭, 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞.
The introduction of Koa reinforces this. The value isn't simply having another powerful reasoning model. It is grounding that intelligence in how businesses actually operate, from processes and workflows to customer and revenue context.

4. 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐠𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥.
Our conversations at Accordion reinforced this for me. From AI spend and revenue recognition to moving AI from roadmap to production and supporting different monetization models, the underlying revenue architecture still matters.

author_headline: Sales Director @ Quadrant Technologies | Partner Engagement, Trusted Business Partner
summary: Quadrant Technologies' Philip Pankov recaps Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei and Marc Benioff talks, arguing agentic AI now hinges on data pipelines and enterprise integration, not model weights.
post_text:
My first Dreamforce - and I really loved it!

A few direct takeaways from the floor at Dreamforce after listening to Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, and Marc Benioff break down where the tech stack is heading:

From conversational wrappers to agentic systems: We’re moving beyond prompt-and-retrieve interfaces. The shift is toward autonomous agents capable of multi-step workflows, tool use, and operational execution without manual babysitting.

The data layer remains the bottleneck: Advanced reasoning engines can't compensate for fragmented, dirty, or siloed data. Structured enterprise pipelines and unified storage are the real prerequisites—not the model weights.

Execution over experimentation: The novelty phase of generative AI is done. The challenge now is deploying models securely into production environments with enterprise-grade governance, deterministic guardrails, and low-latency API layers.

Where the value lands for Quadrant: Enterprises don't just need another SaaS pilot; they need the integration muscle connecting agentic tooling to their existing cloud backbones, core ERP/CRMs, and proprietary data sets to generate measurable operational efficiency.

The architectural direction is set. Now it’s strictly an engineering and delivery problem.

Just wrapped Dreamforce 26’ in San Francisco and I’m pretty sure this year’s event will go down as the one that penetrated mainstream AI culture in Salesforce.

We're at an interesting inflection point. Converging forces like AI-generated change, growing org complexity, and the pressure to stay in control of both are moving faster than most teams' processes were built to handle.

We at Opsera launched our headless delivery platform for Salesforce orgs at Dreamforce to solve precisely these challenges. I ran dozens of demos at the booth and 3 key moments stood out:

1. Mapping an org's entire metadata, live, so every component and every connection is visible in one view. More than one developer told us they'd never seen their own org laid out that way before.

2. Seeing the full history behind any component; who changed it, when, and why that matters for a rollback or an audit. That kind of embedded trust, a record that's simply there without anyone maintaining it, was the clearest signal of what people actually want right now. 

3. An object carrying 15 to 20 legacy validation rules, all still active, no one quite sure why. We ran the impact analysis, showed where they overlapped, and helped consolidate them down to a fraction of that number. All of it, live! 

The best part is that none of it needed new tooling to adopt. There's no complex dashboard to learn, no custom scripts to maintain, nothing to install before you can start with our Headless platform. 

Want to implement a Jira? Just ask. 
Need to know if a change is safe to deploy? Just ask. 
Want to see what breaks before you touch a functionality? Just ask. 

Feature branches, deployment, compliance, every part of it works the way we ran the demo: through plain conversation. 

I’m so deeply proud of us, it feels like an understatement because the pure joy I firsthand saw at the booth in people’s eyes when they realized just how incredibly simple to use our platform is and the outsized impact it can generate for their Salesforce teams was so exciting to witness.

author_headline: Strategy & Business Development | Digital Transformation | Platform Engineering | AI & Data-led Solutions | Working with Global Enterprises
summary: Compunnel's Abhishek Salwan argues Agentforce 360's launch shows AI agents demand human-in-the-loop governance, positioning 'Talent as a Service' as essential infrastructure.
post_text:
Dreamforce 2026 just wrapped up in San Francisco, and if there is one phrase dominating every post-event conversation, it’s the "Agentic Enterprise". With the launch of Agentforce 360, the narrative has firmly shifted from AI as a co-pilot to autonomous AI agents collaborating across sales, service, and marketing.

But here is the reality check we are heavily focused on at Compunnel right now: as AI agents become the new operational baseline, the true competitive advantage shifts entirely back to human capital.

author_headline: Head of Salesforce at St. James’s Place | Platform & Engineering Leader | Salesforce CTA
summary: St. James's Place Salesforce architect Ram Babu Singh lists ten wealth-management takeaways from Dreamforce on APIs, MCP, agent governance, and client-data foundations for AI advisers.
post_text:
Thank you, Salesforce, for another excellent Dreamforce. It brought together some of the biggest names in AI and a busy week of announcements.

The highlight for me was the people. I caught up with friends and former colleagues from around the world. I also had valuable conversations with product leaders, architects and business leaders, particularly in wealth management and financial services.

Here are my takeaways, seen through a wealth management lens:

1.	More adviser and client questions will start outside the CRM, in collaboration tools, AI assistants and other interfaces.

2.	The opportunity is real: more time for advisers to spend with clients, and faster, better informed conversations.

3.	Trust remains central. The adviser to client relationship has to be enforced in the platform and the APIs, not left to the interface.

4.	APIs remain the contract. Partner APIs need to be well designed, versioned and share only the data each partner needs.

5.	MCP is a useful additional layer for AI assistants. It complements APIs rather than replacing them, and it does not make AI deterministic on its own.

6.	In an advice business, predictable outcomes come from good design, including clear schemas, validation, approvals and audit.

7.	Conversational experiences will sit alongside good screens, not replace them. The same capabilities can serve client portals, mobile apps and AI assistants.

8.	Starting with read and prepare use cases, such as client review preparation, makes sense. Anything touching client money, advice or communications should keep a human firmly in the loop.

9.	As firms use more than one AI platform, consistent governance across agents will matter.

10.	Data foundations still decide success: accurate client data, clear consent and good records.

The principle I am taking away is API first, agent ready and governed by design, with the focus on better outcomes for advisers and clients.

author_headline: CRM + AI + People = Digital Transformations for Humans Breaking down complex legacy technology challenges & rebuilding Sectors: Financial Services, Energy, Utilities & Logistics
summary: Consultant Marshall Cram contrasts Dreamforce's Benioff-McConaughey keynote with HubSpot Unbound's Yamini Rangan, noting both framed AI as entering an agentic 'Outcomes' era.
post_text:
Many of those that attended the conferences this week will be heading home today. I am not sure about those that attended Unbound (formerly Inbound), but for many of those that attended Dreamforce, a quiet weekend to recover is likely in the cards. I was able to stream many of the sessions, including the keynotes, from both events. I can say the keynotes, while completely different, did not disappoint.

These two events and the main keynotes could not be more different. Dreamforce showed its size and market cap of around $210 billion, with slick production. Salesforce kicked off the keynote with a well-produced video of Matthew McConaughey, Creative Advisor, being paid around $10 million annually, to build excitement. While the streaming of Unbound lacked that level of production, and let's be honest, it could use a bit, the keynote by Yamini Rangan was as compelling as that of Marc Benioff's but completely different.

On one side, the Salesforce keynote was technology-focused. Benioff set out to dispel the notion of ‘SaaSagedon,’ i.e., the end of SaaS, by presenting the power of AI and Salesforce combined. AI, being a probabilistic system that can be prone to error, is best paired with a deterministic system, i.e., Salesforce.

In sharp contrast to the Salesforce keynote, Yamini Rangan didn’t start off with a video or by talking about Hubspot’s success, growth, or technology, but went straight into the challenges we've all faced in the AI era. She compared where we are to the ‘maxing phase,’ the precursor stage to actually realizing value, just like when we ‘max’ in training, and the results follow the stage, not in the stage. Rangan argued that we are entering what she frames as the ‘Outcomes’ era, following this maxing stage. Instead of mastering the technology, we can now start to leverage it and focus on what outcomes we want to achieve.

So what was the common theme then? Both keynotes took aim at how their respective solutions help organizations unlock trapped value. Both posit that the Agentic era is upon us and that AI is there to help people and organizations.

In my next post I will dive into the Salesforce keynote and follow up with more on the Hubspot keynote.

The big question is which one resonates with you and your team and ultimately meets your needs.

summary: Founder Sudheer Kiran lists Dreamforce announcements—AIforce, Claudeforce, Agentforce, Koa, and AWS/Google Cloud integrations—plus a Sam Altman talk on AI trust and governance.
post_text:
Yesterday, I wrote about what I saw at HubSpot UNBOUND 2026 and why I think marketing is moving from AI-assisted workflows toward agentic AI.

Then came Salesforce Dreamforce 2026.

And the story got even clearer.

What caught my attention wasn’t the number of AI announcements. It was the direction behind them.

AI is moving deeper into the systems where marketing, sales and customer operations actually happen.

A few things stood out to me:

→ AIforce: Salesforce is pushing the CRM beyond its traditional interface, allowing AI to work with Salesforce data, workflows and business logic.

→ Claudeforce: The Salesforce + Anthropic partnership brings Claude together with Salesforce context, workflows and actions.

→ Agentforce: The conversation is shifting from AI assistants that answer questions to agents that can actually execute work.

→ Koa: Salesforce is building reasoning specifically around CRM and business context.

→ AWS + Google Cloud: Salesforce is also making its data and agents increasingly connected to the broader technology ecosystem.

And then there was the conversation with Sam Altman, which added another dimension to the discussion: as AI moves from generating answers to taking actions, trust, governance and human oversight become much more important.

What I find most interesting is how closely this connects with what we saw at HubSpot UNBOUND.

HubSpot showed us AI getting closer to the buyer and marketer.

ChatGPT Ads, AI visibility, CRM context and AI-driven execution.

Salesforce is showing us AI getting deeper into the enterprise.

CRM context, reasoning, agents and execution.

Put the two together and I think we’re seeing a much bigger shift.

The question is no longer simply:

“What can AI help marketers do?”

It’s becoming:

“What does AI understand about our business, and what are we willing to let it do?”

That’s a very different conversation.

I shared my full take on what Dreamforce 2026 means for marketers and why I think the CRM is becoming something AI can operate through.

author_headline: CEO at Redtag
summary: Redtag CEO Nazar Mykytyn highlights Marc Benioff's Dreamforce keynote quote on grounding probabilistic AI models in Salesforce's deterministic corporate data.
post_text:
Salesforce just shared the key Dreamforce takeaways, and this is the most important one 

Enterprises can’t run on models alone. AI models are powerful but probabilistic — they understand the world, but not the rules that govern your business. As Salesforce Chair and CEO Marc Benioff put it at the keynote: “They kind of know what’s going on, but they’re not grounded in a single set of truth like your traditional Salesforce apps. The idea really is, how can you bring that probabilistic world of the AI world to the deterministic world? The deterministic world is where all that corporate data is, where the single source of truth is.” Connecting model intelligence to your workflows, policies, permissions, and context is how you get agents that can act with trust.

🇺🇲 Busy week! Dreamforce & 2 new certifications: Sharing & Visibility Architect e Data Architect!!

Sharing models, OWD, role hierarchies, matching rules, and identity resolution. Is it invisible work? Yes, but it is precisely this invisible work that underpins everything else (honestly, I wish the Lucas of 2018 knew what I know today...).

An AI agent seeing the wrong record because the sharing model is poorly designed isn't an AI problem—it’s a data architecture problem. Amid the daily rush and project pressures, many fail to consider how to solve this before scaling. A Data Cloud pipeline that conflates different customer identities doesn't stall due to a lack of technology; it stalls for lack of expertise in hybrid profiles, unification, and foundational governance.

Anyway, I'm happy to have managed to get both! There's still one more to go this year... :)

Just wrapped up Dreamforce , and honestly, there's a lot to unpack this year. Sharing the highlights:

🔹Enterprise AI Harness - brings together six Salesforce products (Informatica, Data 360, Tableau, Salesforce Guardian, MuleSoft, Agentforce Studio) into one "AI Control Plane."
🔹Koa - Salesforce's own CRM-built AI model (built with NVIDIA), made for Sales, Service, and Marketing work. In pilot now, with a wider rollout planned later in 2026.
🔹Job-Ready Agents - 7 pre-built agents businesses can deploy out of the box. 6 are already live: Casey & Fin (customer service, Fin also works with third-party CRMs), Paige (employee IT/HR help), Carter (shopping assistant), Marshall (back-office/finance process builder), and Piper (inbound B2B lead qualification). Hunter (sales pipeline) is still in pilot, GA expected Nov 2026.

The direction is clear: less time logging into Salesforce apps, more AI doing the work where you already are. Exciting times to be in this ecosystem.

post_text:
Salesforce launched Claudeforce with Anthropic at Dreamforce 2026. What every IT Manager using Salesforce must understand.
Salesforce and Anthropic expanded their strategic partnership and unveiled Claudeforce, a new way for salespeople to access critical data directly from inside Anthropic's Claude chatbot. Source: CNBC September 15, 2026.
On the same day, Salesforce and Nvidia announced a new reasoning model for Agentforce built on one of Nvidia's open-weight Nemotron models. Source: CNBC September 15, 2026.
For IT Managers, two announcements from the world's largest software conference matter for your enterprise stack.
Claudeforce: if your organisation runs Salesforce, your CRM data is now directly accessible from inside Claude. That creates a data governance question your IT and legal teams need to answer immediately. Which Salesforce data classifications are permitted to flow through Claudeforce? What audit logging exists for Claudeforce access to CRM data? What happens to that data in Anthropic's infrastructure?
Agentforce on Nemotron: Salesforce has embedded Nvidia's open-weight AI directly into its agentic platform. That means AI agents operating inside your Salesforce environment are now powered by a model whose open-weight architecture carries different security characteristics from Claude.

author_headline: Salesforce Certified Application Architect at furuCRM Inc.
summary: Salesforce Architect Dung Huynh summarizes Adam Olshansky's session '5 Mindset Shifts for the AI Era,' detailing shifts like Resistance to Evolution and Doer to Director.
post_text:
One session I really enjoyed at Dreamforce was “5 Mindset Shifts for the AI Era” by Adam Olshansky.

What I liked most was that AI is not simply helping us work faster. It is changing our role in tech.

Here are my takeaways from the 5 mindset shifts:

1. Resistance → Evolution

When I first started using AI, I was a little hesitant.

I’m quite fast when doing things manually, so my first thought was often: “It’s just a small task. I can do it faster myself.”

Giving AI enough context also felt troublesome.

Then one of my colleagues showed me different ways to provide context so AI could understand the problem better.

That was when I learned how to “bully” AI 😂

The productivity improvement was impressive. I no longer had to write every line of code myself, which gave me more time for things I knew I should do but never had enough time for.

2. Solo Builder → Team Player

When I first started working with Salesforce, there were so many things I didn’t understand.

My boss wasn’t always available, and senior members were busy with their own projects. I spent a lot of time researching or waiting for someone to confirm my approach.

Now, AI can be another teammate.

Instead of just asking for answers, I can ask it to challenge my approach, question my assumptions, and find what I might have missed.

3. Doer → Director

This was my favorite part.

Adam described AI as a “brilliant high-speed intern”: extremely fast, but it doesn’t understand your business without enough context.

AI might do 80% of the work. The remaining 20%, including review, business knowledge, and direction, is where our value comes in.

Try asking AI to write a test class that covers every necessary case correctly on the first try.

Some unnecessary cases will probably be there, while important ones are somehow missing 😅

Our role is shifting from simply doing the work to knowing what should be done and whether AI did it correctly.

4. Specialist → Polymath

Just look at the App Store and Google Play. More people without a coding background can now build applications with AI.

Not knowing a technology or programming language is no longer as big a limitation as before.

The ability to learn quickly, ask the right questions, and connect knowledge across different areas becomes more important.

5. Staying Ahead → Become Your Own Replacement

Instead of worrying about AI or someone else replacing you, replace the old version of yourself with one that knows how to use AI better.

Maybe the question in the AI era is no longer:

“What can I do?”

but:

“What can I direct AI to do?”

There is something grounding about moving from conversations about the future of technology to being alongside teams doing the hard work of making transformation real.

And then… Dreamforce.

If there was one shift that Dreamforce 2026 made unmistakable, it was this: enterprises are moving from AI-assisted to truly agentic.

AI is no longer just answering questions or assisting employees — it’s reasoning, acting and orchestrating work across trusted enterprise data. From AIforce and Claudeforce to Koa, the future is open, contextual and increasingly embedded in the flow of work.

The question is no longer simply “What can AI do?” but “How do we operationalize it at scale — and turn it into measurable business impact?”

For me, Dreamforce reinforced that the real opportunity isn’t the technology alone. It’s how we bring it together with people, process and industry context to create meaningful outcomes.

And that brings me to perhaps my favorite part of Dreamforce — the people.

It is a rare opportunity to connect with clients, partners, colleagues, leaders and practitioners from across the ecosystem. Some of the most valuable moments weren’t on a stage or in a keynote. They happened in hallways, over coffee, in customer meetings, at partner sessions and in conversations with colleagues I don’t often get to meet face-to-face.

Those conversations are where announcements turn into possibilities — where we start asking what this means for our clients, what we can build differently, and where AI can genuinely transform an experience or an operating model.

As I wrap up these 10 days, I’m leaving with much more than notes from Dreamforce — new ideas, stronger relationships, renewed client context and plenty to take back to our teams.

Salesforce announced Koa, a reasoning model built on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super, during a Dreamforce event, demonstrating open-source AI deployment in enterprise CRM systems.

• Koa was built by post-training NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Super on a proprietary synthetic dataset drawn from nearly three decades of enterprise CRM deployments.
• Koa utilized supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with NVIDIA NeMo RL, NeMo Gym, and NeMo AutoModel. The model runs entirely within Salesforce's infrastructure, ensuring no customer data is used during training or inference.
• In Salesforce’s CRM Bench, Koa matches or exceeds leading model performance on CRM actions, demonstrating 3x fewer errors compared to benchmarks.
• The training corpus covers synthetic enterprise scenarios across 14+ industries, including manufacturing, financial services, healthcare, and travel. Customer pilots start in October with clients like Formula 1 and UChicago Medicine.

Why it matters: The use of open models like Nemotron allows enterprises to fine-tune and run complex reasoning models entirely within their private cloud infrastructure, maintaining strict data control and maximizing security for sensitive customer data.

summary: Zach N., a Salesforce public sector leader, describes his DF26 talk on open, multi-framework government portals using React, Agentforce Vibes, Claude Code, Data 360, MuleSoft and Informatica.
post_text:
I had the absolute pleasure of taking the stage at Dreamforce #DF26 to share a product vision for the future of state & local government digital service delivery! This was particularly special for me because I was able to demonstrate the progress we at Salesforce are making on a number of key capabilities that our public sector customers and the civic tech community have been requesting from vendors for a very long time!

Here are a few core takeaways from the stage:
- The Future of the Salesforce Platform is OPEN: With our headless toolkit and multi-framework support for React, governments can now build and host React portals on our governed platform. This enables agencies to own the design in-house and stand up exceptional human-centered portals using open source U.S. Web Design System or state design system components! Good human-centered design = increased civic engagement 🙂
- Best of Both Worlds: Multi-framework allows governments to pair open-source tools (like Code for America’s SNAP work requirements screener) with Salesforce hosting, data, workflows, security, and governance. Paired with Agentforce Vibes and Claude Code, agencies can now stand up accessible, standardized portals in days rather than months. Lots of possibilities for new constituent-centered experiences that were previously too much effort or cost prohibitive.
- Low-Burden, High-Impact AI: To reduce resident friction on paperwork-intensive tasks, agencies can use Agentforce to build AI prompts directly into workflows. These can both be incredibly impactful and make for great initial use cases. For instance, directing AI to analyze a photo of a volunteer hours log and pre-fill forms with resident confirmation before they submit.
- Delivering Connected Experiences: Data 360, MuleSoft, and Informatica provide a foundation to master data, unify identities, and harmonize constituent records across systems. Paired with opt-in for residents and data sharing agreements, this pre-populates known information, cuts down on resident friction, and can help deter fraud.
- Free, Democratized Learning via Trailhead: Salesforce Trailhead remains free for everyone, whether you hold a Salesforce license or not. Program teams can learn everything from core platform skills to AI concepts and business strategy.

Including a reference to Code for America's Human-Centered Work Requirements Screener for SNAP that I mentioned in the demo: https://lnkd.in/gW_f-tM3
I encourage customers to consider embedding it via multi-framework or Salesforce Flow!

Finally, a big thank you to public servants working tirelessly to deliver for residents every single day 💙

(P.S. For more on SNAP, Medicaid, and how policy expands work requirements, check out Jennifer Pahlka’s podcast, Friction is the Feature: https://lnkd.in/gcBbdq2d, it inspired many of the ideas in my demo!)

author_headline: Director of Sales and Marketing Technology at CBIZ
summary: CBIZ's Curtis Shelton recaps Steve Simpson's session on career architecture, arguing Salesforce professionals must shift from executor to architect as AI agents handle execution.
post_text:
One of my biggest takeaways from Dreamforce  wasn't actually about a particular Salesforce product. It was about how our jobs are changing.

I had the opportunity to hear Steve Simpson talk about architecting your career for an AI-driven workplace and architecting Salesforce in the AI era.

Follow Steve Simpson on LinkedIn⁠: https://lnkd.in/gFppkkfP

One concept really stuck with me:
As AI agents become capable of doing more of the execution, our value increasingly shifts toward architecture, orchestration and ownership of outcomes.

Steve talked about the evolution from being an executor toward becoming a strategic engineer and ultimately thinking like an architect. His Dreamforce sessions also explored how AI is changing the way we plan, design, build, test and deliver Salesforce solutions.

We're already living in a reality where we're sitting in front of our multiple monitors with four or five different agents working simultaneously:

One is analyzing data.
One is building something.
One is testing it.
Another is researching or troubleshooting.
Another is our helper "rubber ducky" agent that helps guide us on how to guide our other agents.

Our job has become:
What am I asking them to accomplish?
What context do they need?
How do these systems connect?
What guardrails do they need?
How do I validate the results?
What happens when something goes wrong?
And ultimately—who owns the outcome?

That last question is the important one.

AI can execute.
Humans still have to own the outcome.

And that means the scope of what it means to be a “technical person” is about to get much broader.

It can't just be:
Salesforce Admin → Salesforce Developer → Salesforce Architect

We're increasingly going from:
Platform → Data → Integrations → Security → Business Process → AI Agents → Governance → Outcomes → The Integration Architect

Not necessarily someone whose job title is Integration Architect. Rather, a person who understands how people, systems, data, APIs, AI agents and business processes fit together—and takes responsibility for the result.

You don't have to be the world's best developer.
You don't have to know every Salesforce feature.
You don't have to be an expert in every system.
But you increasingly need enough breadth to understand the connections between them.
That's a pretty significant shift in what it means to build a technology career.

And honestly, it's one of the most exciting things I took away from Dreamforce.

Thanks to Steve Simpson for putting some of these ideas into perspective. His work is a great reminder that architect thinking isn't just about designing technology anymore. It's about designing how technology works together.

author_headline: Partner, Salesforce Tech Solutions
summary: Partner Gustavo Tanure argues (in Portuguese) AI projects fail on process/data not tech, listing Salesforce agents like Casey, Piper, Hunter, Carter and Marshall plus a Headless Experience Layer.
post_text:
Depois de 3 dias de Dreamforce, mais de 45Km percorridos (é… a gente anda um bocado) e dezenas de sessões, e a cabeça está a mil. Muita inovação, muita coisa por fazer. Separei o que fez mais sentido pra mim.

Uma coisa apareceu logo no primeiro dia e não saiu mais da minha cabeça: a maioria dos projetos de IA que travam não travam por tecnologia. Travam por processo e dados. Caso de uso escolhido porque dava pra fazer e não porque valia a pena. Piloto que nunca sai do papel porque ninguém preparou a empresa pra absorver aquilo em escala.
Salesforce que não estava preparado para Agentes. 
É isso mesmo…. Os projetos agora devem ser orientados ao agente. Regra de negócio embutida no LWC? Esquece. Não escala. Agente não lê UI. 

A Salesforce, pra ajudar nisso, hoje já vem com agentes por finalidade:

Atendimento e Suporte

	•	Casey (Help Agent): resolve atendimento ao cliente, automatizando devoluções, rastreamento de pedidos e perguntas frequentes.
	•	Paige (IT & HR Agent): atende chamados internos de TI e RH.

Vendas e Marketing

	•	Piper (Inbound Pipe Gen Agent): engaja, qualifica e converte leads que chegam de forma passiva pelo site ou caixa de entrada.
	•	Hunter (Outbound Sales Agent): prospecção ativa, buscando leads e criando oportunidades de ponta a ponta.

Operações, Comércio e Back-Office

	•	Carter (Shopping/Commerce Agent): assistente de compras, sugere produtos e ajuda a fechar o carrinho.
	•	Marshall (Supply Chain Agent): otimiza a cadeia de suprimentos, gerenciando fornecedores.
	•	Fin (Customer Experience Agent): gerencia e personaliza a jornada do cliente na plataforma (que suporta áudio e anexos).

E, claro, o canal. A interface saiu do Salesforce e foi pra onde o cliente está — Teams, Slack, Claude, GPT, WhatsApp. Por isso a Salesforce criou o Headless Experience Layer: mesmo conteúdo e mesma experiência, independente do canal.

Por isso a pergunta mudou. Não é mais "dá pra fazer um agente pra isso" — agente todo mundo faz. Bom agente, muito poucos.
A pergunta agora mudou: qual agente fazer, pra quê, qual necessidade de negócio ele resolve de fato, onde estão as informações que ele vai usar, e o que ele pode ou não pode fazer sozinho e qual canal estará?

Deixou de ser ferramenta de produtividade. Virou arquitetura de negócio.
