author_headline: I make commercial strategy executable. Product Marketing at DealHub AI | CPQ, Quote-to-Revenue, and the AI systems that run modern GTM | Microsoft, Amazon Business
summary: DealHub AI marketer David Held argues Salesforce's own keynote language describing revenue infrastructure migration as "a rebuild," not an upgrade, undermines its switching-cost lock-in advantage.
post_text:
As I watched the Dreamforce keynote this week, one phrase stopped me in my tracks and hasn't allowed me to move on.

"It is not an upgrade. It is a rebuild."

That was Salesforce describing what it takes to move to their new revenue infrastructure. Not a migration. Not a lift-and-shift. A rebuild.

For two decades, the argument for staying on the Salesforce platform has been switching cost. The longer you are on it, the deeper the wiring, the harder it is to leave. But switching cost only works if the alternative is building something new. If, in the context of SFCPQ,> RCA, the vendor is already asking you to rebuild inside their own tent, the math collapses.

You are not preserving sunk cost. You are paying to demolish and reconstruct on someone else's timeline, with someone else's new blueprint (AI consumption), so you can keep paying rent on land you already bought.

Being around business applications for over 20 years, I have seen enough platform migrations to know that "rebuild" is the honest word vendors use when "upgrade" would be a lie. And when a vendor gets that honest in public, it usually means the foundation required more than a renovation.

If they are already rebuilding the foundation, are they asking you to buy the land or sign a longer lease?

author_headline: Salesforce Consultant
summary: Tiago Freitas details Dreamforce's Claudeforce launch, explaining Salesforce in Claude's 37 sales skills and a separate ~40-skill developer plug-in for Apex, deploy and metadata.
post_text:
O plug-in oficial da Salesforce coloca o Claude Code criando metadado, escrevendo Apex e rodando deploy na sua sandbox, sem você sair do terminal.

Saiu no Dreamforce, dia 15 de setembro. E não confunda: Claudeforce é o nome da parceria Salesforce + Anthropic, e o primeiro produto dela é o Salesforce in Claude, com 37 skills para quem vende. O plug-in de desenvolvimento é outra coisa: cerca de 40 skills para metadado, Apex, deploy, retrieve e revisão de segurança.

O que eu configuro antes de soltar isso num projeto:

1. Conecto só em sandbox.
2. Libero rede por comando, o sf CLI só fala com a org e o login.
3. No MCP, uso usuário de integração com permissão limitada.
4. Time todo na mesma versão. A 2.1.275 quebrou quem usa gateway e a 2.1.276 corrigiu no dia seguinte. Rode claude --version e, se for a 275, rode claude update.

Dica de time: coloque "autoUpdatesChannel": "stable" no settings.json. O canal stable atrasa cerca de uma semana e pula versão com regressão grande.

Mini glossário:
• Skill: pacote de instruções que ensina uma tarefa ao assistente.
• Plug-in: conjunto de skills e ferramentas.
• MCP: padrão que liga o assistente a outros sistemas, como o Salesforce.
• sf CLI: linha de comando da Salesforce, usada no deploy.
• Sandbox: cópia da org para testar sem mexer em produção.
• Gateway: servidor da empresa que fica no meio do caminho até a IA.

A versão longa está no blog A.I. Foil.

author_headline: Helping companies save 30%+ in costs with ACX Framework | CEO & Co-founder @ Teleperson
summary: Teleperson CEO Jesse Hollander cites a Harness survey of 700 engineering leaders showing high confidence but low actual tooling for AI agent discovery, testing gates and kill switches.
post_text:
Four companies shipped an AI "control plane" in eight days. One survey explained why none of it will matter yet.

Salesforce announced one at Dreamforce — register, govern, observe, and cost-control agents across Salesforce and third-party platforms. Genesys named one the same thing last week. WSO2 released an open-source one under Apache 2.0. Dipp AI shipped a runtime data gateway.

Then Harness surveyed 700 engineering leaders. 75% already run agents in production. 

Here's what they found:

1️⃣ 77% are confident they have a complete inventory of every agent, MCP server and LLM in their environment. 44% run discovery tooling that could verify it.

2️⃣ 74% are confident their testing would catch a production-impacting failure. 19% have a gate that automatically blocks a bad release.

3️⃣ 76% believe they could shut down a misbehaving agent in under 15 minutes. 33% have a kill switch.

And the one that should stop you: 

4️⃣ 87% had an agent-related security event this year — and confidence didn't predict who did. The group that said their agents were secure end to end had incidents at 88%. Against 87% for everyone else.

That's not a weak correlation. That's no correlation. 

Whatever enterprises are currently using to assess their agent security posture is measuring something else.

The control plane became a product category this month. It has not yet become a practice.

Two things worth doing this week: run discovery and see what's actually running. Then time your kill switch and write the number down.

post_text:
“AI won’t wipe your tears.” — Reese Witherspoon

I went to Dreamforce expecting to hear a lot about AI. And I did. A LOT about AI.

New technology, tools, integrations and demos of what’s possible now and what’s coming next.

But that isn’t what I’m leaving San Francisco thinking about.

Across speakers from the UAE’s Minister of AI to Sterling K. Brown, Tony Robbins, Reese Witherspoon and many others, I kept hearing the same current:

Our humanity matters. Maybe more than ever.

Technology should make people’s lives better. We need to be intentional about how AI changes the skills we value and not automate for the sake of automating.

We can’t lose our creativity, curiosity or ability to solve problems in new ways.

The theme I heard over and over was energy.

The energy we bring to other people. Finding inspiration. Leaning into our relationships and enjoying the journey while we’re building whatever comes next.

There’s so much possibility in what AI can do. I left Dreamforce thinking just as much about what we choose to do with it, and what we make sure stays distinctly human.

And yes, being thoroughly entertained along the way with amazing coworkers definitely helped my energy.

summary: Wavelength co-founder Pranav Mallampalli argues AI-driven digital CS needs reasoning beyond Customer.io, Iterable, Gainsight or ChurnZero, citing a Josh Allen analogy and Databricks/Hubspot example.
post_text:
"I want an AI like Josh Allen (shoutout Buffalo Bills) that can read a defense, determine an audible to call or pick a play, and run" That's what someone told me at #dreamforce and honestly, for digital customer success, I AGREE and so does my fantasy team 🏈 

Customer.io crossed 100M ARR and Iterable has raised hundreds of millions for their orchestration systems (they're really good btw). You can trigger an email whenever a user or prospect takes an action, segmented down by a CRM attribute, and personalized to what they've done. 

OG CSP's like Gainsight and ChurnZero create systems of record that could also trigger these outreach campaigns, but based off of health scoring and directional attributes instead of just specific ones. 

But after chatting with dozens of CS leaders, one of their biggest issues getting an AI to reason about if that account needs to be talked to. The football reference translated to a CS workflow: "give me a list of customers that match an upgrade flow from Databricks, that haven't been marketed to via Hubspot, and create a personal play to send IN A CHANNEL THEY'LL READ!"

That's the gap we're building Wavelength to fill. A digital CSM that can reason, personalize, and orchestrate the right campaigns, in-app messages, and more. The best digital CS programs won't be built inside a CSP or a lifecycle tool alone. They'll be built on a reasoning layer that can do both simultaneously.

But for most growing businesses, the real question isn’t:

“What’s the newest Salesforce feature?”

summary: Fuse AI co-founder Saurav Bubber recounts his first Dreamforce, hearing Jensen Huang, Dario Amodei, Sam Altman and Tony Robbins, predicting AGI within 36 months and headless enterprise software.
post_text:
Just attended my first Dreamforce and it was nothing short of incredible! 

It felt like the Super Bowl for tech - Marc Benioff managed to bring together some of the most inspiring leaders from across across the world:

Jensen Huang
Dario Amodei
Sam Altman
Tony Robbins, Matthew McConaughey, and many more.
Star-studded lineup.

The coolest part for me was actually getting to spend time with leaders from some of the largest enterprises and hearing how they’re thinking about enterprise-wide AI transformations.

A few key takeaways:

1. We are probably <36 months away from something that looks like AGI.
But the tone has definitely shifted from “this is coming one day” to “you should probably start preparing now.”

2. The top enterprises are re-evaluating everything and are looking to the best startups in every sector to help. Legora for legal, Rillet for enterprise finance, Profound for martech, Listen Labs for user research and many more are leading the way.

Interestingly enough, it was the first conferences we went to where folks started recognizing Fuse AI for being one of the emerging leaders in sales-tech. 🏎️ 🏎️ 

3. Organizations are becoming headless
 The future probably isn’t employees logging into 20 different SaaS tools every day. The tools sit underneath.
The data, permissions, workflows and actions get exposed.
Then the interface becomes Claude, Slack, Salesforce, an internal agent, or whatever comes next.
The UI matters less.
The infrastructure underneath matters a lot more.

4. Tokenmaxxing is becoming a real thing in GTM too
If something can be solved by throwing more compute, more research or more agents at it, companies are increasingly going to do that.

A lot of work that used to take hours is quickly becoming cheap enough to just run continuously through AI agents, with AI-native teams focusing on high leverage activites.

5. Humans are still the future
This was probably my favourite part.
I don’t think the future is just replacing everyone with AI, it's giving great people significantly more leverage.

As AI adoption expands, this means higher quality products for enterprises, great access to software, and the ability to solve problems we didn't think where possible before. This will create more and higher impact work for humans, not less.

To drive this transformation, humans will still bring the vision, execution, taste, creativity, judgment, relationships and ambition.

Dreamforce made one thing pretty clear:

The next few years are going to be some of the most EXCITING years in history and we are still very early!

- Saurav, Co-Founder @ fuseai.com

post_text:
Leaving #DF26, I’m struck not just by the pace of innovation, but by how fundamentally the enterprise technology model is being reimagined.

→ The interface is changing.
AIforce particularly caught my attention. The traditional CRM UI may no longer need to be the destination. Intelligence can increasingly meet people where they work — while securely connecting to the data, workflows and business logic underneath.

→ The architecture is changing with it.
Combine that with Data 360, Agentforce and increasingly specialized reasoning models, and we are moving beyond simply adding AI to applications. We are beginning to rethink how humans, agents, data and enterprise capabilities work together.

→ For healthcare, that leads to an even more important question: what does this mean for the patient experience?
Patients shouldn’t have to understand the systems behind their journey. They should experience something connected, contextual and proactive — with intelligence behind the scenes and human interaction when it matters most.

→ Greater capability also requires greater trust.
As technology becomes more autonomous, trust, governance, interoperability and accountability become even more important. They aren’t barriers to innovation — they are what allow innovation to scale responsibly.

→ Ultimately, innovation isn’t the outcome.
The goal isn’t more AI pilots. It’s turning innovation into trusted capabilities that create meaningful, measurable outcomes — responsibly and at scale.

Great conversations and learning with colleagues and the broader Takeda team throughout #DF26.

What a time to be in technology — and to help shape what comes next.

summary: Josh Smith, enterprise systems executive, says AI outputs depend on data/semantic layer, warns "garbage in, gospel out," and notes selling moving outside CRM UI.
post_text:
Great week in San Francisco at Dreamforce - ran into old colleagues, had great meetings with my team, our partners, and our Salesforce account team.

Key themes from this year:

1) AI outputs are only as good as your underlying data and semantic layer. While there was a lot of talk about AIforce, Claudeforce, Koa, Agentforce, etc., one thing was clear across the board. You win and lose at the foundation. Don’t build the base correctly and the house crumbles.

2) To that end, a quote stuck with me this week. “Garbage in, garbage out” has now turned into “Garbage in, gospel out”. In other words, folks are taking AI outputs at face value. Frontier models are often seen as all knowing and outputs are trusted blindly without questioning the data and context underneath. That’s a dangerous, slippery slope. This is why the contextual layer and AI-ready data underneath are so important.

3) In the same way that we are seeing web content be consumed differently - I.e. most traffic now coming from bots, less traditional search or directly going to websites, selling and success motions are moving out of the CRM UI directly and into AI as well. This is thought provoking - I.e. getting AI tools into the hands of the end users more quickly to help drive revenue.

Overall, great week. Now it’s time to go put this into action!

For those of you who were also there or tuned in virtually, what were your takeaways?

summary: Yanqi Luo, Salesforce ML scientist, recaps Dreamforce talks by Reese Witherspoon on Hello Sunshine, Omar Sultan Al Olama, will.i.am and Matthew McConaughey on AI and humanity.
post_text:
I saw Reese Witherspoon speak at Dreamforce, and my first thought was:

She really is Elle Woods in real life! 💗

Warm, feminine, optimistic — but also incredibly ambitious.

Before this, I mostly knew Reese through her movies. I knew much less about the entrepreneur behind Hello Sunshine.

She shared how frustrated she became with the roles and stories available to women in Hollywood. At one point, she asked studios how many female-led movies they were making — and realized just how few there were.

One line from her stuck with me:

“Rage can be a good motivator.” 🔥

Instead of waiting for the industry to change, she eventually decided to build something herself.

Sometimes when you keep looking around thinking, “I could do this differently. I could do this better,” frustration is actually telling you something.

Maybe you build.

She also talked a lot about human connection — how the people who stay with you tend to be the ones who share your vision. 

Her story about her book club made that tangible. She didn’t initially realize how much simply choosing and amplifying a book could change an author’s life — helping someone build a career, support a family, and reach an audience they might never have reached otherwise.

That theme of humanity kept showing up throughout Dreamforce in very different ways.

H.E. Omar Sultan Al Olama talked about bringing innovators into regulatory roles — so people who understand what it means to build technology can also help shape the rules around it.

I also liked the UAE’s broader framing: keep conversations open, coexist with different approaches, and ultimately come back to a simple question:

Is this technology actually improving people’s lives? 🌍

Then will.i.am and Matthew McConaughey brought up another side of the AI wave: imagination, presence, and the micro-moments of life.

We talk endlessly about agents, productivity and automation. But the small moments — noticing something, imagining something, being fully present with someone — are part of what makes us human.

Are we using AI — or are we letting AI use us? 🤖

And the All-In conversation brought in responsibility. Moving fast doesn’t remove the need to understand failures, do real root-cause analysis, test what we build, and take responsibility for the consequences.

For a conference filled with conversations about AI, my biggest takeaway was actually about humanity:
 
Build when you think something can be better.
Protect your imagination. 💭
Take responsibility for what you create.
Value human connection. 🤝
And don’t let the AI wave make you miss the micro-moments of life.

And yes, I left even more convinced that Reese Witherspoon is basically the real-life Elle Woods. 💗

#Dreamforce #AI #DF26 #Humanity #ResponsibleAI

Dreamforce 2026 has wrapped, and the direction of travel is hard to miss: Salesforce wants its data and business logic sitting underneath the tools people already work in, not behind its own screen.

2. Koa, Salesforce's first CRM reasoning model, built on NVIDIA Nemotron and now in pilot. Notably, trained on simulated enterprise scenarios rather than customer data.

4. Seven prebuilt job-ready agents (Hunter, Casey, Paige, Carter, Marshall, Piper, Fin) move the conversation from building agents to deploying digital workers.

5. The Trusted Enterprise AI Harness puts governance front and center, with deterministic execution as the safeguard. Agents reason where flexibility helps, then fall back to governed workflows and approvals the moment an action carries real risk.

post_text:
Sharing a few tidbits I've learned as I reflect on my time at #Dreamforce this week - Let's Talk #Slack. 

Many of us already spend a meaningful part of our day in Slack - just a few practical use cases to further streamline your day:

⭐ Catch up quickly: Use AI in Slackbot to summarize what you missed, rather than work through every message (especially useful with many threads)

⭐ Find prior context: Search past channel conversations and events you have access to—making it easier to reuse decisions and knowledge that may otherwise be buried.  (For example: You joined a new company and want to learn from how an event was run last year.)

⭐ Create reusable skills: Set up repeatable prompts for common actions, such as notifying a group when new cases arrive.

⭐ Mobilize faster: Let's say your website went down and you need to fix it, fast...Slack can help pull together the right people, context, and actions in one place.

⭐Prepare with less effort: You can use Agent marketplace to download #Agentforce agents to provide notifications ahead of a call with quick context, read emails and pre-generate draft responses, and generate executive updates 

⭐ Collaborate on building: Emerging AI-powered coding capabilities can allow teams to prompt, create, and improve solutions together - directly in Slack.

There is also an important watch-out: as organizations create more agents and skills, clear naming conventions, reusable patterns, and governance will matter. Otherwise, teams can quickly recreate the very complexity they are trying to solve.

Special thanks to Brett Stineman and Christine McHone, our Slack experts 🏆, for your insights in facilitating the Salesforce and Slalom roundtable on the latest AI innovations in #Slack!

summary: LuMay AI's Surekha Chikoti details takeaways from Gaurav Kheterpal and Ishita Mathur's session on AI agent evaluation, testing, tracing and monitoring using LLM-as-Judge.
post_text:
Dreamforce was packed with learning across the AI journey — from keynotes and customer stories to deep technical sessions. A big thank you to Salesforce and Dreamforce for bringing together such a strong community of builders, leaders, and practitioners.

One session that stayed especially close to me was on AI Agent Evaluation, Testing, Tracing & Monitoring.

I have followed Gaurav Kheterpal’s Dreamforce sessions for years. In many ways, he has been a virtual mentor to  me, and I continue to be inspired by the practical depth he brings to the Salesforce ecosystem.

A few takeaways that stood out:
* Evaluate agent quality across groundedness, factuality, completeness, and policy adherence
* Build strong test cases with expected behavior, actions, and responses
* Use LLM-as-Judge for automated evaluation, supported by human validation and calibration
* Trace failures across retrieval, reasoning, tools, and generation
* Monitor operational signals such as engagement, response, and escalation rates
* Use alerts and investigation workflows to identify the root cause
* Continuously Build → Test → Monitor → Optimize as part of the refinement loop

The biggest reminder for me: post-production monitoring is just as important as deployment itself. Once agents go live, teams need continuous visibility into quality, behavior, failures, thresholds, and improvement opportunities.

Learning Path: Evaluate → Validate → Trace → Monitor → Alert → Monitor

Continuously improve while keeping the continuous lifecycle around it is important.

At LuMay AI, this is also a core part of how we think and build enterprise AI solutions— testing, evaluation, observability, monitoring, governance, traceability, human oversight, and continuous improvement across the production lifecycle.

A special thank you to Gaurav Kheterpal and Ishita Mathur for creating such a strong applied learning experience that made a complex topic practical and easy to follow.

Enterprise AI is not just about getting agents into production. It is about continuously understanding, monitoring, and improving how they perform.

summary: BCG's Shalini Unnikrishnan recaps moderating a session with Rwanda's ICT Minister Paula Ingabire on AI scaling, citing Zipline drones and BioNTech's mRNA manufacturing partnership.
post_text:
One of the most substantive events that I had a chance to moderate at Dreamforce was a session with Paula Ingabire, Rwanda's Minister of ICT and Innovation, on how AI is being unlocked in Rwanda and scaled across Africa. I came away energized by how far the country has moved on this agenda.

Minister Ingabire framed Rwanda as a proof-of-concept country for Africa. A regulatory environment built for testing new technology, then scaling successful pilots across the continent. Zipline's drone delivery and the mRNA manufacturing partnership with BioNTech both grew out of exactly that model.
 
What I'd like to highlight is the discipline in Rwanda's approach. They deliberately ask whether AI is even the right tool for a given problem, rather than treating it as the default answer. That kind of clarity is what turns a proof of concept into something durable.
 
Thank you to Minister Paula and everyone in the room for one of my most memorable conversations of the week.

author_headline: Founder & CEO | Artificial Intelligence Leader, Advisor, & International Speaker | ex-Amazon AI Lead | 10+ years in AI/ML | UC Berkeley
summary: AI leader Raj Muhar analyzes Jensen Huang's Dreamforce remarks on AI safety and against new regulation, arguing instead for impact-scaled rules, builder liability, and diverse stakeholder input.
post_text:
Jensen Huang spoke at Dreamforce this week and two of his points stand out to me.

"If you build a product or a service and you're not confident in its functionality, capability, or safety, then don't release it...Safety is paramount in a lot of ways. It’s job one...Innovation, speed and safe products, it’s a false choice. You could definitely have both at the same time.”

I agree with this. A frontier AI system deserves the same discipline as any typical engineering release: a variety of evaluations, red-teaming, staged rollouts, and monitoring after launch. In my own work shipping AI at big tech and startups, rigorous evaluation has always been a gateway to launch. Meticulous and thorough testing is a part of how you build something that works sustainably across all edge cases.

The second point is where we differ: "We don't need any new laws. We don't need new regulations." His view is that market forces already handle this.
A handful of companies now control the frontier models, the compute, and much of the distribution. This concentration of power is THE case for well-designed regulation. Markets are good at pricing what buyers can see and poor at pricing harms that fall on people outside the transaction, which at this scale, these "externalities" reach the entire economy.

The regulation I'd like to see rests on three principles:
1) Rules scaled at the impact layer, so smaller/emerging AI companies can still innovate, giving customers more choices in models, harnesses, and the application layer that best suit their needs. 
2) Clear liability for harm caused, so the cost of risk sits with the builder.
3) A diverse set of stakeholders at the table: researchers, civil society, smaller builders, and the public, alongside the largest labs.

Good engineering + research and good governance reinforce each other, it’s not an either or.

I walked in not fully knowing what to expect, I left full of ideas, new connections and honestly, a little bit of FOMO for next year already.

First and foremost, a huge thank you to the customers and partners who took the time to be there. Your energy, honesty and stories made the week what it was, and none of this means much without you in the room.

A few highlights that stuck with me:

 🎤 Dreamforce Main Keynote: how powerful it was watching the vision for the "Agentic Enterprise" come to life on stage with Anthropic's Dario Amodei and NVIDIA's Jensen Huang. Takeaway: the interface is becoming the conversation. Instead of clicking through a dashboard, you just tell the system what you need and it acts.

👩‍💻 Marketing Keynote: from headless marketing to agents that manage your budget and your data quality and content for you. 
Takeaway: marketing is shifting from "build the campaign" to "supervise the agents running it."

🌍 Booking.com session on Data 360 Headless: how impactful hearing directly from Nina Timmer on how they're unifying data across every surface to actually act on it. 
Takeaway: trust in AI scales only as fast as the data governance underneath it.

🔆 A Conversation with Reese Witherspoon: an unexpected favorite. 
Takeaway: even in an AI-first world, the best pitches are still just good stories, well told.

💕 SWN Fearless Forward: Power Breakfast where I got inspired by role models like our COFO Robin Washington, CRO Alexa Vignone, CPO Nathalie Scardino and CEO South Asia Arundhati Bhattacharya on ambition, perspectives, allyship and representation. Just WOW! 

But frankly, some of the best moments of the week weren't on any agenda. Grabbing coffee or a meal and hearing real, unfiltered stories about what's working (and what isn't) on the ground was worth as much as any session.

author_headline: KanaliA.io
summary: Sergio Zuñiga of KanaliA.io reflects on Dreamforce, proposing companies map a frequent customer query end-to-end to reduce repeated data requests using agentic AI.
post_text:
¿Cuántas veces le pedimos al cliente información que la empresa ya tiene?

El número de pedido que recibió por correo.
Los detalles del problema que explicó por WhatsApp.
La factura que está en otro sistema.
El contexto que se perdió cuando lo cambiaron de área.

Vuelvo de Dreamforce pensando en esa fricción y en cómo usar la capa agentica para reducirla.

Tomemos una consulta simple: “¿Dónde está mi pedido?”

Para resolverla, hay que identificar al cliente, consultar el estado actualizado, entender si existe un retraso y determinar qué acción corresponde. Si hace falta escalar, alguien debe recibir el caso completo y hacerse responsable.

Cada paso obliga a aterrizar una conversación que a veces dejamos demasiado suelta:

→ “Tenemos los datos”. ¿Están actualizados y disponibles cuando se necesitan?

→ “Tenemos el proceso”. ¿Está claro qué hacer cuando el pedido aparece como entregado y el cliente dice que nunca llegó?

→ “Tenemos una integración”. ¿Permite ejecutar la acción necesaria o solamente consultar información?

→ “Tenemos atención humana”. ¿El asesor recibe el contexto o empieza desde cero?

Mi propuesta para llevar esto a nuestros clientes: elegir una consulta frecuente y recorrerla de principio a fin. Contar cuántas veces el cliente repite información, cuántos sistemas consulta el equipo y cuántos cambios de responsable ocurren antes de resolverla.

Ese recorrido nos daría prioridades concretas para un piloto y una base contra la cual medirlo.

Por eso me gustan los workshops y los hands-on training. Me gusta remangarme, probar y entender qué hace falta para que una idea funcione en la operación.

El resultado que me gustaría perseguir después de Dreamforce es muy concreto: que resolver algo con una empresa le cueste menos esfuerzo al cliente.

¿Qué información siguen pidiendo a sus clientes que ya existe dentro de la organización?

summary: Kyle Brierley argues Salesforce's Dreamforce news lets customers work in Claude or Slack while Salesforce stays the control plane, criticizing overlapping branding like AIforce, Agentforce, Coworker, Koa.
post_text:
I've been trying to make sense of all the Dreamforce announcements, figured I'd chime in with some warm (not quite hot) takes. 

Salesforce is basically telling customers: you might not need to open Salesforce anymore.
Start working in Claude, Slack, or another interface, while Salesforce stays underneath with the customer data, permissions, business logic, and actions.

That's kind of a wild thing for a software company to admit, but it's also a smart platform move. If someone else is going to own the screen or the UI, make sure your platform is still the control plane every agent has to call.

But the naming and branding of this stuff is getting a little ridiculous. AIforce, Agentforce, Claudeforce, Slackforce, Coworker, Koa... They're not all the same thing technically, but I'm not sure the average user could tell you where one ends and the next begins. Also, every non-AI company has their own 'human named agent' now which is just wrapping another named agent (claude, codex, etc.). It's a lot. 

Once a lot of products run on the same small group of foundation models, the details matter more: what job the agent owns, what context it gets, when it needs permission, how it explains an action, and whether someone can undo it.

I'm all for a good mascot (shout out #muse). But at this point I'd rather see the demo where the agent gets something wrong, explains what happened, and lets me undo it.

Source: https://lnkd.in/gmDXxQz6

author_headline: EVP + Chief Experience Officer at Salesforce
summary: Rachel Kobetz, Salesforce's Chief Experience Officer, recaps her first Dreamforce, citing her 'New Mandate' talk, Camp Design, and the True to the Core panel.
post_text:
My first Dreamforce is in the books. And I get it now.

There is an energy here that is hard to understand from the outside. Customers, builders, partners, employees, and Trailblazers packed into a few blocks of San Francisco, talking about what’s possible, what isn’t working yet, and what needs to come next.

It was a pretty incredible way to mark my seventh week at Salesforce.

I had the chance to share The New Mandate: Designing for the Agentic Era, join the Salesforce+ broadcast, spend time with customers and partners, visit Camp Design, our XD home base for the week, and close Dreamforce on the True to the Core panel.

That was a fitting way to end the week: customers and Trailblazers asking direct questions, in public, about what matters most, and leaders answering for what we’ve built, where it needs to improve, and where we’re headed.

That kind of candor matters. Listen closely enough, and it should change the work.

The agentic era is opening an enormous new design space.
How can work begin before the prompt?
How does work change when people and agents collaborate as one team?
How does work move across products and surfaces without making the customer carry the seams?
How far can we expand agency while keeping people firmly in command?

One idea came into sharper focus for me this week: the more agency we give software, the more legible its context, authority, and consequences have to become.

That raises the bar for the entire experience. Systems need to understand the work, carry context across surfaces, make action and uncertainty visible, and preserve the ability to intervene and recover.

Salesforce has a rare combination of strengths for that future: deep customer relationships, trusted enterprise data and workflows, platform depth, Slack as the front door to the Agentic Enterprise, and a community willing to tell us exactly where the seams are.

The work ahead is to turn those strengths into one coherent Salesforce experience that feels intuitive, trusted, and as ambitious as the platform beneath it. That is exactly the kind of challenge I came here to take on.

Thank you to everyone who challenged an idea, shared what isn’t working, told me what you want Salesforce to become, came to the talk, watched an interview, pulled me into a conversation, or simply said hello.

And especially to XD: I saw just how much talent, care, craft, and coordination it takes to make a week like this happen.

Now, back to building.

And none of it happens without the people who show up and do the work. To the entire Conga #marketing team — what you pulled together for this event was exceptional. And to Karina Estrada, Conga's Global Partner Marketing leader — you showed up at Dreamforce the way you show up every single day: with energy, precision, and genuine partnership. Working alongside you is one of the highlights of building this ecosystem. Thank you. 

Cheers to a weekend to recover!

More posts to come from the week ahead.

summary: Omar Qureshi details Accenture's Agentic SDLC showcase at SPIN, demonstrating three scenarios with Cursor/SpaceXAI covering UI change, design change and incident remediation.
post_text:
Heading home from Dreamforce, where we ran our Agentic SDLC for Salesforce showcase at Accenture’s SPIN experience space.

The opportunity is to shorten the path from business need to working software, absorb change without restarting delivery and resolve incidents more efficiently.

We demonstrated this through three scenarios: a recorded business discussion becoming a governed Salesforce UI change; a React experience on Experience Cloud absorbing a mid-cycle design change; and an AMS incident being investigated and remediated, with an engineer approving the pull request before deployment.

Different scenarios, but the same outcome: greater pace and capacity, with human decisions visible throughout. People continue to own the business, architecture, quality and release decisions.

Model capability is less of a constraint than it was. The challenge is applying it effectively across a live programme. That requires a harness of skills, rules, delivery standards and quality gates, supported by a Digital Brain grounded in business context, org metadata and proven delivery practices.

Much of today’s agentic tooling focuses on the build step. Our approach extends from the initial business need through architecture, build, test, release and support.

It was brilliant to have the Cursor team, now part of SpaceXAI, on the floor with us. Our partnership with Cursor, alongside our work with Salesforce, is helping us bring this approach to our clients.

Huge thanks to Navita Sharma, Abhishek Sharma  and Sammy Basha for their support, and Cameron Cronin for leading us through it. Thank you to our ATCI innovation team for the weeks of build and rehearsal behind the scenes, and to Mitesh Mistry and the wider team.

Thank you to Justin Santilli, Charles Addai-Appiah, Ryan Anderson, Jordan Stein and the SpaceX team for their massive support. Thanks also to the Accenture events team, and to the account and Market Unit teams who brought their clients along.

summary: BTG Pactual's Felipe Tolipan Sidsamer describes a 150-executive Latin America Day 0 in Berkeley and Marc Benioff's Claude Force conversation with Anthropic's Dario Amodei on AI ROI.
post_text:
Estou muito feliz por ter participado do Dreamforce 2026, uma experiência marcante, com quatro dias intensos de imersão em São Francisco.
O primeiro deles foi um convite especial: o "Day 0", um encontro exclusivo em Berkeley reunindo apenas 150 executivos de toda a América Latina, uma oportunidade rara de troca antes mesmo do evento principal começar.
Dali em diante, três dias de conversas relevantes e a chance de trocar ideias com outros líderes de negócio sobre para onde a IA está levando as empresas.
Um dos momentos mais interessantes foi a conversa entre o Marc Benioff (CEO da Salesforce) e o Dario Amodei (CEO da Anthropic) com o lançamento do Claude Force, parceria da Anthropic com a Salesforce. Dario comentou que, mesmo se a evolução da IA parasse hoje, ainda teríamos anos de ganhos pela frente, já que usamos uma fração pequena do potencial atual da tecnologia (e ele brincou que não pretende parar). Marc fez um paralelo com omundo corporativo: a maioria das empresas ainda não conseguiu transformar o uso daIA em ROI concreto, e é por isso que a Salesforce está investindo em facilitar essa implementação.
Esse é justamente o ponto que mais me chamou atenção. Adicionar IA a um processo só faz sentido se gerar retorno real, e poucos players ainda conseguiram fazer essa transição de forma consistente. O mercado ainda está aprendendo — inclusive entendendo como os clientes vão reagir a esse novo modelo de relacionamento. Mas a oportunidade já está clara: ganhar eficiência para o assessor de investimentos, liberando tempo para o que realmente importa, o relacionamento com o cliente. E é esse ganho que o cliente precisa sentir na prática.
Saio do evento com a convicção de que 2027 será um ano de avanços concretos para a assessoria de investimentos — tanto para clientes quanto para assessores —, sempre com o mesmo objetivo final: fortalecer o relacionamento com o cliente.

 ⭐ Leaders guide the story; individuals write it. AI is accelerating career-defining "sliding door" moments daily—they're happening all around us.  ⭐ The "my dance space" mentality is officially over. AI and new ways of working cracked something open this year—a real appetite for collaboration over territory. Slack was our sherpa for that all week. One of my favorite moments was following our global field marketing team's live thread, filled with real-time photos, event updates, and customer wins celebrated with a flood of emojis. Kaitlyn Kopetski rocked it! That same spirit of gratitude carried everywhere, including our Platform Customer Golf Appreciation Event, where strategic conversations between security sales leaders John Beck, Ryan Patten, Brian Larimer, Chris F., Jen Courtney & Mark Church kept dissolving into genuine laughter and mutual appreciation. As security moves from a checkbox to the center of every AI conversation, their role is shifting from sellers to trusted advisors, a change that showed up on the course and in every room.

 ⭐  Security is the bedrock, not the afterthought, of the agentic enterprise. Dreamforce showed vision and execution moving in lockstep. On the main stage, Sam Altman drove home why AI safety and alignment can't be an afterthought. In parallel, our Security Keynote, brought to life by Gagan Gulati, Marla Hay, Pete Thurston and Iain Mulholland gave the practical blueprint: enterprise security has to outpace raw model capability. Enterprises now face a dual mandate: secure the AI itself (the data, models, and agents) while also defending against AI-driven threats in real time. Salesforce is setting the standard so every enterprise can step into this frontier with real, ironclad trust.

To my global field marketing team: Sarah Jecmen, Katie Parrotta, Brooke Newman, Kris Carter, Jaina Katechia, Jennifer Smith & Jo Birtle celebrate this feeling of accomplishment. author_headline: Regional Sales Director @ Salesforce | Helping companies grow through world-leading technology
summary: Salesforce's Mark Boesen notes 1,600 sessions, Salesforce going "headless" across Claude/Slack/CRM, Dario Amodei's Anthropic keynote, and seeing Tony Robbins speak live.
post_text:
An unforgettable Dreamforce is drawing to a close, and I'm leaving genuinely blown away by the energy, ambition, and drive that we've seen across 1,600 sessions (!) over the past few days. I cannot thank our customers enough for making the trip across the pond to spend a crazy few days with us in the name of AI & Innovation. 

As I reflect on the innovation shown and the discussions we've had, a few key themes stand out. 

1) You no longer need to log in to your CRM to run your sales business
Salesforce has gone headless. You can now work in the interface of your choice - whether that's Claude, Slack, or directly in CRM. This is a massive deal. Less admin time for sales reps to spend time on what they (we) love most: talking to customers.

2) SaaSpocalypse? Not so fast. 
We're not at the end of software. But we may well be at the end of software that makes humans do all the work. Having Dario Amodei from Anthropic on the keynote was a special highlight, and hearing how Anthropic uses Salesforce as a core pillar of their own GTM was a fascinating and full-circle moment.

3) Danish companies are ready to innovate and we have the talent to do it. Throughout this week I've had the privilege of meeting exceptional people from Danish companies and our partner ecosystem. Our eagerness to innovate thoughtfully and responsibly genuinely stands out. A key question we kept returning to: what truly separates the companies creating real value from AI from those that don't - and where do you start? I look much forward to continuing those discussions on home turf starting Monday morning. 

On a personal note I fulfilled a life-long dream of seeing Tony Robbins live. That was a special few hours. It has truly been a remarkable week and I'm going home energized for what's ahead. 

An extraordinary thank you to everyone who joined us and made Dreamforce what it is. See you next year 🤩

author_headline: AI Delivery Lead, Director | Technology | Transformation | Salesforce
summary: Salesforce's Cynthia Tam describes serving as sighted escort for Kristy Schenderlein and Michael Hess of Blind Institute of Technology, and attending a neurodiversity accessibility session with Kurt Iobst.
post_text:
Celebrities, Trailblazers, and Puppies!

I was fortunate to attend my first #Dreamforce as a new hire. While it was highlighted by Jammin' up close with Ziggy Marley, the real stardom was serving as a sighted escort for Kristy Schenderlein, alongside Michael Hess, #goldenhoodie winner and Founder of Blind Institute of Technology (BIT). I lost count of how many people approached asking for a picture with Mike, and hearing their personal stories was inspiring. Attending sessions like “Neurodiversity, Accessibility, and the Access Issues AI Fixes” gave me a fresh perspective as an AI Delivery Lead at Salesforce. I appreciated how Dreamforce gave Kurt Iobst, CPACC a platform to present Neuroforce, Salesforce’s employee resource group (#ERG) for neurodiversity, and how Luis Salazar's deep dive into his personal experience offered a real-world example on executive function (EF) .

What started as a 3-hour shift with my fellow sighted escort Bruce Behrens turned into our enthusiastic request to accessibility coordinator J. Stan Hjartberg to stay on for the full 9-hour day.  It concluded with Kristy and Mike taking the stage to discuss BIT’s success in supporting professionals with disabilities, building an untapped talent pool of Salesforce Admins. BIT’s structured Apprenticeship Program, paired with Salesforce’s genuine partnership, is what real support looks like, reflected in the full panel of speakers from both sides: Lucia Rios, Colin Chinery, Luis Salazar, and Valerie Brown from Salesforce, and Kristy Schenderlein, Michael Hess, and Andrew Johnson from BIT. I love that this isn’t about filling jobs; it’s about accelerating careers with real growth potential. My own career was kickstarted by structured support through my university’s career center and its industry relationships, and I’m proud to work at a company that extends that same support to everyone in our Ohana.

Walking among thousands of attendees at large events can feel intimidating so I appreciate how my team made me feel welcomed, like at the keynote with Alberto Valcarlos, Mark Slaney, Shane Sigler (left to right). A special thank you to our Salesforce Database (#SDB) Social Coordinator Christopher Drexelius for creating a sense of belonging as I joined y’all at Dreamfest (left to right: Aditya Kamble, Sanoop Nambiar, Christopher Drexelius, Vaibhav Arora, Dimpy Chhabra, Parul Lakhotia, and Aneesh Raman (not pictured) — plus a few good-natured folks who got caught in our fun photo op). The puppy breaks were delightful moments of calm and rounded out my Dreamforce experience perfectly.
